articles.title: The ex-Secret Service agent who flipped a hacker is now raising a second $250M cybersecurity fund
articles.body:
Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO.
Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners, a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says.
Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out. Another is the size of his firm’s debut fund late last year: a whopping $250 million fund, which he closed with co-founder Gur Talpaz. A third reason is his résumé, which includes a stint with the Coast Guard, nine years in the Secret Service, and CISO jobs at TIAA and Home Depot before he ever thought about investing.
One proof point that suggests the combination is working is SGNL, the identity security startup CrowdStrike agreed in January to buy for $740 million, 11 months after Brightmind led its Series A.
Now Ward is raising a second fund, targeting roughly the same size as the first one. This time, though, he’ll be doing it without Talpaz, who left in April along with another early colleague, leaving Ward as the firm’s sole general partner. He’s betting on himself at a moment when early-stage cybersecurity startups are raising more money than later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade.
His unemotional approach to exits traces back to an unlikely career. Ward says he grew up in northwest New Jersey between two farms, in a family that couldn’t afford college for his older brothers. After high school, he joined the Coast Guard, inspired by a commercial of a man jumping out of a helicopter, though he says he barely knew how to swim at the time. He spent four years in search and rescue.
Afterward, he studied criminal justice at Seton Hall in New Jersey and thought half-heartedly about law school. “I didn’t know what I wanted to do,” Ward told me last week over Zoom, wearing a pale hooded sweatshirt and looking more like a basketball coach than a venture capitalist. “I was kind of lost. I missed the military and the camaraderie and all of that.”
After graduating in 1998, he says, he mailed out some 300 résumés but no one responded. A Seton Hall professor who was also a chaplain to Secret Service personnel, as well as to members of the FBI and CIA, began introducing him around, and the Secret Service called first.
The Secret Service has two primary missions: protecting people and investigating financial crimes. Ward gravitated to investigations, then to “cyber” after the September 11 attacks in 2001. That year, he married a former college classmate, an American-born Syrian Muslim. Colleagues warned him the background check would be “miserable.” (They’re still happily married.)
What came next took Ward’s life down an unexpected path. Stationed in New York, he arrested a hacker who’d pulled off the largest credit card data theft of that era. Instead of charging him, however, Ward flipped him, turning him into an informant and running him for about three years. But the hacker kept hacking behind Ward’s back, and after he was caught again, he told the agency, as a diversionary tactic, that Ward was in on it.
By that time, Ward had left for the private sector, and he ultimately spent roughly 18 months clearing his name. “It was hard to get out of bed,” he said of that period, describing the investigation as “almost like a spouse cheating on you,” given his love of the agency. The hacker ultimately received a 20-year sentence, and Audible bought the rights to the story, turning it into an eight-episode podcast called “Operation Firewall.”
Ward’s corporate career has been a success by most measures, though he describes it as a series of jumps he really wasn’t qualified to make. His first private-sector job at J.P. Morgan, where he was recruited in 2007 to build a cybersecurity unit, was the hardest transition of his career, he says. He felt like “the dumbest person in the room,” missed his Secret Service crew, and twice thought about going back, unaware he was still under investigation. He stuck it out and now calls the investment bank the “best management school.”
Six years as CISO at the financial services company TIAA followed, and then two years at Home Depot starting in 2019. But in 2021, feeling burned out, he quit without anything lined up for the first time since age 16.
That chapter didn’t last long. The founders of Wiz, whose security software Ward had used at Home Depot, put him on a short list for a job at their company. Jeff Horing, a venture capitalist at Insight Partners, which had co-led Wiz’s $100 million Series A round in late 2020, interviewed Ward for the role, then offered him one at Insight instead.
It’s a good-news, bad-news story, given that Wiz was acquired last year by Google for $32 billion. When I asked him about it last week, Ward observed that the friend who took the Wiz job “made life-changing money,” but said it doesn’t bother him.
Regardless, he spent just three years at Insight, where he says he worked on Wiz, Abnormal Security, and Elisity, which IonQ agreed in October to buy for up to $1.3 billion. Then, at age 49, he thought about striking out on his own for the first time.
He says people told him it was a young man’s game. He left anyway and began cold-emailing limited partners. Ultimately, fewer than 20 LPs filled the fund, including Horing.
Ward started Brightmind in 2024 with Talpaz, a CrowdStrike corporate development executive whose deals overlapped with Ward’s during his time at Insight. Tayler Sipperly, another CrowdStrike corporate development alum, was the firm’s third employee.
The partnership ended this past spring. Asked what happened, Ward, using carefully worded legalese, cited “differences in opinions regarding operations and the future of Brightmind.” In August, Talpaz and Sipperly co-founded a new venture firm with Elia Zaitsev, CrowdStrike’s global CTO for the past three years. Called Cognition, it’s now reportedly targeting a $170 million first fund to back cybersecurity startups.
Brightmind’s first fund has made 14 investments to date, with one exit: that SNGL sale.
Some investors asked why Brightmind didn’t ride out that bet even longer. But Ward says he’s seen enough across his career that he feels confident in warning founders when they’re “going to race past the turn.”
In cybersecurity, he says, the best sales come between a startup’s third and seventh years. Indeed, he says his team tracks every security acquisition and what buyers are building versus buying. If Palo Alto Networks is likely to buy something, he says, CrowdStrike will experience “FOMO, then Zscaler is going to look over and go, ‘What did they just do? I should probably do the same thing.’”
Understanding how the pieces fit together is the trick, Ward explained, offering some hypotheticals. If CrowdStrike is building a product, he said, it’s unlikely to buy a portfolio company that makes something similar. Palo Alto Networks might love a company, but not if buying it would force its customers to switch away from something it bought five years ago.
“It’s very easy to go, ‘Good match,’ ‘terrible match,’” he said. “And that’s really what we spend a ton of time figuring out.”
He has timing on his side, at least. Early-stage cybersecurity startups are outraising their later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade, according to PitchBook, which counts $4.7 billion worth of seed-through-Series B deals through September.
That total is already ahead of the entirety of 2025, even though the number of deals fell to 248 from 358 last year. Seed rounds in particular are ballooning, per PitchBook. The average cybersecurity seed round jumped to $8.4 million in the first nine months of this year, from $5.54 million a year earlier.
Ward questions how much of that money is really going to AI security. By PitchBook’s count, 278 deals in the first half of 2026 were bucketed as such, but his team’s manual review found only 30 true ones. He doesn’t think Anthropic or OpenAI will “take over the security world,” but instead will do “just enough.”
For real-time protection, which he terms “zero second,” he favors cyber-specific models that run locally on a customer’s own systems, like that of Empirical Security. He also looks for startups that could trounce established companies that he considers vulnerable, name-checking 27-year-old Qualys and 24-year-old Tenable.
Ward says Brightmind’s second fund won’t be entirely cybersecurity, focusing about 20% on AI infrastructure deals. He expects a meaningful number of teams to come from Israel, too. (Roughly 40% of the debut fund’s startups are based in Tel Aviv.)
Asked about the founders he’s most comfortable backing, the response is immediate: second-time founders who stick together.
Brightmind is comprised of five people right now: COO Iva Messy, also a Seton Hall graduate, came from venture firms Felicis and Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) on the recommendation of Ward’s cousin, Carl Eschenbach, a former Workday CEO who is now back at Sequoia. Sven Wollschlaeger, a Midwesterner whom Ward calls one of the hardest-working people he’s known, spent three years alongside Ward at Insight and is a principal at Brightmind.
CTO Jamie Mneimneh, whom Ward first hired at Home Depot as a distinguished engineer, is the most technical person of the team. He built the cloud computing environment on AWS where the firm tests startups’ products. Mneimneh also built the AI agents that now source most of Brightmind’s deal flow, which is how the firm avoids hiring a bench of analysts and keeps management fees down, says Ward.
Taylor Cleveland, Ward’s chief of staff at Home Depot, joined the firm a few months ago.
For all the career changes, Ward says the real force driving him hasn’t changed. He grew up without money and still worries it could happen again, saying he’s being paid to produce a “3x net fund,” and he’s “not going to celebrate until we get that.”
Said Ward: “I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I have a level of being very naive to like, not being qualified to do something. I’ve just always looked at people and been like, ‘Okay, you know more than me today, but tomorrow, it’s going to be a little less, and the day after that, it’s going to be less, and eventually, I’m going to catch you and surpass you, and I’m going to know more than you.’ That’s how competitive I am.”

articles.title: US government warns of ‘ongoing cyber threat’ amid mass hacks of industrial retail and military freezers
articles.body:
The U.S. government is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” facing industrial refrigeration units, after reports of cyberattacks targeting freezers and fridges in supermarkets around the world, U.S. military bases, and at least one blood bank.
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and several other federal government departments warned in a joint statement on Thursday that hackers are targeting and compromising internet-connected refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries.
“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn.
The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers.
Hackers also targeted a blood bank in France, causing its refrigerated units to boost temperatures in its cold units containing donated blood supplies — but were stopped before the attack could compromise blood stores. The U.S. Department of Defense is investigating a spate of hacks targeting freezers run by the military, according to Reuters. The hacks were first reported by Signal and Silence.
The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit.
CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor.
In a separate fact sheet, the departments said that hackers may attempt to “force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”
“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said CISA’s acting cybersecurity chief Chris Butera.

articles.title: Hugging Face's CEO Says His P(Doom) Is 'Close to Zero'
articles.body:
Future AI risks are most likely to come from big companies building in secret while open models play defense, Clément Delangue, CEO of Hugging Face, said Wednesday at the WIRED World Fair in Miami.
“Most of the risk is actually created by a couple of players building behind closed doors,” Delangue said. “Most of the mitigation of this risk will be the full ecosystem, meaning everyone being able to build in the open.”
Hugging Face is one of the first companies to be attacked by a rogue AI. This July, agents being tested by OpenAI broke free of their sandbox and chose to attack the startup in search of answers to problems they had been set to solve. The company used an open-weight Chinese model called GLM-5.2 to investigate and counter the onslaught.
Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too.
Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.”
In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said.
Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems.
Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users.
Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks, a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI.
Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future.
“We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.”
Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

articles.title: ‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
articles.body:
On Tuesday night, Democrats made history as they took control of the House and the Senate, and a blue wave swept through traditionally red and swing states — with the nation’s first Black woman governor elected in Georgia, the country’s first Native American woman governor elected in New Mexico, and a Maine Senator ceding to a Democrat after 30 years in office. In these and other campaigns, one theme kept coming up: holding AI companies accountable to the American people. Now, the AI industry is left considering the prospect of regulation, data center construction slowdowns, and more.
‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
AI companies have a new threat: a wave of Democrats who campaigned against them.
‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
AI companies have a new threat: a wave of Democrats who campaigned against them.
Publicly, most major AI company CEOs have remained silent. OpenAI and Anthropic did not provide comments to The Verge; Elon Musk’s call on X to vote “red” for the midterms — the SpaceX CEO had spent close to $450 million backing Republican campaigns for the election — vanished after results poured in.
Privately, CEOs have discussed significant compute capacity constraints for their companies after Tuesday’s results, particularly OpenAI, per The Wall Street Journal. Meta’s platforms president, Dina Powell McCormick, says many are considering moving data center construction abroad. AI executives are reportedly privately nervous about the results but may also be able to blame them for not delivering as much revenue to investors. Many of the incoming leaders have promised to drag CEOs to testify. On X, a popular post by former X product lead Nikita Bier warned that “This is going to be like the Nuremberg Trials but for AI researchers.” (On Tuesday night, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman did post about how “people should always be in control of the future,” but he spent other parts of the evening talking about RAM.)
Tuesday’s results were a “total repudiation” of the AI field, says Wes McEnany, the former Deputy Labor Policy Director of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, & Pensions, who now works with the nonprofit Future of Life Institute. He said that AI touches “every aspect of people’s lives,” whether they’re applying for jobs, using social media, or even paying electricity bills while living near a data center, and that they’re tired of not having “any agency in that conversation.”
The bipartisan backlash against data center construction is the most tangible manifestation of that backlash. It’s going to be unquestionably more difficult to build them across the country, after 43 out of 44 local data center moratoria on Tuesday’s ballots passed, sending a clear message to AI companies. In Texas, the fastest-growing data center buildout area and a key battleground state, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she plans to “issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans.” Similar promises have been made in a handful of other key states.
“Data centers were clearly on the ballot,” said Guru Sethupathy, GM of AI governance at Optro.
In recent months, there’s been an increasing number of protests and collective bipartisan action to battle data centers being built in a wide range of states. Residents are concerned about noise pollution, electricity bill rate hikes, and more. When NBC News polled voters on Tuesday, 76 percent opposed data centers in their communities.
“The data center backlash is one of the most bipartisan political issues I’ve ever seen,” Shaunna Thomas, co-founder and director of the Guardrails Alliance, a Super PAC pushing for AI regulation.
“Data centers are an entry point to looking at this broader corporate accountability lens of, ‘My bill is going up, why?’” said Kyle Jacobs-Morse, deputy executive director at The Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit tech industry watchdog. “People found that it was big tech companies that were the culprit.” He added that particularly in the gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, Democratic campaigns prioritized potential local issues stemming from data centers, including “spillover costs” for local residents, communities, and state governments.
“I do think we’ll hear more questions about who benefits from and who pays for AI, especially as it pertains to infrastructure, but what I’m more curious about is what changes we can expect around regulation,” said François Ajenstat, CEO and founder of Golden Analytics.
Experts say the midterm results have likely ended Trump and congressional Republicans’ repeated attempts to bar state-level AI restrictions. Thomas considers the idea “completely dead,” while McEnany said “any member who votes to wipe out state AI laws is going to be looking for a job in the next [election].” Jacobs-Morse expects to generally see more “tech accountability bills.”
OpenAI recently began calling its data centers “compute campuses,” and President Trump in September attempted to change the name of AI as a technology to “super intelligence.” But midterm results suggest that a significant portion of American voters aren’t buying the rebranding efforts.
“I don’t think it was working, and I think the prospect of it working is extremely low after the election,” Thomas said.
“The Trump idiosyncrasies around some of this stuff… they did not play well at the ballot box,” Jacobs-Morse said.
But some in and around the tech industry are taking the news more positively than others. One X user wrote that “we’re *maybe* back to being a rational, steady hand as a country and can really lead,” while others wrote that the recent results could be good for preventing an AI bubble burst. Katie Barr, CEO of Glen Echo Group and a partner at Orchestra, said she wouldn’t “over-read” the results as an overwhelming tech rejection but rather a reckoning on “affordability, jobs, safety, and whether people have a say in what’s happening in their communities and their lives.”
Analysts at Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note that though tech investors should prepare for “major hurdles for AI and tech legislation” and a slowdown of the planned construction of up to 1,000 data centers across the country, there could be a “slight positive” in that it could help avoid a bubble and slow capital fundraising flooding the market.
There will also likely be a reckoning on AI safety. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) was reelected after campaigning for AI safety policy, and in a victory speech Tuesday by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ossoff said, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.” Some AI safety legislation is already being considered, like the bill to “ban superintelligence” introduced in September by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas).
President Trump has dismissed the idea of a safety crisis in AI as a “hoax,” writing on social media that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” After the midterms, however, Republican lawmakers will need to decide whether to fall in line or negotiate with Democrats on safety-focused policy measures. Either way, Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of Chamber of Progress, a pro-tech industry advocacy group, said he expects AI safety legislation to continue to happen in blue states.
“There’s a lot of open questions about where democrats go next on tech policy. Do we revert to the Biden era war on tech, the Obama era tech honeymoon, or something in between?” Kovacevich said.

articles.title: The Poison and the Cure the Life and Afterlife of French Theory
articles.body:
The Poison and the Cure
The Life and Afterlife of French Theory
The Frenchmen: Or, My Life in Theory by Emily Eakin
School of the South: The Colonial Roots of French Theory by Onur Erdur
In 2005, Alain Badiou argued that in the second half of the 20th century, there was a “French philosophical moment” comparable to the peaks of classical Greece and Enlightenment Germany. Badiou was not an impartial observer—he described himself as perhaps the era’s “last representative”—yet no one would seriously dispute that les trente glorieuses produced a blaze of intellectual activity that radiated around the world, transforming not only academic study but the wider cultural atmosphere. There, however, consensus stops.
Was this “moment” purely, or even primarily, a philosophical one? It was born with an anthropologist, Claude Lévi-Strauss, borrowing a framework from linguistics, and among the central aims of the resulting method, “structuralism,” was to topple a philosophical movement: the existentialism of Jean-Paul Sartre and others. And while many of the leading thinkers who embraced structuralism were educated, like Lévi-Strauss, in philosophy, they also worked in other areas of the humanities and social sciences. Roland Barthes was concerned with mass culture and canonical literature; Louis Althusser with interpretations of Marx; Jacques Lacan with Freudian psychoanalysis; and Michel Foucault with history, and excavating the logics underpinning a range of institutions and practices—medicine, psychiatry, prisons, sexuality. The writing of Jacques Derrida, meanwhile—for a time “the sexiest philosopher on the planet,” in the words of the literary critic Terry Eagleton—amounted less to a conventional contribution to philosophy than a thoroughgoing critique of its founding assumptions. “I never thought I had something to say philosophically,” Derrida reflected in 1991—and his example was chiefly followed by literary critics.
Such a range of interests and allegiances called for a broader rubric. As Fredric Jameson put it, considering the debate about whether Foucault was a philosopher or a historian, “Well, that is why we have the word ‘theory.’ We don’t have to decide.” The catch-all term helped to smooth over other terminological wrinkles. “Structuralism” was a label its putative exponents tended to reject, or outgrow. Foucault complained in the English edition of The Order of Things (1966), his “archeological inquiry” into the changing conditions of knowledge, that he had been unable to persuade the “tiny minds” of “certain half-witted ‘commentators’” that he had “used none of the methods, concepts or key terms that characterize structural analysis.” Barthes, having been a notably fastidious practitioner of the structuralist mode known as semiotics, developed into a representative of a free-spirited offshoot or usurper, “post-structuralism,” promoting readerly experiences of “plaisir” and “jouissance” (a near-sexual frisson).
“Theory” also encompasses a strikingly elastic pantheon of thinkers, as illustrated by a pair of recently published books. The New York Times editor Emily Eakin, in The Frenchmen, her convivial mixture of memoir and popular history, and the Berlin-based historian Onur Erdur, in his more scholarly and tendentious School of the South, both give space to Foucault, Derrida, and Barthes. Otherwise, their attentions diverge. Eakin, being concerned with “America’s theory craze,” writes about Lévi-Strauss, Althusser, Lacan, Gilles Deleuze, and the Belgian-born literary critic Paul de Man, whereas Erdur, exploring the formative impact of colonial experiences on postwar French thinkers, offers a different supporting cast, including Pierre Bourdieu, Jean-François Lyotard, and Hélène Cixous.
But the greatest divergence, or source of dissent, concerns whether the period constituted a golden age: one of the things that has always distinguished French theory is the extremity of its reception. Having achieved international prominence in the mid-1960s, theory underwent what the historian François Cusset describes as an “anarchic expansion” in the ’70s. Converts found it exhilaratingly radical and innovative, uncovering new techniques and areas of study, but Marxists, such as Jameson and Eagleton, were more skeptical. Others charged it with meretricious obscurity and dismissed its italicized neologisms and occasional quasi-mathematical formulae as a travesty of scientific inquiry. Theory was a favored target of conservative philosophers in polemical mode. Roger Scruton wrote of “a boiling tide of nonsense” that would “eliminate the possibility of rational argument” and “annihilate meaning.” Alan Bloom, in his bestselling broadside The Closing of the American Mind (1987), accused the French theorists of abetting “the suppression of reason and the denial of the possibility of truth.” The rehabilitative slant of Eakin’s and Erdur’s accounts indicates theory’s reputation has not recovered. To this day, Erdur writes, French theorists are accused of being “the intellectual originators of destructive social phenomena such as ‘fake news,’ ‘cancel culture,’ wokeness’ and ‘identity politics,’” suggesting that the record, more than two decades after the first postmortems began to appear, is still in need of straightening.
The origins of French theory are typically traced to Lévi-Strauss’s discovery in 1942 of Course in General Linguistics, a series of lectures delivered by the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure and published by his students in 1916 a few years after his death. Saussure studied language “synchronically”—not as it had evolved over time, or as it manifested in individual speech, but as a hermetic, structured system whose principal unit was the sign, composed of the “signifier” (sound-image) and the “signified” (denoted concept). The connection between these, he argued, was contingent and based in convention. Words do not have intrinsic meaning; sense is relational, an artifact of a word’s position in a system of differences: “cat” being distinct from “bat” and “mat” and so on.
Beginning with his technical tome The Elementary Structures of Kinship (1949),Lévi-Strauss turned this conception of language into a way of interpreting non-linguistic phenomena, such as marriage customs. Structuralism was akin to a kind of Copernican revolution. Language preceded, determined, and all but displaced the “subject”—the autonomous human being, the Cartesian cogito, the political actor, the intending author—in what amounted to a repudiation of Sartre’s stress on the idea of individual freedom. The goal of the human sciences, Lévi-Strauss declared in The Savage Mind (1962), was to “dissolve” Man––or as Althusser suggested in For Marx (1965), reduce the myth of man “to ashes.” Others transposed Saussure’s insights to their own specialisms, notably Barthes who, in a series of newspaper columns collected under the title Mythologies (1957), illustrated that everything from royal cruises to laundry detergent could be decoded as a sign-system.
But the authority of structuralism was soon thrown into question, when in 1966, Derrida, then a relatively unknown 36-year-old, derailed its launch party in the US—a splashy conference backed by the Ford Foundation and held at Johns Hopkins in 1966 to which he had been belatedly invited. His lecture “Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences,” which closed the conference, was a “demolition job,” in Eakin’s words, of the paradigm pioneered by Lévi-Strauss (who was apparently invited but couldn’t make it), later mythologized as the dawn of post-structuralism.
Trained in the predominantly German phenomenological tradition, Derrida was exercised by the notion that Western philosophy was beholden to what he called “a metaphysics of presence.” This involved positing a “privileged Origin that commands, guarantees, and perpetuates meaning,” as Edward Said explained, a telos toward which all thought aspired—truth, Being, reality, essence, substance. By showing that meaning was not pre-given but a shifting emanation of relationships, structuralism had successfully ruptured this illusion. Yet in his Johns Hopkins address, Derrida argued that its elevation of language was in danger of reinstating the first principles it had supposedly diffused into a network of differences.
It was in Baltimore that Derrida first met Paul de Man. Their friendship would become a key axis in theory’s post-structuralist phase—and in its conquest of the American academy. De Man arranged a visiting position for Derrida at Yale, where “deconstruction,” the philosophical mode of close—many would say myopic—reading that Derrida patented took particular hold. The Johns Hopkins paper was an early exhibition of this technique, which sought to show how the logic of a given text is not only underpinned by, but—the key difference from structuralism—undermined by relegating or excluding one term in a series of classic binaries: writing and speech, male and female, center and margin, or in Lévi-Strauss’s case, nature and culture. Taking The Elementary Structures of Kinship as an example, Derrida argued that Lévi-Strauss’s discussion of the incest prohibition undoes the opposition on which his text relies—the taboo, in Lévi-Strauss’s account, being at once norm-based (cultural) and universal (natural). Derrida used one of his notorious neologisms, différance, conjoining the ideas of “difference” and “deferral,” which he later deployed as a lever to wrench apart the binaries in which structuralism was still caught: to convey the idea that meaning was both produced by differences and unstably distributed among them, and could therefore never be firmly located, the relations between words constituting an infinite chain.
To Derrida, structuralism’s “nostalgia for origins” and residual “desire for a center” presented a limit to what he called “play,” and to embrace play would be truly to “pass beyond man.” A similar shift—from hermetic structures to the affirmation of what escapes them—can be seen in Barthes’s evolution in the years after the Johns Hopkins conference, from the technical analysis of The Fashion System (1967) (“nearly unreadable,” in Eakin’s view), via S/Z (1970), his painstaking and exorbitant book-length commentary on a Balzac novella, to the teasing fragments of The Pleasure of the Text (1973), which championed an “erotics” of reading, emphasizing bodily enjoyment over hermeneutic closure.
The mid-60s saw the publication of a volley of landmark books in France—Foucault’s The Order of Things and Lacan’s Écrits; two by Althusser (For Marx and Reading Capital); and three by Derrida, Writing and Difference (which collected the Johns Hopkins lecture), Speech and Phenomena, and Of Grammatology, the last containing commentaries on both Lévi-Strauss and Saussure. The explosive rise of this critique of reason seemed to prefigure the revolutionary unrest of May 1968, which in turn lent the ideas momentum, even though, unlike Sartre, many of the intellectuals associated with theory did not join the students and strikers.
The novelty of Erdur’s School of the South is its suggestion that the decisive political context incubating this mode of thought was not les événements but decolonization, in particular the Algerian War (1958–62), which, Erdur writes, precipitated “the collapse of a certain political and cultural order in French society.” A striking number of French theorists spent time in French North Africa, serving in the army or teaching; several were born there, including Cixous, Jacques Rancière, and Derrida, who grew up in a French-speaking Sephardic family in Algiers.
Erdur’s objective is to show that such experiences shaped their thinking, but the details of his case are unevenly convincing, the connections more robust, or intimate, in some instances than others. Derrida was expelled from his school in Algiers at the age of 12 under the Vichy Jewish quotas and never felt at home in Paris, later describing himself as a “child in the margins of Europe.” It is easy to see how his background sharpened his philosophical sensitivity to what he called the “violent hierarchy” embedded in the binaries of Western thought. But the fact that Foucault taught in Tunisia for a couple of years, or that Barthes vacationed in Morocco and resolved to write an autobiographical novel while in Casablanca, is less persuasive evidence for the “colonial roots of French theory,” as Erdur’s subtitle has it. (Barthes’s “vision of a literary existence” was less a development of his theoretical work, which predated his visits to Morocco, than an expression of dissatisfaction with it.)
Eakin is the more skillful and ambitious storyteller, her 48 punchy chapters weaving intricately back and forth in time, lighting on key friendships and rivalries and critical exchanges—Derrida attacking Foucault’s reading of Rousseau, de Man later challenging Derrida’s. The resulting mosaic enlivens—if also simplifies—what Eakin admits can seem an “intentionally rebarbative” body of thought. Like Erdur, Eakin writes extensively about the theorists’ lives, including their personal lives, aiming to recover what she calls “the hidden human element beneath their often stringent antihumanism”—we learn that Barthes was “prone to a potbelly” and that Lacan was holding a “plate of coleslaw” when he had a run-in with Derrida at Johns Hopkins. Another leavening ingredient is the book’s autobiographical arc, which traces Eakin’s sophomore bewitchment with theory to postgraduate disenchantment, when she abandons her PhD in favor of a career in journalism.
Eakin’s memories of her student days are not exactly rife with dramatic incident—essay crises predominate, reaching a climax with her senior thesis (she fortunately earns “a generous magna cum laude plus,” despite some mixed feedback). But her trajectory is emblematic, a prism through which she surveys the wider story of the Anglosphere’s infatuation with French theory. Though individually notable in their native land, it was in the US, via popularizers such as Jonathan Culler and abettors such as de Man, that theory became a coherent and dominant force within the academy. (In Britain, the philosopher Christopher Norris and the contributors to the film journal Screen alsotook up the cause.) Why did American literature departments prove so hospitable, or susceptible? An affinity must have been suggested by theory’s exaltation of language, congenial to scholars who regarded words as their métier. Theory also promised to lend an aura of rigor to literary study, a congenitally insecure discipline which since its inception in the early 20th century had been scouring for ways of legitimizing itself via approximating scientific discourses, hoping to dismiss charges that it was too intuitive and hedonistic to be a serious subject.
In Cultural Capital: The Problem of Literary Canon Formation (1993), John Guillory argued that the embrace of French theory was the product of a larger crisis. The social value of a literary education was being eroded by the rise of a “professional-managerial class,” which was usurping the old bourgeoisie. Theory appeared to present solutions: the technical fastidiousness of deconstruction mimicked “the technobureaucratic labor” of the ascendant PMC. It not only added a philosophical luster to the measly scrutiny of poems, it licensed the study of any “text,” to use the vogueish term, enlarging the embattled category of literature to colonize other fields, to the degree that literary study could seem not the fusty means to an obsolete sentimental education but the Ur-discipline underlying all the others.
If these were some of the priming circumstances, what were the subjective attractions of this body of work? It provided a political outlet, a subversive enclave as neoliberalism and neoconservatism asserted themselves. “Politics had gone dormant,” Eakin reflects of the late 1980s. “Theory made thinking feel like doing.” It was also glamorously difficult and overtly heterodox, its Nietzschean dash an invigorating contrast to the staid temper of Anglo-Saxon rationality. The “essential” enemies, Barthes wrote in Mythologies, were “bourgeois norms,” and all the theorists were—at different scales and in different domains—leery of or hostile towards the givens of the social world, and of the seemingly natural or self-evident (“what-goes-without-saying,” in Barthes’s formulation). It was a mode of thought that traded in the exposure of hidden forces—from the silent workings of domination through institutions (what Althusser called “ideological state apparatuses”), to the unacknowledged partitions and exclusions that underlie thinking itself, the madness buried in the foundations of reason (the “rifts” disturbing “the deepest strata of Western culture,” as Foucault wrote in The Order of Things).
To identify as a theory-head “marked you as a member of the counterculture, different from—and critical of—the docile horde,” Eakin reflects. Semiotext(e), the small press founded by Columbia professor Sylvère Lotringer, did much to enhance theory’s punkish glow, extending its frontiers beyond elite universities. Its Foreign Agents series, launched in 1983, published English translations in sleek minimal editions—On the Line by Deleuze and Félix Guattari, and Simulations by Jean Baudrillard—which, as the cultural theorist McKenzie Wark noted, helped make theory “the lingua franca of creative workers, avant-garde artists, and downtown bohemians.” Eakin remembers feeling that she was “perched at the frontiers of thought.”
Education systems, Althusser, Bourdieu and Foucault stressed in different ways, are engines for reproducing inequalities and oppressive norms, and theory’s distance from the academic establishment conferred a dissident charge, as did its stylized insouciance toward disciplinary boundaries. In learning to “do” theory, one was not becoming a specialist but undergoing a holistic intellectual training, less acquiring knowledge than transforming one’s relation to it. Theory’s refreshment of perception—a classic aim of avant-garde art—and demystifying methods seemed applicable to virtually every aspect of modern life, including one’s inner life, its implications intimately existential: “What seemed merely an intellectual exercise was actually a way of being,” Eakin reflects.
But what seems to have seduced readers above all was theory’s style—the excitements of the prose itself, some of which resembled a species of experimental literature. Perry Anderson compared Lacan to the poet Mallarmé, Lévi-Strauss to Wagner, Foucault to Artaud and the theologian Bossuet. Introducing the collection Structuralism and Since (1979)—one of many introductory books published in these years—the critic John Sturrock stressed that Lévi-Strauss, Barthes, Foucault, Derrida, and Lacan were “also writers.” Dan Sperber, in the opening essay, is yet more emphatic: “Lévi-Strauss is not simply a scholar; he is also an artist.” The anthropologist’s memoir of his fieldwork in Brazil, Tristes Tropiques (1955), considered a literary masterpiece, concluded with a nearly page-long sentence of rising lyricism, clinched by a humorous swerve, summoning:
“the possibility, vital for life, of unhitching, which consists—Oh! fond farewell to savages and explorations!—in grasping, during the brief intervals in which our species can bring itself to interrupt its hive-like activity, the essence of what it was and continues to be, below the threshold of thought and over and above society: in the contemplation of a mineral more beautiful than all our creations; in the scent that can be smelt at the heart of a lily and is more imbued with learning than all our books; or in the brief glance, heavy with patience, serenity and mutual forgiveness, that, through some involuntary understanding, one can sometimes exchange with a cat.”
Foucault began The Order of Things with a reference to a Borges story and a bravura analysis of Velázquez’s Las Meninas, and concluded it with a sonorous peroration which looked ahead to “some event of which we can at the moment do no more than sense the possibility” that might erase man “like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea.” The closing words of Derrida’s “Structure, Sign, and Play” evoke an impending transformation with similarly heady foreboding: “the as yet unnamable which is proclaiming itself and which can do so, as is necessary whenever a birth is in the offing, only under the species of the nonspecies, in the formless, mute, infant, and terrifying form of monstrosity.”
But Theory’s style was also a source of revulsion. If the idiosyncratic demands of Derrida’s writing—with its coinages, convoluted syntax, and highly self-reflexive patterning—were a thrilling indication of intellectual rigor among his acolytes, they were merely proof of self-indulgence to the uncharmed. Like many of the theorists, unsurprisingly given their hyper-attentiveness to language, he used and made much of wordplay, ingeniously and fruitfully in some cases, but issuing in free-associative binges in others. Glas—his 1974 book that is printed in two columns, one devoted to Hegel, the other to Jean Genet—is a particular offender: “The phallic flower is cuttable-culpable. It is cut [se coupe], castrated, guillotined, decollared, unglued”; “Remain(s)—to (be) know(n)—what causes shitting” etc.
To lay even admiring emphasis on rhetorical skill tends to be double-edged. Jameson introduced Deleuze to his students by remarking, “He is a great writer, and this is a marvelous experience. I don’t care how true or false it is. . . . I would like you to feel the excitement of this stuff, even when you don’t necessarily understand it.” The enthusiastic recommendation entails bracketing the substance. Anderson made a similar point, in a more cautionary tone: “The potential cost of a literary conception of intellectual disciplines is obvious enough: arguments freed from logic, propositions from evidence.” And note the chilly thesis of Hayden White’s essay on Foucault in the Sturrock collection: “The authority of Foucault’s discourse derives primarily from its style (rather than from its ‘factual evidence’ or rigor of argument).”
A central tenet of deconstruction was that the suspicion of style implicit in these qualifications is rooted in philosophy’s age-old distrust of writing itself. In Derrida’s telling, since Plato, writing has been denigrated as an ambiguous, unreliable derivative of speech; in his reading of the Phaedrus, he lights on the Greek word pharmakon, which he glosses as both cure and poison. Philosophy’s diminishment of writing was a way of managing—by compartmentalizing—the disturbing instabilities of all communication, of language itself. The dry austerity of analytic philosophy could be seen as an expression of this defensive impulse, an effort to deny or overcome its status as writing.
If French theory’s rhetorical qualities dented its philosophical credentials in some quarters, in others, it was this very conjunction that seemed so original and freeing. For Jameson, it was the “possibility of writing philosophy in a wholly new way” (which he traced to the pathbreaking versatility of Sartre) which constituted a “liberation from philosophy, a liberation toward theory”: an écriture that vaults over the guardrails between discourses. Part of what distinguished Barthes, Sturrock noted, was that he “showed that criticism, too, could be written, could offer verbal and conceptual excitements of its own while still engaging with the chores of interpretation” (or while shirking them: “I am offered a text. The text bores me. It might be said to prattle,” Barthes writes in The Pleasure of the Text).
The literary pretensions of these theoretical texts didn’t only ignite their reception, they shaped and arguably distorted it. That the corpus was often filtered through literature departments meant that it was often read out of its original context. Reading Derrida without any firsthand exposure to the philosophical tradition he was attempting to dismantle meant lacking an informed vantage point from which to detect straw man arguments or exaggerated claims to novelty. The result, as the English philosopher Peter Dews noted in his critical study Logics of Disintegration (1987), was “an astonishingly casual and unquestioning acceptance of certainly extremely condensed—not to say sloganistic—characterizations of the history of Western thought, as if this history could be dismissed through its reduction to a set of perfunctory dualisms.” Eakin writes that she blushes at the memory of “my college-age self, earnestly parroting Derrida’s critique of Plato’s Phaedrus . . . despite having only a glancing familiarity with the ancient Greek text.” This was surely part of theory’s attraction for the literature student––it was a springboard to the forbidding world of philosophy, without having to trawl through years of specialized instruction.
However crucial to its appeal, the style of French theory also poses what might be called difficulties of inheritance. The work was often resistant to paraphrase. It is hard to describe deconstruction without recourse to bespoke vocabulary like différance (which Derrida helpfully explained was neither a word nor a concept). As Said noted, the “nearly maniacal complexity” of Derrida’s prose “defies translation and perhaps even description.” That left emulation. John Guillory argues that style was “the actual mechanism of [theory’s] replication,” not least because the “fortunes of theory” were closely linked to the “charismatic persona of the master theorist”—ironic, given the end of the “author” proclaimed by both Foucault and Barthes, as well as the anti-humanist bias and anti-authoritarian impetus of French theory as a whole. The historian Tamara Chaplin, in Turning On the Mind, emphasizes the transformative effect of television on postwar French culture, giving new prominence to the “physical image” of the writer, who was now being sold along with their books. The magnitude of Derrida’s and Foucault’s celebrity is remarkable. The biographical approach of Erdur’s and Eakin’s books is telling in this respect. Framed by both as an attempt to historicize and humanize their protagonists, the interest in their personal lives is also indicative of the fame that can make them seem intellectually untouchable. For Guillory, their prose style—an “imitable effect”—transmitted their charisma, which was key to producing “discipleship.” “I had disappeared into theory,” Eakin recalls, “crudely aping the Frenchmen rather than thinking for myself.” In the introduction to The Years of Theory, Jameson wrote that “Hegel would not have wanted me to theorize the end of this very rich and exciting period with the contingent deaths of its ‘master-thinkers’”—many were dead by 1990, including Foucault, Barthes, and de Man—but this logic seems hard to resist, given their personal magnetism, performing to packed lecture halls and photographed in magazines.
The Frenchmen records two key moments in Eakin’s deconversion: In 1996, she was working at Lingua Franca,the publication that broke the story of a hoax in which the scientist Alan Sokal successfully submitted a jargon-rich parody of theory to the journal Social Text. The final tie was cut with Derrida’s death in 2004, when Eakin, while on maternity leave from her job as an “ideas” reporter at the New York Times, greenlit a caricatural obituary, prompting an outraged letter signed by thousands of scholars. It is as though Eakin needed to betray theory in order to expel it and recover from her delirium—“a multiyear breakdown I hadn’t realized I was having,” one by which “the entire culture had been touched.” Eakin’s volte-face mirrors the wider cultural retaliation, emboldened by the discrediting of several star theorists. Althusser strangled his wife to death in 1980; in 1987 came the revelation of Paul de Man’s wartime journalism for Nazi-controlled Belgian newspapers, providing a symbolic denouement in The Frenchmen.
By this time, post-structuralism had been damaged by the culture wars, in which it was blamed for giving rise to identity politics and besieging the Western canon, or, in the more extreme neocon counterattacks, charged with a relativism and nihilism that threatened civilization. French theory also drew criticism from the left, which saw it as abetting the “culturalization” of politics and its splintering into micro-interest groups, occluding shared conditions of exploitation. The “synchronic” bent of Saussurean linguistics had likewise, critics charged, led to a neglect of historical processes. Deconstruction’s fixation on details of texts such as a single pair of words, meanwhile, could be seen as extractive, its methodical subversion of cherry-picked oppositions amounting to an all-purpose, unassailable maneuver that silkily placed itself beyond critique.
However intellectually galvanizing, the critique of reason and overthrow of the subject clearly had politically incapacitating consequences. “Prefer what is positive and multiple, difference over uniformity, flows over unities, mobile arrangements over systems,” Foucault wrote in his foreword to Deleuze and Guattari’s The Anti-Oedipus (“hands down the weirdest stuff in the French theory canon,” Eakin writes), with its anti-Freudian celebration of the creative, oppositional power of desire (or “desiring-machines”). The affirmative focus on multiplicity, dynamism, and proliferating differences could paradoxically evoke an undifferentiated, impregnable mass, lacking the contradictions or strategic focal points through which power could be breached.
Theory could seem to transgress everything without transforming anything. In this, Terry Eagleton argued, it bore the marks of the spectacular but unconsummated “insurrectionary élan” of May 1968. Iconoclastic in impulse but shrinking from presenting a positive alternative to the existing order, theory reflected the abortive uprising’s vertiginous “blend of euphoria and disillusionment, liberation and dissipation, carnival and catastrophe,” a “kind of intellectual backwash to a tumultuous political era.” Theory may have struck a chord precisely because it chimed with the emergent late-capitalist reality it was gesturally ranged against. Its dissolution of the subject matched the dispersal of the classical agent of collective struggle under the neoliberal assault, with no obvious successor. Perhaps there was also something constitutionally ephemeral about a body of thought resistant to structures, something unsustainable about its institutionalization. As Peter Dews reflected, “Totalizing anti-totalization is just too contradictory a stance to last for very long.”
In many ways, however, the “French philosophical moment” never ended. Far from being overthrown, theory—not unlike neoliberal common sense—has been so comprehensively metabolized, achieved so thoroughgoing a hegemony, that it has become invisible, its “influence no longer obvious because it is everywhere,” as Eakin writes. There are the substantive legacies within academic study—what Cusset calls theory’s “detachable concepts,” now in wide circulation, from Lacan’s “mirror stage” and Foucault’s “biopower” to Bourdieu’s “cultural capital,” as well as the new disciplines which drew inspiration from it, including postcolonialism and cultural studies; its underground influence, too, persisted into the 2000s in the UK blogosphere spearheaded by Mark Fisher. And it has left a mark on popular culture—at least two generations of prominent novelists, among them Jonathan Franzen and Ben Lerner, bear the imprint of their theoretical education.
Eakin has in mind a more pervasive if intangible footprint. “For better and for worse,” she argues, “we are in some ways all like the Frenchmen now, expert decoders of our tirelessly signifying universe.” The better, for Eakin, is that theory “taught us a new way to think. Be skeptical. Be alert. Pay very close attention.” Such imperatives are hardly unique to French theory; they are surely ingredients of virtually any form of thought that seeks to question—to “denaturalize”—what we take for granted. The self-scrutiny implied by post-structuralism’s interrogation of reason and “scrupulous attentiveness to language’s complexities and contradictions,” as Eakin puts it, is a more distinctive bequest. “The quality and fecundity of a discourse,” Derrida argued at Johns Hopkins, can be gauged by how rigorously it probes its “inherited concepts”—and by extension, its inherited authorities. White’s suggestion that “the authority of Foucault’s discourse derives primarily from its style” implied that rhetorical craft is an underhand or domineering means of producing authority—not as transparent to reason, and not as consensual as evidence or argument. But, whether or not they advertise or acknowledge it, all forms of discourse have a style from which their authority partly derives. In this sense, the élan of French theory radicalizes and encourages us to reflect on a general problem of how to relate to imposing predecessors.
The contagion of style has not secured theory’s long-term legacy, but the ebbing of its authority and the charged atmosphere surrounding it ought to make room for a more level-headed, realistic, discriminating approach. We no longer have to pick a side, and so can acknowledge that enthusiasm and aversion are not mutually exclusive reactions but may be warring impulses, and can explore the middle ground between dismissal and wholesale acceptance. As with artistic avant-gardes, theoretical traditions are inherited in part by being outgrown: selectively adopted, repurposed and rejected—all of which requires a degree of distance. Indeed, the practice of thinking outside an author’s terms and finding one’s own is necessary not only to criticize their work but to appreciate it.
Jameson was onto something in his 1972 book The Prison-House of Language: “A genuine critique of structuralism commits us to working our way completely through it so as to emerge, on the other side, into some wholly different and theoretically more satisfying philosophical perspective.” Theory, in this vision, would be more than a phase, less something you grow out of than grow through, parsing its contributions from its limitations and its insights from its distractions. By questioning one’s awe as well as one’s impatience, one can develop a more nuanced attitude, not only independent-minded but even overtly self-interested. You can find the energy and confidence and irreverence of this creative, controversial “moment” inspiring without needing to declare your allegiance to French theory as a whole, instead revisiting the still-fresh texts that can still help us think, and before which we need be neither cowed nor contemptuous but are free to be curious, and productively ambivalent.

articles.title: Nasdaq plummets 4% into correction territory
articles.body:
Stocks plummeted on Thursday, erasing the sharp gains from the rally seen in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, as investors accelerated their move away from technology stocks on fears of a data-center buildout slowdown.
The Nasdaq Composite declined 5.52% to close at 24,315.00. The tech-heavy index slid into correction territory, falling more than 10% below a record set last month. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to end at 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and settled at 51,523.06.
The Dow more than wiped out its advance from Wednesday's massive postelection rally. All three major averages posted their worst day since April 2025.
The small-cap Russell 2000 index decreased 4.45% and also entered a correction.
Stocks related to the artificial intelligence trade, particularly those linked to the chips industry and data centers, slid for a second day. Investors fear that a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress as well as victories in key gubernatorial races could decelerate the data center buildout.
For instance, Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont — who caucuses with Democrats — has called for a national data center moratorium. In a post on X Wednesday evening, Sanders wrote that "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
Chipmakers Broadcom and Nvidia respectively fell 10% and 9% Thursday, while software stock Oracle moved lower by almost 7%. Another chip stock, Qualcomm, reported earnings that beat estimates, but the stock dropped 9% on a weaker-than-expected earnings outlook. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down more than 12% for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
Shares of neocloud companies also retreated, with CoreWeave losing almost 10%. Nebius and Iren slid about 15% and almost 17%, amid worries about a backlash to the industry in light of the election results in various states.
Investors are "stepping away until they get a better sense of the implications of the midterms around the AI capex cycle in particular, which is the biggest economic tailwind we've had going for us for the last, call it, three years," said Tim Holland, chief investment officer at Orion. "It's about tone and tenor from the party that did really well, incredibly well, at the federal level and at the state level."
Thursday's selling pressure was so intense that it spread to other parts of the market. Shares of industrial giant Caterpillar declined 6%, while financial stock JPMorgan fell 4%. Aerospace name Boeing and athletic apparel giant Nike pulled back 2%.
"Unlike yesterday, you're just seeing that the sell-off in tech, the size of it, is now feeding itself into the broader market," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Wealth. "The rubber band is becoming increasingly stretched."
On Wednesday, the Dow jumped more than 1,500 points to notch its best day since April 2025 after a decisive midterm win for Democrats. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite also popped more than 1% each. Areas related to AI were under pressure, however, while economically-sensitive stocks rose.

articles.title: Nvidia Kubernetes Engine (NVKE)
articles.body:
Run a managed Kubernetes service on your own NVIDIA GPU infrastructure.
NVIDIA Kubernetes® Engine (NVKE) provides the management plane that platform teams install to create and
operate Kubernetes clusters for their customers. Each workload cluster has its
own Kubernetes control plane, etcd and node pools. You operate the NVKE management
plane; your customers use their clusters through the Kubernetes API and kubectl.
Preview: NVKE is available as a preview. APIs, configuration and behavior can change between releases, and we do not recommend NVKE for production workloads. See Preview status and known limitations.
Get started · Documentation · Contribute · Get help
The local quickstart runs on a Linux host or VM, amd64 or arm64, with at least
6 CPUs, 12 GiB of free memory and 100 GiB of free disk. It requires Docker,
virtual TPM support and the tools listed in the guide. Follow its setup through
workload-cluster creation and confirm the cluster's nodes report Ready.
On macOS, use the local site guide, which runs
the evaluation inside a Colima virtual machine.
For a real installation, you supply the machines, networking, node images and registries, and configure access to NVIDIA Infra Controller (NICo). NICo is the sole compatible infrastructure provider at preview. The platform and version reference lists validated combinations and pinned dependencies.
- Creates independent workload clusters. Request clusters through the NVKE
API or nvkectl; NVKE provisions machines through NICo and forms Kubernetes
clusters with their own control planes.
- Manages workload cluster lifecycle. Create, scale and delete node pools, upgrade Kubernetes and replace nodes. See the node pool guide for the manual steps and preview limits on replacement and upgrades.
- Establishes node identity. Nodes attest through SPIFFE/SPIRE using their TPM before receiving join credentials. Encryption of etcd data is available per cluster.
- Connects builds to deployment. Its companion project, NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes (NVKR), builds node images and NVKE components from pinned inputs. NVKE deploys those artifacts; NVKR owns their build and release evidence.
The preview needs explicit operator configuration: API authentication is off and the API uses plain HTTP after installation. Configure API authentication and protected access before admitting callers. The management cluster does not upgrade, scale or replace itself, and there is no management-plane upgrade or backup/restore procedure. FDE node images are for evaluation and provide no data-at-rest confidentiality. Read the known limitations before choosing an evaluation or installation path.
The diagram shows the NVKE product family, how it sits on NICo and your GPU machines, and which components talk to each other.
NVKE is not a Kubernetes distribution and not a Cluster API flavour. It is a self-hosting factory for Kubernetes clusters: a throwaway seed cluster stands up a management cluster, and the management plane on it then provisions and lifecycle-manages many isolated workload clusters on demand.
An installation has two kinds of Kubernetes cluster:
- The management cluster runs the NVKE management plane and infrastructure
controllers. nvkectl forms it using a temporary seed cluster; installing the
management-plane services is a separate step.
- Workload clusters run customer applications. The management plane creates and operates them through NICo, Cluster API and the node agent.
Read What is NVKE for the operator workflow and Architecture for the implementation and data flows.
Use Go 1.27.3, the version pinned in go.work, and GNU Make 4 or later. Public Go modules must be reachable on the first build. Flox is optional and supplies the repository's development tools; on macOS, it also supplies GNU Make 4. See Development for toolchain setup.
git clone https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke.git
cd nvke
make build
This builds the workspace and writes nine binaries to bin/: agent,
updater, controller, nvkectl, capd-reboot-controller,
nvke-os-image-check, management-engine, tenant-api and operator-api. Building does not start a
management plane or create a cluster. The node agent runs on Linux.
The workspace guide explains the modules and outputs.
For local services and test environments, see Local development setup.
Before submitting a change, follow CONTRIBUTING.md and run
make preflight; it selects checks for the modules you changed.
The documentation index links the remaining guides and references.
Contributions, bug reports and documentation improvements are welcome. Start with CONTRIBUTING.md; open an issue before substantial work so maintainers can agree on the approach.
- Questions: GitHub Discussions.
- Chat: the #nvke channel in the DSX AI Factory Slack.
Get an invite.
- Bugs and feature requests: GitHub Issues.
- Security vulnerabilities: follow SECURITY.md and report privately.
- Community: Code of Conduct, Governance, Maintainers and Support.
- Releases: release process.
- CI health: the CI dashboard shows the last thirty runs of every workflow and refreshes hourly.
Kubernetes® is a registered trademark of The Linux Foundation in the United States and other countries. NVIDIA and the NVIDIA logo are trademarks and/or registered trademarks of NVIDIA Corporation in the U.S. and other countries. Other company and product names may be trademarks of the respective companies with which they are associated.
Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE and NOTICE.

articles.title: Lippitt-Knoster in Practice (Field Notes for Managing Complex Projects)
articles.body:
"Lippitt-Knoster" is one of those things where if you've worked with me during the last 10 years, you've likely heard me mention it. You might even be reading this because I needed somewhere to point you. In which case, Hi! 👋
The Lippitt-Knoster Model for Managing Complex Change was originally written to describe a way of navigating large organizational shifts, but I’ve found that it’s also useful as a diagnosis tool for any kind of large and long-running project. After all, every project is a "change" in a microcosm. You might not have a complex organizational change to manage every day, but everyone is involved in long-running projects of some size and shape in a company. So that’s what I use it for, and it is useful indeed.
The beauty of the model is that you don’t need an MBA or a special issue of the Harvard Business Review to explain it. It says that any complex project requires six components to succeed, and if one or another is missing, you’ll have some specific and corresponding failure.
It can be summed up in a simple chart but also rewards you with some deeper insights as you apply it:
- Vision is the purpose and endpoint of a project. Vision tells you where you’re going and why. If the vision is missing, there will be confusion about what is being done and why work is happening.
- Consensus is a team's agreement and alignment around the vision. If a team lacks consensus, people will not want to do the thing and they will sabotage you.
- Incentives are the motivation or reasons for why people support the work and prioritize it appropriately. If not everyone is incentivized properly, there will be resistance. Resistance is the passive sibling of sabotage.
- The Action Plan is the practical set of steps to get from vision to finish. If you lack an action plan, your team will experience a routine set of false starts and treadmills, which is another way of saying that it will look like work is happening but nothing actually moves forward. You won’t make progress.
- Resources are the organizational capacity (people, budget, time) needed to accomplish the work. Lacking resources is a close cousin to lacking skills; it leads to frustration in trying to do something you know you're capable of, but with an unrealistic set of operating constraints.
- Skills are the ability to do the work necessary to complete the project. If a team lacks the necessary skills, you'll have a lot of questions around if this work is possible, leading to anxiety.
Vision, consensus, and incentives are all Strategic Concerns. They involve abstract political work: ideas, relationships, people, and an understanding of the business. The action plan, skills, and resources are all Tactical Concerns. They are focused on the practical details of “how” something gets done.1
One mistake I often see people make is to focus primarily on one concern or the other. For example, a product manager or corporate strategist might spend too much time focused on the strategic side of things without understanding if the team or company is able to execute. Consequently, their ability to build consensus will be negatively impacted by not knowing what is possible or probable. Line managers and software engineers typically make the opposite mistake. They focus too much on the ‘how’ instead of the ‘why’. They’ll prove that something is possible and how it can be done, without realizing that sometimes the team or business doesn't want to do the thing they’re proposing. Neither myopia ends in a successful project.
The order of the model components matters – they flow into each other – but can be managed in either direction. For example: you might start with a vision, build consensus, arrange the right incentives for everyone to act, create a plan, provide adequate resources and timeline to accomplish that plan, and make sure it is staffed with people who have the skills to execute on it. Easy peasy!
You could also navigate the components the other way, working through a series of questions: is something possible? Do skills exist to accomplish the thing? Do those skills (people) have excess capacity that can be allocated to this idea? Can it be done without budget? Can that group of people be small enough that they organically develop their own plans? And if so, are they incentivized to take on this kind of work outside their daily responsibilities? Does it need sign-off from anyone? If you’ve found confirmatory answers along the way, congratulations: you can carve out a secret R&D initiative within your team or your company. (This is also 'effectuation' in practice.)
You can also read the model from the perspectives of both cause and effect. Reading it one way creates a checklist before kicking off any major work: “Here are the six prerequisites for success, are we all set?” (A causal, prescriptive reading – given starting parameters, what will be the end result?) Reading it backwards turns it into a troubleshooting tool. For example, if someone comes to you mid-project complaining that "We keep going in circles and the team is anxious! What can I do?" you might look at the model and respond, "Well of course! You don't have an action plan. Or maybe, it hasn't been adequately distributed and communicated and people feel that they lack the skills to accomplish something so big. Let's break it down into manageable pieces that we do have the skills for." It’s pretty quick to go between looking at the failure states and looking at the necessary components to diagnose what’s going on with a project. (A diagnostic reading, reasoning backwards.)
The model is a fantastic tool for making sense of things. But that leaves the hard work to start after you've made sense of things. How do you drive consensus? How do you align folks around a vision? How do you build up skills, or break down big projects into smaller pieces for which skills exist? How do you win resources, or align incentives?
Some of those answers are obvious, but most are not. Many of the answers are best understood as the manifestation of tacit expertise — a ‘feeling’ for the right move in any particular context, a form of expertise that comes from having been around the block a few times.
And like with most tacit expertise, you’ll find that there are no one-size-fits-all answers to any scenario, but there are plenty of good practices and useful observations.
So here are some of mine:
Strategic Concerns
The most common and important questions that come up after someone lays out a vision are “Why should we do this?” and permutations around the follow-up details. If you see those questions, that’s “confusion”, which is another way of saying you’ve presented a fantasy instead of a vision (or perhaps, the vision is missing entirely). That’s because many people confuse vision for having a colorful and inspiring imagination, making their picture too colorful, unrealistically grand, or too far off.2
My experience is that you make more progress by simply providing adequate context and letting people derive their own vision. The art of context is giving people breadcrumbs to get from where you are today to where you want to be in the future, and giving them some good reasons to follow those breadcrumbs with you. There’s nothing more effective than a self-motivated team that thinks they’re the ones who came up with the idea, that they saw what things could be like. That’s vision.
Similarly, consensus is a straightforward concept, but strangely elusive in most organizations. Any organization beyond a certain age and size will typically have a 'minimally viable consensus' while practically being at odds with itself. Departments often turn into silos with their own internal logic for what should happen. Job security encourages teams to think about what’s best for them instead of for the company. And companies don’t do a great job tying “what’s best for the company” with “what’s best for the individuals within, or the communities around”,3 which makes most employment mercenary: people naturally find a balance between what they’re paid and how much to care about the thing in question. (In that sense, incorporated businesses are kind of like democracy: a bad choice, but among the best of the options available for coordinating large groups of people to accomplish things.)
Recognizing that, one amateur mistake people make is trying to build consensus in a group setting. It just doesn't happen that way. You’re either going to have everyone nodding along and afraid to say their piece in front of everyone else, or you’re going to have one guy (and it’s usually a guy – sorry, my dudes) start pulling some “what about”-ism and dragging the conversation into a black hole of details that you never intended to argue about but find yourself frustratingly debating anyway.
In either scenario, the meeting will end without consensus.
In Japanese business culture there is a concept called “nemawashi”, which translates roughly to “tending to the roots” or “laying the groundwork”. It’s a good analogy because the practice of creating consensus requires a lot of political skill, footwork, trust-building, and private conversation. It means giving people space to tell you everything that’s wrong with your idea, finding ways to address those concerns, and making sure everyone is aligned before the alignment actually happens. The group meeting when everyone signs off in agreement should be the result of careful stage management — you should know and have already addressed everyone’s concerns, including second-order effects of how addressing one person’s issues will impact others.
There should be no surprises; it is theater, not improv.
That said, you might not be able to get to consensus. Perhaps your boss wants the “thing” to happen but there’s another department that’s actively against it. Maybe you're encroaching on their turf, or it will reduce their capacity in some zero-sum resource bucket. Maybe they just have a different perspective on the world and the approaches the business should take. Maybe you've wandered into a long-running feud and this project is just one of many different battles being waged. Who knows, people can be both petty and complicated!
If you can't get their buy-in, they will sabotage it in all sorts of creative ways. Because sabotage and resistance are close cousins and are political (in the sense of not being open conflict), monographs on activism and subterfuge can be read as useful primers. Consider James C. Scott's Weapons of the Weak and the OSS's Simple Sabotage Field Manual for what kinds of foot dragging, malicious compliance, noncompliance, evasion, sowing confusion, slander, useless meetings, arbitrary hurdles, revisiting decisions, and moving goalposts to expect.
My advice for these scenarios is to try one of two things. Your first option is to get to the bottom of why there is no consensus and figure out if you’re in a position to address that root cause. Often, you’re not in a position to address those things; if you pursue resolution, you’re going to use up a lot of your political capital or burn out trying to get the project moving forward. And success can be fleeting – projects can continue to be sabotaged even after launch. I once had a project launch only to have all of its resources immediately pulled, forcing its premature death.
Not even chief executives are immune to this; sometimes the solution to a lack of consensus and active sabotage is to simply fire the people in disagreement. (Obviously, use this technique sparingly — you’re scorching the earth.)
