So I recommend most people take the second approach, which is to just drop it. Move on. It’s a lost cause. Don’t be the sailor with a bucket trying to dump water off this Titanic. Quitting things and dropping things is a totally acceptable thing to do; life isn’t a video game where you’re striving for 100% completeness on every side quest. Move on to things where you’re actually making a difference.
But let’s say everyone agrees. Now you need to make sure that things are prioritized appropriately. You’re not going to make any progress if this is low on everyone’s priority list. So you incentivize teams and people.
Positive incentives typically work better than negative incentives, but most people are not in a position to offer meaningful (financial) incentives to push a project forward. Instead, you can rely on horse-trading (“if you help me move this project forward, I’ll help with your thing”), you can help people resolve their problems, and you can paint a compelling-enough end-state that people also want to reach that goal with you.
Otherwise, people are going to be resistant, which is a passive form of sabotage: sabotage without commitment, or general apathy. It might not even be malicious. It’s just… well, you’re just one more project for people to care about and work on. Why should they do it above all else?
And more importantly, resistance can turn into sabotage when incentives are not just missing, but misaligned. Misaligned incentives can break consensus when you're sweating the details.
Tactical Concerns
Now, let’s say you figured out the strategic bits and you’re working through the implementation portion. Some projects are simple enough that you can just describe what needs to be done, and you can count those requirements on a single maimed hand. We’re not talking about those projects.
Any complex-enough project requires coordination of requirements, dependencies, timelines, people, and other details. I’ve written a bit about those issues in “When Everything is Important But Nothing Is Getting Done”, so I don’t want to retread too much ground.
But one thing worth highlighting is how skills and anxiety are coupled, and how to navigate a lack of skills. Any ambitious project is at some point going to run into a lack of skills or prior experience because the work wouldn't be ambitious if you'd done it before. So in many regards, it is an existential question for any project: are you and your team able to do what needs to be done? If not, you’ll get a very stressed team, or you’ll get a simulacrum of what you expected.
There are ways to compensate for a lack of skills. I rely on three techniques:
First is up-skilling people. Education, mentorship, and training are effective ways to turn juniors into seniors, low-skilled employees into high-skilled employees. While there are a variety of documented techniques for this (see: accelerated expertise, tactical decision games), the caveats are that (a) this typically takes longer than the time-span of a single project and (b) you need to find people who are interested in learning.
So the second technique is atomization: break the requirements into smaller pieces that meet the level of skill available rather than trying to get people to rise to the required level. Instead of making everyone work harder, just make the requirements easier. Instead of asking people to “cut database reads by 50%” or “create a capacity forecasting model for the next 12 months” (where they may not even know where to start), give them smaller tasks and directions for what to do to accomplish that. Point folks in the right direction, explain the what and the why, turn big asks into a series of steps, a recipe to accomplish something. This is in itself a form of teaching, and it is more project-sized (see what I did there?).
The third technique is to roll up your sleeves and contribute. I’ve learned from many effective leaders that there is no work below your pay grade. What makes many great leaders "great" is their willingness to spend extra time doing “glue” work, filling in the holes between roles, and making sure all assumptions are bridged back to real expectations. They are never too good to personally write up a project document, to manage a tracker, to make sure that people are talking to each other. They often know as much or more about the details than subject matter experts, but they don't needlessly meddle – they support where needed and use gaps as up-skilling opportunities.
Much of the work of compensating for skills gaps is directly translatable into managing budget, time, and effort tradeoffs to navigate the “resources” component of Lippitt-Knoster. And your ability to solve for skills and resources directly translates back into the specific action plan you need to put together. For example: you may decide not to spend $100,000 on a vendor because you can reverse engineer a single feature you need for a project, but you need to add time to the plan for that.
These considerations become a calculus of risks, rewards, and effort, which in turn underpins the strategic portions that we talked about earlier: sure, you might think you can lead a team to rebuild the hot new vendor in house in two months, but have you earned organizational political capital to place those chips on the table?
So there you have it, Lippitt-Knoster in practice. Lead on!
1 - This grouping is not present in most Lippitt-Knoster model descriptions I’ve come across; it is my one humble contribution.
2 - A realistic vision that is too far into the future is its own type of risk – every day presents new opportunities for conditions to change, starting conditions to be led astray. The likelihood of any far-off future has too many compounding variables... too many things have to go right and be true for it to be reliable enough to pin your hopes to.
3 - These things are usually at odds with each other. There's a big literature about how "equity" is a tool to get employees to care about corporate success, but most startup equity goes to zero; for the average employee, a bonus or a pay raise is more useful. Public company equity presents a different issue: it is dependent on public market behavior, and less on your individual ability to impact it – being in a public company, you're likely one of thousands-plus of employees.
Thanks for reading
Useful? Interesting? Have something to add? Shoot me a note at roman@sharedphysics.com. I love getting email and chatting with readers.
You can also sign up for irregular emails and RSS updates when I post something new.
Who am I?
I'm Roman Kudryashov -- I help healthcare companies solve challenging problems through software development and process design. My longer background is here and I keep track of some of my side projects here.
Stay true,
Roman

articles.title: Republicans Learn X Is the Echo Chamber
articles.body:
There's a BlazeTV YouTube video whose thumbnail shows the presenter with his arms around Anakin Skywalker and a gender-flipped Draco Malfoy called Malfoid. “Total Chud Victory?” It says. The video's title: “Young Right is Reclaiming Culture and Liberals Are Mad About it.”
BlazeTV posted the video on November 2, the day before Democrats swept the midterms and started a political realignment in America so overwhelming that Republicans lost control of all the most powerful state positions in Texas.
The video is a profound misreading of the political and cultural moment. It reminded me of stories of the Bolsheviks seizing the Winter Palace to discover tarot card playing courtiers who had no idea a revolution was happening in the streets.
The American version was watching defense contractor Palmer Lucky dress up like Harry Potter on Halloween while standing next to his Malfoid wife. And it was Elon Musk — who spent roughly half a billion on the election only to see his chosen candidates fail — posting an AI generated picture of Anakin Skywalker sitting at the head of a happy fascist Star Wars family two days before the midterms.
The online right has dominated American culture for a decade, or at least has dominated political narratives picked up by the mainstream media. Its memes and conspiracies drove news cycles. At first, the right’s memes filtered from random people on obscure Discord channels to Reddit’s r/the_donald or 4chan to Trump’s Twitter feed. More recently they’ve come from AI slop farms, from Musk, or from the administration itself. Powered by a well-funded media and podcast ecosystem, Fox News (and a propensity for shamelessness) its comedians, podcasters, and pundits became powerful celebrities and influencers, at least within Elon Musk’s X.
This insular, often inscrutable world has given us Ben Shapiro, Nick Fuentes, Gamergate influencers, the streamer Asmongold, and a revolving door of characters who have shuffled interchangeably between Twitterverse celebritydom and actual government; Kash Patel, DataRepublican, Laura Loomer, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr., Dan Bongino, the list goes on.
It has been said many times that “Twitter is not real life,” and that posting too much anywhere will rot your brain. Never has that been more apparent than now: Much of Trumpworld spent the week before an election in which they would get utterly trounced using AI to generate barely legible Anakin and Malfoid memes for an inconsequential ingroup on the social media platform run by the biggest loser on the planet.
“It certainly seems like it has had its high water mark and that reality has FINALLY caught up with the Republican Party,” Michael Senters, a research assistant at the Anti-Defamation League who studies online and gaming culture, told 404 Media.
In 2016, 4chan posters talked about “meme magic” — the pseudo-ironic belief that pictures on the internet could manifest great change in reality. According to legend, Trump strategist Steve Bannon was running a World of Warcraft gold farm when he realized the angry gamers could be harnessed into a powerful reactionary political force. Bannon and others would successfully parlay Gamergate into an endless culture war that’s dominated online life in the Trump era.
During the midterm livestream of Bannon’s War Room podcast, his guest read exit polls that suggested the right-wing had lost young men — a group long thought to be its strongest soldiers. The split between the parties was even, the guest explained. “That can’t be right,” Bannon whispered, signalling he’d lost touch with the constituency he’d harnessed on behalf of Trump ten years ago. As the election results began coming in, right-wing podcasters, livestreamers, and newscasters across the internet went through at least a few of the stages of grief. First they struggled to understand what was happening, suggesting the votes must be wrong. Eventually, many of them ragequit.
"Okay, I'm going to be honest. I'm absolutely rage quitting. I'm so frustrated. I am so unbelievably frustrated. I'm so mad. I think Trump didn't do 50 different things he should have done. I think he should have gone a thousand times harder. I think that he wasted his time selling trinkets and nonsense,” Asmongold said as the returns came in. He lives in Texas where Democrats swept in a shock victory.
“I wish that there were more people who thought like me that weren’t sorry about it. But you know what? There’s not. So it’s just me. And that’s fine. It’s fine. It’s OK,” he said, his voice catching in his throat.
Many right-wing personalities went into Tuesday somehow expecting to win despite a disastrous war, a disastrous economy, disastrous polls, and a doddering president whose closing argument seemed to be more about his ballrooms, golf courses, and the Reflecting Pool than anything else. Since Trump was re-elected, these same people have called everyone else out of touch, convinced by their X algorithm and prediction markets that no blue wave would materialize. The media has similarly spent many thousands of words suggesting that Bluesky is an out-of-touch leftist echo chamber while mostly failing to suggest anything of the sort about the AI-pilled Silicon Valley executives, bots, and racists shitposting on X. Tuesday’s election wipeout highlights how detached from reality the Malfoid/Anakin-shipping, X-brained billionaires and their acolytes have actually become.
“Blueskywave. Those of us on here, across the board, were out of touch. I see no other conclusion,” Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg's Odd Lots podcast (who is a serious, good journalist), said in a post on X after the election amidst a sea of Anakins tonguing Malfoids.
The meme game and general demeanor of Trump and his followers has grown wildly tiresome in his thus far-disastrous second term. Under the guidance of White House Communications Director Steven Cheung, official government accounts have posted racist Halo memes, used AI to put a studio Ghibli face on anti-immigrant propaganda, and fully embraced Malfoid and Darth Vader as cultural heroes. The base on X loved this stuff. No one else did.
As our friend Gita Jackson over at Aftermath wisely put it immediately before the election, "The idea that they can meme magic their way into a red sweep by posting about Anakin Skywalker a lot is pure desperation [...] Their values have been rejected by popular culture at large, and they are now resigned to exist in the margins.”
Senters said the midterms showed the hard limits of memes as a political tool. “The power that memes have has always been, in my opinion, the power to help define linguistic and community lines in the amorphous space of the Internet. You create a community when you ‘get the joke’ behind a meme but memes generally don't persuade,” he said. “I'll be curious to see if the government accounts will continue to post these far-right cultural memes in the wake of the defeat or if they'll change their tune at all. Like do they double down on the meme posting to try to rally their base? Because it very clearly had ZERO appeal to anyone outside their base.”
Yet the right-wing has spent the last ten years acting as if their memes had moved the country politically. “They deluded themselves into believing that memes carry persuasive power and that their bubble on X represented material reality in a meaningful way when that was no way close to the truth,” he said. “They saw how many ‘numbers’ the Malfoid and Anakin memes did on X and convinced themselves that this was a real cultural awakening moment and that the volk were on their side.”
Alyssa Mercante, an internet culture reporter who is writing a book about politics and video games called Rage Game, agreed. “I think what it's really showing is that when you start to get a little bit too deep in the weeds of this hyper online culture war stuff, it cannot escape the internet,” Mercante told 404 Media. “It is not working anymore. The material reality of America is just not good enough.” Gas prices are up. Everything is more expensive. And ICE has killed Americans in the streets.
“This conspiratorial mindset is wrecker mentality. It is just destructive for the sake of destruction. There is no goal beyond pulling away any sort of legitimacy from the media or from democracy,” Mercante said. “When you get so deep in the weeds of this anti-establishment conspiratorial thought process, you just can't make anything or do anything of value. You're just upending tables and pointing at them and laughing.”
Democrats crushed Republicans who leaned into the online culture war during the midterms. Bo French — an overt racist who ran for railroad commissioner in Texas — sent text messages to voters that depicted himself as Master Chief from Halo. His opponent beat him by more than a million votes.
In Nevada, Halo composer Martin O’Donnell ran as a Republican for a House seat and lost to incumbent Susie Lee. O’Donnell announced his campaign on Discord and leaned hard into an extremely online gamer identity. “He’s like, ‘I wrote the Halo music and I’m voting for Trump and you should too.’ He did a Halo LAN party campaign fundraiser. The imagery was him as Master Chief,” Mercante said. “This dude is like: ‘My personality is gamers, gamers are not woke and they're resisting this [...] and Trump is the person that is going to help us resist,’ and he's polling like absolute dog water.”
It’s been 12 years since Gamergate set the tempo for online culture wars and a decade since Trump won in 2016. In 2026, Star Wars, Halo, Harry Potter feel dated in a way they didn’t back then. “What 22-year-old kid is going to be like ‘they took Halo from me.’ They don’t know Halo to have it taken away from them,” Mercante said.
She stressed that so much right wing online culture is about distraction — she likened it to jingling keys to capture the attention of a baby. “If the economy is the number one issue for both Democrats and Republicans going into the midterms, no amount of Malfoid scissoring Anakin Skywalker is going to change that need for people to be in a better financial position,” Mercante said. “The tech oligarchs pushed this stuff straight into our eyes for two years straight unfettered [...] And I wake up and gas is this expensive? I don’t care if you take a Taylor Swift song and make JD Vance walk out to it.”
“[They] really thought that this would just last forever,” she added. “When you build up a meme presidency, eventually the cards just collapse underneath you, and there's just nothing to show for it.”
Though this midterm signals a move away from Gamergate-style culture war politics, both Senters and Mercante cautioned that this type of rhetoric is still dangerous, and can still be destructive. “They’re still very good at doing propaganda on the internet — they wrote the book in many cases,” Mercante said.

articles.title: Chomsky and the Two Cultures of Statistical Learning
articles.body:
derided researchers in machine learning who use purely
statistical methods to produce behavior that mimics something in the
world, but who don't try to understand the meaning of that
behavior. 
It's true there's been a lot of work on trying to apply statistical models to
various linguistic problems. I think there have been some successes, but a lot of failures.
There is a notion of success ... which I think is novel in the history of science.
It interprets success as approximating unanalyzed data.
Chomsky's remarks were in response to Steven Pinker's question about the success of probabilistic models trained with statistical methods. This essay is a response to Pinker and Chomsky, and will address these questions:
For example, a decade before Chomsky, Claude Shannon proposed probabilistic models of communication based on Markov chains of words. If you have a vocabulary of 100,000 words and a second-order Markov model in which the probability of a word depends on the previous two words, then you need a quadrillion (1015) probability values to specify the model. The only feasible way to learn these 1015 values is to gather statistics from data and introduce some smoothing method for the many cases where there is no data. Therefore, most (but not all) probabilistic models are trained. Also, many (but not all) trained models are probabilistic.
As another example, consider the Newtonian model of gravitational attraction, which says that the force between two objects of mass m1 and m2 a distance r apart is given by
F = G m1 m2 / r2
(This example brings up another distinction: the gravitational model is continuous and quantitative whereas the linguistic tradition has favored models that are discrete, categorical, and qualitative: a word is or is not a verb, there is no question of its degree of verbiness. For more on these distinctions, see Chris Manning's article on Probabilistic Syntax.)
A relevant probabilistic statistical model is the ideal gas law, which describes the pressure P of a gas in terms of the the number of molecules, N, the temperature T, and Boltzmann's constant, K:
P = N k T / V.
The equation can be derived from first principles using the tools of statistical mechanics. It is an uncertain, incorrect model; the true model would have to describe the motions of individual gas molecules. This model ignores that complexity and summarizes our uncertainty about the location of individual molecules. Thus, even though it is statistical and probabilistic, even though it does not completely model reality, it does provide both good predictions and insight—insight that is not available from trying to understand the true movements of individual molecules.
Now let's consider the non-statistical model of spelling expressed by the rule "I before E except after C." Compare that to the probabilistic, trained statistical model:
P(IE) = 0.0177 P(CIE) = 0.0014 P(*IE) = 0.163 P(EI) = 0.0046 P(CEI) = 0.0005 P(*EI) = 0.0041
Accuracy("I before E") = 0.0177/(0.0177+0.0046) = 0.793
Accuracy("I before E except after C") = (0.0005+0.0163)/(0.0005+0.0163+0.0014+0.0041) = 0.753
A more complex statistical model (say, one that gave the probability of all
4-letter sequences, and/or of all known words) could be ten times more
accurate at the task of spelling, but does not offer concise insight into how spelling
works. Insight would require a model that knows about phonemes,
syllabification, and language of origin.  Such a model could be trained (or not) and
probabilistic (or not).
As another example of insight, consider the Theory of Supreme Court Justice Hand-Shaking: when the supreme court convenes, all attending justices shake hands with every other justice. The number of attendees, n, must be an integer in the range 0 to 9; what is the total number of handshakes, h for a given n? Here are three possible explanations:
Now let's look at some components that are of interest only to the computational linguist, not to the end user:
Clearly, it is inaccurate to say that statistical models (and probabilistic models) have achieved limited success; rather they have achieved an overwhelmingly dominant (although not exclusive) position.
Another measure of success is the degree to which an idea captures a community of researchers. As Steve Abney wrote in 1996, "In the space of the last ten years, statistical methods have gone from being virtually unknown in computational linguistics to being a fundamental given. ... anyone who cannot at least use the terminology persuasively risks being mistaken for kitchen help at the ACL [Association for Computational Linguistics] banquet."
Now of course, the majority doesn't rule -- just because everyone is jumping on some bandwagon, that doesn't make it right. But I made the switch: after about 14 years of trying to get language models to work using logical rules, I started to adopt probabilistic approaches (thanks to pioneers like Gene Charniak (and Judea Pearl for probability in general) and to my colleagues who were early adopters, like Dekai Wu). And I saw everyone around me making the same switch. And I didn't see anyone going in the other direction. We all saw the limitations of the old tools, and the benefits of the new.
And while it may seem crass and anti-intellectual to consider a financial measure of success, I note that the intellectual offspring of Shannon's theory create several trillion dollars of revenue each year, while the offspring of Chomsky's theories generate well under a billion.
This section has shown that one reason why the vast majority of researchers in computational linguistics use statistical models is an engineering reason: statistical models have state-of-the-art performance, and in most cases non-statistical models perform worst. For the remainder of this essay we will concentrate on scientific reasons: that probabilistic models better represent linguistic facts, and statistical techniques make it easier for us to make sense of those facts.
A dictionary definition of science is "the systematic study of the structure and behavior of the physical and natural world through observation and experiment," which stresses accurate modeling over insight, but it seems to me that both notions have always coexisted as part of doing science. To test that, I consulted the epitome of doing science, namely Science. I looked at the current issue and chose a title and abstract at random:
Chlorinated Indium Tin Oxide Electrodes with High Work Function for
Organic Device Compatibility
In organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), a stack of multiple organic layers facilitates charge flow from the low work function [~4.7 electron volts (eV)] of the transparent electrode (tin-doped indium oxide, ITO) to the deep energy levels (~6 eV) of the active light-emitting organic materials. We demonstrate a chlorinated ITO transparent electrode with a work function of >6.1 eV that provides a direct match to the energy levels of the active light-emitting materials in state-of-the art OLEDs. A highly simplified green OLED with a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 54% and power efficiency of 230 lumens per watt using outcoupling enhancement was demonstrated, as were EQE of 50% and power efficiency of 110 lumens per watt at 10,000 candelas per square meter.
It certainly seems that this article is much more focused on "accurately modeling the world" than on "providing insight." The paper does indeed fit in to a body of theories, but it is mostly reporting on specific experiments and the results obtained from them (e.g. efficiency of 54%).
I then looked at all the titles and abstracts from the current issue of Science:
I said that statistical models are sometimes confused with probabilistic models; let's first consider the extent to which Chomsky's objections are actually about probabilistic models. In 1969 he famously wrote:
But it must be recognized that the notion of "probability of a sentence" is an entirely useless one, under any known interpretation of this term.
His main argument being that, under any interpretation known to him, the probability of a novel sentence must be zero, and since novel sentences are in fact generated all the time, there is a contradiction. The resolution of this contradiction is of course that it is not necessary to assign a probability of zero to a novel sentence; in fact, with current probabilistic models it is standard practice to do smoothing and assign a non-zero probability to novel occurrences. So this criticism is invalid, but was very influential for decades. Previously, in Syntactic Structures (1957) Chomsky wrote:
I think we are forced to conclude that ... probabilistic models give no
particular insight into some of the basic problems of syntactic structure.
This criticism is correct, but it is a criticism only of Markov-chain models, not of probabilistic models (or trained models) in general. Since 1957 we have seen many types of probabilistic language models beyond the Markov-chain word models. Examples 1-4 above can in fact be distinguished with a finite-state model that is not a chain, but other examples require more sophisticated models. The best studied is probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG), which operates over trees, categories of words, and individual lexical items, and has none of the restrictions of finite-state models. We find that PCFGs are state-of-the-art for parsing performance and are easier to learn from data than nonprobabilistic categorical context-free grammars. Other types of probabilistic models cover semantic and discourse structures.
Every probabilistic model is a superset of a deterministic model (because the deterministic model could be seen as a probabilistic model where the probabilities are restricted to be 0 or 1), so any valid criticism of probabilistic models would have to be because they are too expressive, not because they are not expressive enough.
In Syntactic Structures, Chomsky introduces a now-famous example that is another criticism of finite-state probabilistic models:
Neither (a) 'colorless green ideas sleep furiously' nor (b) 'furiously
sleep ideas green colorless', nor any of their parts, has ever occurred
in the past linguistic experience of an English speaker. But (a) is
grammatical, while (b) is not.
But regardless of what is meant by "part," a statistically-trained finite-state model can in fact distinguish between these two sentences. Pereira (2001) showed that such a model, augmented with word categories and trained by expectation maximization on newspaper text, computes that (a) is 200,000 times more probable than (b). To prove that this was not the result of Chomsky's sentence itself sneaking into newspaper text, I repeated the experiment, using a much cruder model with Laplacian smoothing and no categories, trained over the Google Book corpus from 1800 to 1954, and found that (a) is about 10,000 times more probable.
Furthermore, the statistical models are capable of delivering the judgment that both sentences are extremely improbable, when compared to, say, "Effective green products sell well." Chomsky's theory, being categorical, cannot make this distinction; all it can distinguish is grammatical/ungrammatical.
Another part of Chomsky's objection is "we cannot seriously propose that a child learns the values of 109 parameters in a childhood lasting only 108 seconds." (Note that modern models are much larger than the 109 parameters that were contemplated in the 1960s.) But of course nobody is proposing that these parameters are learned one-by-one; the right way to do learning is to set large swaths of near-zero parameters simultaneously with a smoothing or regularization procedure, and update the high-probability parameters continuously as observations comes in. Nobody is suggesting that Markov models by themselves are a serious model of human language performance. But I (and others) suggest that probabilistic, trained models are a better model of human language performance than are categorical, untrained models. And yes, it seems clear that an adult speaker of English does know billions of language facts (a speaker knows many facts about the appropriate uses of words in different contexts, such as that one says "the big game" rather than "the large game" when talking about an important football game). These facts must somehow be encoded in the brain.
It seems clear that probabilistic models are better for judging the likelihood of a sentence, or its degree of sensibility. But even if you are not interested in these factors and are only interested in the grammaticality of sentences, it still seems that probabilistic models do a better job at describing the linguistic facts. The mathematical theory of formal languages defines a language as a set of sentences. That is, every sentence is either grammatical or ungrammatical; there is no need for probability in this framework. But natural languages are not like that. A scientific theory of natural languages must account for the many phrases and sentences which leave a native speaker uncertain about their grammaticality (see Chris Manning's article and its discussion of the phrase "as least as"), and there are phrases which some speakers find perfectly grammatical, others perfectly ungrammatical, and still others will flip-flop from one occasion to the next. Finally, there are usages which are rare in a language, but cannot be dismissed if one is concerned with actual data. For example, the verb quake is listed as intransitive in dictionaries, meaning that (1) below is grammatical, and (2) is not, according to a categorical theory of grammar.
Steve Abney points out that probabilistic models are better suited for modeling language change. He cites the example of a 15th century Englishman who goes to the pub every day and orders "Ale!" Under a categorical model, you could reasonably expect that one day he would be served eel, because the great vowel shift flipped a Boolean parameter in his mind a day before it flipped the parameter in the publican's. In a probabilistic framework, there will be multiple parameters, perhaps with continuous values, and it is easy to see how the shift can take place gradually over two centuries.
Thus it seems that grammaticality is not a categorical, deterministic judgment but rather an inherently probabilistic one. This becomes clear to anyone who spends time making observations of a corpus of actual sentences, but can remain unknown to those who think that the object of study is their own set of intuitions about grammaticality. Both observation and intuition have been used in the history of science, so neither is "novel," but it is observation, not intuition that is the dominant model for science.
Now let's consider what I think is Chomsky's main point of disagreement with statistical models: the tension between "accurate description" and "insight." This is an old distinction. Charles Darwin (biologist, 1809–1882) is best known for his insightful theories but he stressed the importance of accurate description, saying "False facts are highly injurious to the progress of science, for they often endure long; but false views, if supported by some evidence, do little harm, for every one takes a salutary pleasure in proving their falseness." More recently, Richard Feynman (physicist, 1918–1988) wrote "Physics can progress without the proofs, but we can't go on without the facts."
On the other side, Ernest Rutherford (physicist, 1871–1937) disdained mere description, saying "All science is either physics or stamp collecting." Chomsky stands with him: "You can also collect butterflies and make many observations. If you like butterflies, that's fine; but such work must not be confounded with research, which is concerned to discover explanatory principles."
Acknowledging both sides is Robert Millikan (physicist, 1868–1953) who said in his Nobel acceptance speech "Science walks forward on two feet, namely theory and experiment ... Sometimes it is one foot that is put forward first, sometimes the other, but continuous progress is only made by the use of both."
After all those distinguished scientists have weighed in, I think the most relevant contribution to the current discussion is the 2001 paper by Leo Breiman (statistician, 1928–2005), Statistical Modeling: The Two Cultures. In this paper Breiman, alluding to C. P. Snow, describes two cultures:
First the data modeling culture (to which, Breiman estimates, 98% of statisticians subscribe) holds that nature can be described as a black box that has a relatively simple underlying model which maps from input variables to output variables (with perhaps some random noise thrown in). It is the job of the statistician to wisely choose an underlying model that reflects the reality of nature, and then use statistical data to estimate the parameters of the model.
Second the algorithmic modeling culture (subscribed to by 2% of statisticians and many researchers in biology, artificial intelligence, and other fields that deal with complex phenomena), which holds that nature's black box cannot necessarily be described by a simple model. Complex algorithmic approaches (such as support vector machines or boosted decision trees or deep belief networks) are used to estimate the function that maps from input to output variables, but we have no expectation that the form of the function that emerges from this complex algorithm reflects the true underlying nature.
It seems that the algorithmic modeling culture is what Chomsky is objecting to most vigorously. It is not just that the models are statistical (or probabilistic), it is that they produce a form that, while accurately modeling reality, is not easily interpretable by humans, and makes no claim to correspond to the generative process used by nature. In other words, algorithmic modeling describes what does happen, but it doesn't answer the question of why.
Breiman's article explains his objections to the first culture, data modeling. Basically, the conclusions made by data modeling are about the model, not about nature. (Aside: I remember in 2000 hearing James Martin, the leader of the Viking missions to Mars, saying that his job as a spacecraft engineer was not to land on Mars, but to land on the model of Mars provided by the geologists.) The problem is, if the model does not emulate nature well, then the conclusions may be wrong. For example, linear regression is one of the most powerful tools in the statistician's toolbox. Therefore, many analyses start out with "Assume the data are generated by a linear model..." and lack sufficient analysis of what happens if the data are not in fact generated that way. In addition, for complex problems there are usually many alternative good models, each with very similar measures of goodness of fit. How is the data modeler to choose between them? Something has to give. Breiman is inviting us to give up on the idea that we can uniquely model the true underlying form of nature's function from inputs to outputs. Instead he asks us to be satisfied with a function that accounts for the observed data well, and generalizes to new, previously unseen data well, but may be expressed in a complex mathematical form that may bear no relation to the "true" function's form (if such a true function even exists). Chomsky takes the opposite approach: he prefers to keep a simple, elegant model, and give up on the idea that the model will represent the data well. Instead, he declares that what he calls performance data—what people actually do—is off limits to linguistics; what really matters is competence—what he imagines that they should do.
In January of 2011, television personality Bill O'Reilly weighed in on more than one culture war with his statement "tide goes in, tide goes out. Never a miscommunication. You can't explain that," which he proposed as an argument for the existence of God. O'Reilly was ridiculed by his detractors for not knowing that tides can be readily and concisely explained by a system of partial differential equations describing the gravitational interaction of sun, earth, and moon (a fact that was first worked out by Laplace in 1776 and has been considerably refined since; when asked by Napoleon why the creator did not enter into his calculations, Laplace said "I had no need of that hypothesis."). (O'Reilly also seems not to know about Deimos and Phobos (two of my favorite moons in the entire solar system, along with Europa, Io, and Titan), nor that Mars and Venus orbit the sun, nor that the reason Venus has no moons is because it is so close to the sun that there is scant room for a stable lunar orbit.)
But O'Reilly realizes that it doesn't matter what his detractors think of his astronomical ignorance, because his supporters think he has gotten exactly to the key issue: why? He doesn't care how the tides work, tell him why they work. Why is the moon at the right distance to provide a gentle tide, and exert a stabilizing effect on earth's axis of rotation, thus protecting life here? Why does gravity work the way it does? Why does anything at all exist rather than not exist? O'Reilly is correct that these why questions can only be addressed by mythmaking, religion or philosophy, not by science.
Chomsky has a philosophy based on the idea that we should focus on the deep whys and that mere explanations of reality don't matter. In this, Chomsky is in complete agreement with O'Reilly. (I recognize that the previous sentence would have an extremely low probability in a probabilistic model trained on a newspaper or TV corpus.) Chomsky believes a theory of language should be simple and understandable, like a linear regression model where we know the underlying process is a straight line, and all we have to do is estimate the slope and intercept.
For example, consider the notion of a pro-drop language from Chomsky's Lectures on Government and Binding (1981). In English we say, for example, "I'm hungry," expressing the pronoun "I". But in Spanish, one expresses the same thought with "Tengo hambre" (literally "have hunger"), dropping the pronoun "Yo". Chomsky's theory is that there is a "pro-drop parameter" which is "true" in Spanish and "false" in English, and that once we discover the small set of parameters that describe all languages, and the values of those parameters for each language, we will have achieved true understanding.
The problem is that reality is messier than this theory. Here are some dropped pronouns in English:
From the beginning, Chomsky has focused on the generative side of language. From this side, it is reasonable to tell a non-probabilistic story: I know definitively the idea I want to express—I'm starting from a single semantic form—thus all I have to do is choose the words to say it; why can't that be a deterministic, categorical process? If Chomsky had focused on the other side, interpretation, as Claude Shannon did, he may have changed his tune. In interpretation (such as speech recognition) the listener receives a noisy, ambiguous signal and needs to decide which of many possible intended messages is most likely. Thus, it is obvious that this is inherently a probabilistic problem, as was recognized early on by all researchers in speech recognition, and by scientists in other fields that do interpretation: the astronomer Laplace said in 1819 "Probability theory is nothing more than common sense reduced to calculation," and the physicist James Maxwell said in 1850 "The true logic for this world is the calculus of Probabilities, which takes account of the magnitude of the probability which is, or ought to be, in a reasonable man's mind."
Finally, one more reason why Chomsky dislikes statistical models is that they tend to make linguistics an empirical science (a science about how people actually use language) rather than a mathematical science (an investigation of the mathematical properties of models of formal language, not of language itself). Chomsky prefers the later, as evidenced by his statement in Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (1965):
Linguistic theory is mentalistic, since it is concerned with
discovering a mental reality underlying actual behavior. Observed use of language ... may
provide evidence ... but surely cannot constitute the subject-matter
of linguistics, if this is to be a serious discipline.
 Plato's answer was that the knowledge is 'remembered'
from an earlier existence. The answer calls for a mechanism: perhaps
the immortal soul ... rephrasing Plato's answer in terms more
congenial to us today, we will say that the basic properties of
cognitive systems are innate to the mind, part of human biological
endowment. 
It was reasonable for Plato to think that the ideal of, say, a horse, was more important than any individual horse we can perceive in the world. In 400BC, species were thought to be eternal and unchanging. We now know that is not true; that the horses on another cave wall—in Lascaux—are now extinct, and that current horses continue to evolve slowly over time. Thus there is no such thing as a single ideal eternal "horse" form.
We also now know that language is like that as well: languages are complex, random, contingent biological processes that are subject to the whims of evolution and cultural change. What constitutes a language is not an eternal ideal form, represented by the settings of a small number of parameters, but rather is the contingent outcome of complex processes. Since they are contingent, it seems they can only be analyzed with probabilistic models. Since people have to continually understand the uncertain, ambiguous, noisy speech of others, it seems they must be using something like probabilistic reasoning. Chomsky for some reason wants to avoid this, and therefore he must declare the actual facts of language use out of bounds and declare that true linguistics only exists in the mathematical realm, where he can impose the formalism he wants. Then, to get language from this abstract, eternal, mathematical realm into the heads of people, he must fabricate a mystical facility that is exactly tuned to the eternal realm. This may be very interesting from a mathematical point of view, but it misses the point about what language is, and how it works.
An excellent overall introduction to the statistical
  approach to language processing, and covers some ground that is not
  addressed often, such as language change and individual differences.
Breiman does a great job of describing the two
  approaches, explaining the benefits of his approach, and defending
  his points in the vary interesting commentary with eminent
  statisticians: Cox, Efron, Hoadley, and Parzen.
Compares finite state, phrase structure, and
  transformational grammars. Introduces "colorless green ideas sleep
  furiously."
A book-length exposition of Chomsky's theory that was
  the leading exposition of linguistics for a decade.  Claims that
  probabilistic models give no insight into syntax.
Claims that the notion "probability of a sentence" is
  an entirely useless notion.
A revision of Chomsky's theory; this version
  introduces Universal Grammar.  We cite it for the coverage of
  parameters such as pro-drop.
I found the Plato quotes in this
  article, published by the Communist Party of Great Britain, and
  apparently published by someone with no linguistics training
  whatsoever, but with a political agenda.
Gold proved a result in formal language theory that
  we can state (with some artistic license) as this: imagine a game
  between two players, guesser and chooser.  Chooser says to
  guesser, "Here is an infinite number of languages. I'm going to
  choose one of them, and start reading sentences to you that come
  from that language. On your N-th birthday there will be a True-False
  quiz where I give you 100 sentences you haven't heard yet, and you
  have to say whether they come from the language or not."  There are
  some limits on what the infinite set looks like and on how 
  the chooser can pick sentences (he can be deliberately
  tricky, but he can't just repeat the same sentence over and over,
  for example). Gold's
  result is that if the infinite set of languages are all generated by
  context-free grammars then there is no strategy for guesser that
  guarantees she gets 100% correct every time, no matter what N you
  choose for the birthday. This result was
  taken by Chomsky and others to mean that it is impossible for
  children to learn human languages without having an innate "language
  organ."  As Johnson (2004) and others show, this was an invalid
  conclusion; the task of getting 100% on the quiz (which Gold called
  language identification) 
  really has nothing in common with the task of language acquisition
  performed by children, so Gold's Theorem has no
  relevance.
Where Gold found a negative result—that
  context-free languages were not identifiable from examples, Horning found a positive result—that probabilistic
  context-free languages are identifiable (to within an arbitrarily
  small level of error).  Nobody doubts that
  humans have unique innate capabilities for understanding language
  (although it is unknown to what extent these capabilities are
  specific to language and to what extent they are general cognitive
  abilities related to sequencing and forming abstractions). But
  Horning proved in 1969 that Gold cannot be used as a convincing
  argument for an innate language organ that specifies all of language
  except for the setting of a few parameters.
The best article I've seen on what Gold's Theorem
  actually says and what has been claimed about it (correctly and
  incorrectly).  Concludes that Gold has something to say about formal
  languages, but nothing about child language
  acquisition.
An excellent article discussing the poverty of the
  stimulus, the fact that all models have bias,  the difference
  between supervised and unsupervised learning, and modern (PAC or VC)
  learning theory. It provides
  alternatives to the model of Universal Grammar consisting of a fixed
  set of binary parameters.
A compelling introduction to probabilistic syntax,
  and how it is a better model for linguistic facts than categorical
  syntax. Covers "the joys and perils of corpus
  linguistics."
Shows working code to implement a probabilistic,
  statistical spelling correction algorithm.
Expands on the essay above; shows how to implement
  three tasks: text segmentation, cryptographic decoding, and spelling
  correction (in a slightly more complete form than the previous essay).
When I set out to write the page you are reading now,
  I was concentrating on the events that took place in Cambridge,
  Mass., 4800 km from home.  After doing some research I was surprised
  to learn that the authors of
  two of the three best articles on this subject sit within a total of
  10 meters from my desk: Fernando Pereira and Chris Manning. (The
  third, Steve Abney, sits 3700 km away.) But perhaps I shouldn't have
  been surprised. I remember giving a talk at ACL on the corpus-based
  language models used at Google, and having Fernando, then a
  professor at U. Penn., comment "I feel like I'm a particle physicist
  and you've got the only super-collider."  A few years later he moved
  to Google. Fernando is also famous for his quote "The older I get, the
  further down the Chomsky Hierarchy I go." His article here covers
  some of the same ground as mine, but he goes farther in explaining
  the range of probabilistic models available and how they are useful.
Cited here for the allegory of the cave.
An enormously influential article that started the
  field of information theory and introduced the term "bit" and the noisy
  channel model, demonstrated successive n-gram approximations of
  English, described Markov models of language, defined entropy with
  respect to these models, and enabled the growth of the
  telecommunications industry.

articles.title: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
articles.body:
GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents
A cybersecurity model trained to find and validate exploitable vulnerabilities, while staying within the scope that researchers set.
We’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.
On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.
These capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities(opens in a new window). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure.
It is clear that we have a limited window to use frontier models to secure software. Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.
GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.
On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, about 16 percentage points higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s 32.1%. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities compared with 32.0% for GPT‑6 Astra.
Daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused 100% of tasks, while GPT‑6 Cyber completed 95%; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the system card(opens in a new window) for full results and evaluation settings.
One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.
We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the system card(opens in a new window) for full results.
One of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the Hugging Face incident. We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.
GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.
We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:
GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:
We have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models. In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report issues to maintainers and vendors.
Our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years:
- Found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and showed that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports(opens in a new window).
- Developing exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities. GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed.
- Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities. We recently discussed a critical vulnerability in Brotli(opens in a new window), a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications.
As models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s intent and authorization.
We added and strengthened these protections alongside the release of GPT‑6 Cyber (see the system card(opens in a new window) for full information):
- Cyber-specific misalignment monitoring. We monitor whether actions match the user’s authorization, while recognizing legitimate exploit development and testing.
- Targeted monitoring for emerging threats. For example, during the coordinated disclosure of critical PHP vulnerabilities, we set up targeted monitoring for attempts to develop exploits against live PHP servers, while preserving support for defenders patching affected systems.
- Private Safety Processing (PSP). We use automated checks to review related interactions for misuse. Standard retention remains the default. API customers using Zero Data Retention(opens in a new window) generally must use PSP(opens in a new window), which reviews encrypted records retained in customer storage for 30 days without exposing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel.
- Protection against stolen credentials. We require IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default, restricting requests to approved networks with limited exceptions. We also monitor credentials for compromise.
- Sandboxing and oversight. As with past models, we recommend sandboxing(opens in a new window), action review(opens in a new window), and human oversight for high-risk workflows.
- Protections against high-risk cyber assistance. We use new checks to block high-risk activity involving critical systems (see below for more).
Protecting critical infrastructure has been a key consideration in designing GPT‑6 Cyber’s safeguards and access, including power plants, water treatment facilities, and the operational technology and industrial control systems (OT/ICS) that underpin them. We simultaneously want to give the teams defending these systems access to our most capable models while also strengthening our safeguards to prevent unauthorized attacks.
First, to equip these defenders, our $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders grant program subsidizes access for resource-constrained teams such as government organizations and essential service providers. We’re also introducing a new group within Daybreak Red (Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure) for approved critical infrastructure defenders, which gives them permissions to conduct authorized testing of critical systems while retaining safeguards against model misalignment.
Second, to prevent misuse of the Daybreak Red and Blue platforms, we have refined safeguards against assistance and capability development that could compromise industrial controls or safety-critical systems, interfere with equipment, or cause serious injury, catastrophic physical damage, or life-endangering service disruption. The figure below compares safeguard label rates across four access configurations, before and after the recent updates we’re rolling out alongside GPT‑6 Cyber.
Higher safeguard block rates are not always better. Many of the techniques in this evaluation are also essential to legitimate security work: understanding systems, finding vulnerabilities, and verifying that fixes withstand attack. We therefore assess these rates alongside support for legitimate research and patching, rather than aiming for 100%.
To evaluate how our models can help defend critical infrastructure, we partnered with Dragos, the global provider for extended operational technology (xOT) cybersecurity. Dragos ran evaluations using cyber-permissive Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab environment. The evaluations covered requests progressing from network discovery and asset enumeration through targeted reconnaissance, sensitive data exfiltration, and unauthorized, potentially dangerous device actions.
We used feedback from Dragos to refine our safeguards, aiming to block harmful assistance without unnecessarily restricting authorized testing. See their final report(opens in a new window) for details on the evaluations. We’re also working to expand partnerships with other offensive security providers and purple teams on penetration testing and red teaming with AI, and with energy companies, other critical infrastructure operators, and national labs to assess our models’ effectiveness and safeguards in industrial defense. We have also increased our investment in threat investigations to detect model usage involving OT/ICS. We’ll continue refining our safeguards with input from partners and the security community, including reports through /feedback when safeguards miss harmful activity or interrupt legitimate work.
GPT‑6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. We will progressively expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon, and are also making GPT‑5.6 Cyber available to all Daybreak Red customers. We’re also expanding Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT‑6 Astra to more organizations and individual security researchers; let us know(opens in a new window) if you’re interested.
New users and organizations can apply for Daybreak and get started with our cyber skills, products, and partners.

articles.title: Meta, Google, and TikTok sue California AG over teen social media law
articles.body:
Meta, Google, and TikTok have each filed lawsuits against California Attorney General Rob Bonta in an attempt to block a law that restricts social media features it deems addictive for users under 16.
California Governor Gavin Newsom signed the bill, known as AB 1709, into law in September, and it’s slated to take effect at the start of the new year.
The law prohibits social platforms from offering autoplay videos and personalized feeds to users under 16, and it requires the platforms to delete these users’ accounts if they don’t turn those features off. If platforms do not comply, they could be liable for fines of up to $50,000 per affected user under 16 years old.
Meta claims that AB 1709 violates the First Amendment by overriding its editorial decisions about how to display content, adding that Section 230 preempts the law. TikTok and Google made similar arguments.
“Meta currently organizes its feeds of content to include personalized content recommendations and to automatically play media, [so] the Act would make it unlawful for Meta to disseminate speech to minors altogether, and would require Meta to delete minors’ accounts, unless it changes these practices,” the company wrote in its lawsuit.
In an emailed statement, a TikTok spokesperson added, “AB 1709 is a blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which book stores, TV networks and streaming services all use.”
AB 1709 follows a trend of legislation around the world that seeks to curb teen social media use in an attempt to improve teen mental health outcomes. However, digital safety experts often caution against these laws because they can inadvertently compromise the privacy of all platform users, including adults, by requiring age verification checks that collect more user data.
“AB 1709 compels platforms to collect even more information from every user, invading everyone’s privacy and frustrating our ability to remain anonymous online,” EFF Associate Director of State Affairs Rindala Alajaji said in a press briefing. “Online surveillance by social media companies is harmful, and yet this bill requires even more of it, further concentrating power in the hands of tech companies rather than actually protecting users.”
Alajaji added that teenagers’ use of social media has been instrumental in enabling impactful digital activism, citing the Parkland shooting survivors’ March for Our Lives and climate activist Greta Thunberg’s global reach.
“As a functional ban on social media for youth under 16, AB 1709 cuts young people off from essential information and experiences, silencing the very voices it claims to protect,” Alajaji said.
These platforms are primed to fight this California law as they navigate similar legal battles in various countries. That’s especially true for Meta, which agreed to pay a settlement of up to $18 billion to resolve children’s safety claims brought by 29 U.S. states.
In December 2025, Australia became the first country to ban social media for users under 16 altogether. France passed a similar law, but its top court struck it down, citing concerns about violations of free expression rights.
These platforms also argue that the law would affect parents’ ability to make decisions about their teens’ internet use through parental controls.
A Google spokesperson noted that autoplay on YouTube is turned off for minors by default, and that parents have the ability to turn off their teens’ access to Shorts altogether.
“We believe parents are best positioned to make the right decisions for their families, which is why we offer a range of protections and tools that put parents in control,” a Google spokesperson said. “Overly broad laws like this actually break the systems we’ve built to help kids find high-quality, age-appropriate videos.”
A representative for Attorney General Bonta said that his office is reviewing the filings and is committed to “defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online.”

articles.title: Motorola Signature 27 with GrapheneOS support
articles.body:
Motorola, a Lenovo Company, is designing to a higher standard with the new motorola signature 27, the company’s most advanced flagship smartphone to date, bringing together distinctive design, category-leading innovation and next-generation AI experiences. From its contoured edges, expressive finishes and refined craftsmanship to the breakthrough technologies within, every detail of the motorola signature 27 was purposefully built to deliver a premium experience without compromise. Featuring Motorola’s most advanced camera system yet, recognized with a DXOMARK Gold Label for image quality performance, the brightest Extreme AMOLED Duo Tandem display¹ available in a smartphone, the Snapdragon® 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 Mobile Platform, making it among the first smartphones to unlock next-generation connectivity and AI experiences, and the only smartphone in-market with Audio by Bang & Olufsen, the motorola signature 27 represents the pinnacle of Motorola innovation.
Motorola’s best camera system yet, recognized for imaging excellence
The motorola signature 27 includes the world’s best camera sytsem launched in 202625, combining advanced hardware, cinematic video, and effortless photography. Awarded the coveted DXOMARK Gold Label in recognition of its industry-leading level of imaging quality performance and outranking all other Android and iOS devices, the motorola signature 27’s camera system delivers eye-catching photos and videos, with:
- A 50MP Sony LYTIA L910 main camera captures exceptional clarity, rich color and deep contrast for vibrant, ready to share results. Combined with LOFIC technology, it records brighter, more balanced video with consistent detail across challenging lighting conditions, whether filming concert stages, neon-lit streets, candlelit dinners or nights out with friends.
- A 200MP periscope telephoto camera with 100x Super Zoom captures everything from distant landmarks and architectural details to wildlife and action unfolding far away with remarkable clarity. Powered by AI, 100x Super Zoom Pro helps preserve natural color, sharpness and details even at extreme distances. The 3x periscope telephoto lens also delivers flattering, natural-looking portraits, while ultra-resolution imaging provides greater flexibility for cropping, reframing, and editing.
- The first ever dedicated EVS action sensor on a smartphone² introduces a new approach to smartphone motion photography, helping capture fast-moving subjects with greater clarity and precision. Working together with the Action Shot feature, it freezes motion while maximizing available light, producing crisp, vibrant images with richer detail and more natural color.
- The 50MP ultrawide camera³ fits more into every frame, transforming tight spaces into expansive compositions and making it easier to capture sweeping landscapes, large landmarks and group photos without stepping back.
- And a 50MP front camera delivers sharp, ready-to-share selfies and supports 4K video recording, so selfie videos feature the same bold colors and clarity as still photos.
For a more cinematic video experience, the motorola signature 27 features a powerful Video Enhancement Engine that uses AI to intelligently optimize color, contrast and dynamic range in real time. Support for Dolby Vision®, the same technology used by leading filmmakers, helps enable richer, more immersive video. Combined with the Qualcomm® Electronic Image Stabilization and 3.5° OIS hardware on the main camera, panning, walking, and handheld recording looks more fluid and stable, so users can stay in the moment while the camera does the hard work.
the brightest display available in a smartphone20
Engineered to unlock the full potential of the latest advances in display technology, the motorola signature 27 features a new Extreme AMOLED Duo display, the brightest display available, designed to provide a premium viewing experience in virtually any environment.
Built with breakthrough Tandem Technology, it combines two emissive layers into one, producing brighter visuals, richer color and greater efficiency. With up to 12,0004 nits of peak brightness, users can comfortably view maps, messages, photos and videos virtually anywhere, whether navigating a sunny afternoon, checking directions on the go or capturing content outdoors, without needing to shield the screen or strain to see it. Plus, 1.5K Super HD resolution and Dolby Vision® bring entertainment to life with exceptional sharpness, contrast and precision.
This advanced display is also designed to be smarter and more durable, delivering up to 34% greater energy efficiency and up to a 121% longer lifespan than traditional AMOLED panels.24 Pantone® Validated color calibration ensures colors and skin tones appear true to life5, while SGS-certified blue light technology helps reduce eye strain.
powering next generation experiences
At the heart of the motorola signature 27 is the Snapdragon® 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 Mobile Platform, making it among the first smartphones to feature Qualcomm Technologies’ latest flagship mobile chipset. Engineered to power breakthrough gaming, advanced camera experiences, ultra-fast connectivity and AI, it delivers the performance needed for today’s most demanding mobile experiences and the next wave of AI innovation.
To sustain peak performance when it matters most, the motorola signature 27 pairs the platform with Motorola’s ArcticMesh cooling system that uses micro-diamond-infused thermal gel and a thermal chamber that is 40% larger than the previous generation⁶ to keep performance running at its best during extended gaming sessions, AI tasks, video recording and intensive multitasking. With a new 6‑antenna design delivering faster 5G downloads, up to 2x faster Wi‑Fi speeds6, Wi‑Fi 8 compatibility, the motorola signature 27 is built to stay fast, capable and ready for next-era AI. And seven years of OS upgrades23 help ensure the experience stays reliable long into the future.
AI that goes beyond assistance
The motorola signature 27 is designed for Gemini Intelligence, which brings the best of Gemini to Android’s most advanced devices, alongside out-of-box Google Gemini experiences and Motorola Qira.
The motorola signature 27 can understand context, help people create, support decisions and move from intention to action across the apps and services they use every day. As Google rolls out these capabilities to Gemini Intelligence⁷ devices globally in the coming months, motorola signature 27 will be ready to bring them to users around the world:
- Whether booking a ride or preparing a grocery order from a shopping list on your screen, Gemini helps users go from intention to action with less effort. Gemini can handle complex, multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf, reducing app switching and helping them stay focused on what matters. Users remain in control throughout, with the ability to view progress, jump in, or stop a task.16
- Rambler17 transforms natural speech into polished messages, letting users think out loud while it refines their words in the background. Rambler removes filler words, edits repetition, and organizes ideas into clear paragraphs or bullet points. Users can correct themselves mid-sentence, switch languages seamlessly, and review everything before sending, ensuring they share exactly what they intend. Afterwards, users can quickly ask Rambler to rewrite, rephrase, translate, or reformat their text.
- Create My Widget18 enables users to create personalized widgets by simply describing what they want to see. Whether it’s a tracker to follow your monthly spending, daily recipe inspiration, or a trip countdown with your travel details, your homescreen can be as personalized as you want it to be.
- Sign-to-Text19 translates American Sign Language (ASL) into written English in real time using the device’s front-facing camera. Integrated with Gboard and Live Transcribe, it opens new ways for users to communicate across digital and in-person interactions.
Right out of the box, the motorola signature 27 also includes powerful Google Gemini⁸ experiences designed to bring new levels of creativity, including Gemini Omni, which enables users to create and edit video through natural conversation, and Lyria which generates custom soundtracks from simple prompts.
In addition, the device features Motorola Qira⁹, a built-in AI system designed to connect and enhance experiences across supported Motorola and Lenovo devices, helping users get more from their broader ecosystem through a single, seamless hybrid AI experience.
the only smartphone with “Audio by Bang & Olufsen”
As the only smartphone in-market to feature Audio by Bang & Olufsen, the motorola signature 27 unlocks an elevated audio experience built on Motorola’s recently announced multi-year partnership with Bang & Olufsen. Combining Motorola’s premium mobile innovation with Bang & Olufsen’s renowned expertise in sound and design, the device is engineered to deliver sound that is meant to be felt, not just heard. Featuring dedicated Sound Modes and an all-new speaker architecture, the device is tuned to preserve the character of the original recording, alongside deep bass, clear vocals and greater fidelity across music, movies and games.
distinctive design, exceptional durability
With the motorola signature 27, Motorola continues the evolution of its signature family design philosophy, that balances aesthetic expression with everyday usability. The device features a sleek aluminum silhouette with contoured edges and a thin profile that feels comfortable in hand, while delivering a distinctly premium look and feel. Complementing the refined design is a seamlessly integrated camera plane, finished in smooth ceramic and brushed aluminum, creating a sophisticated focal point that feels both purposeful and modern.
Precisely crafted with a ceramic and glass construction, the motorola signature 27 is available in two unique, elevated finishes: PANTONE Coal Smoke, which features a tactical weave finish inspired by automotive design and performance materials, and PANTONE Capulet Olive, which features a textile-inspired finish influenced by premium fashion and interior design.
Premium materials and durability come together in the motorola signature 27, featuring Corning® Gorilla® Glass Ceramic 3, an aerospace-grade aluminum frame, military-grade durability (MIL-STD-810H)10, and IP68 and IP69 ratings for enhanced protection against the elements.22
power that gives the freedom to do more
To back up all this powerful innovation, the motorola signature 27 features a 7000mAh battery11, 35% larger than the last generation, so users can stay connected longer, stream and create without interruption, and move through the day without constantly thinking about battery life.
When battery does get low, 90W TurboPower™ charging quickly restores power for the day in just 12 minutes12,13, whether on a coffee break or while getting ready. For a more effortless experience, users can go cord-free with 50W wireless charging, powering 0 to 100% in up to 80 minutes of wireless charging.12,14
Motorola’s first GrapheneOS-supported device, built for privacy and peace of mind
Data privacy matters, and Motorola continues to build on its commitment to security with ThinkShield®, which helps protect users from the factory to the phone, and Moto Secure, a centralized destination for managing privacy and security features.
Expanding that commitment even further, the motorola signature 27 will kickstart a new era of smartphone privacy and security. It will be Motorola’s first device to support GrapheneOS, a hardened, open-source operating system based on the Android Open Source Project. Developed in partnership with the GrapheneOS Foundation, the leading nonprofit in advanced mobile security, the device reflects Motorola’s commitment to bringing cutting-edge security to everyday users across the globe.
That commitment runs deeper than software: GrapheneOS sets demanding requirements for the hardware it runs on and how it’s kept updated, and the motorola signature 27 is built to meet them. The device is Motorola’s first with a performant implementation of ARM Memory Tagging Extension, a new hardware caching mechanism for helping ensure system integrity and privacy. More details on it will be shared in the coming months.
Availability
Motorola signature 27 will be available in markets worldwide in the coming months, with a starting MSRP of $1,599. For local price information and availability, please contact your local PR team.
