articles.title: My gym forced a social media down my throat. So I reverse-engineered its app
articles.body:
My gym forced a social media down my throat. I reverse-engineered its app.
I recently joined a new gym. It’s a pretty good gym, with nice equipment, nice management, nice branding.
And an app.
Now, it’s not some random shitty vibe-coded app. It’s actually pretty good as a product. It has pretty slick UI/UX and a well-thought-out, consistent design language. I found only one bug in it.
For me, though, the only use case is to show a QR code at the turnstile for checking in and out.
However, there is a problem. The home screen of the app is a social feed. Once you check out, it prompts you to post a story of your session. The home feed is full of people’s gym selfies. Every time I open the app, I’m forced to see something that essentially looks like Tinder.
Now, my friend thinks this is a genius business idea. According to her, people who work out really want to flaunt their bodies, but posting that on normal social media is frowned upon. So this gym company really found a good product-market fit.
I think she’s right.
However, I’m super aggressive about social media and feeds I don’t control. Any app that shows me a feed I can’t turn off, sort, or filter—I take that as psychological warfare against me.
I haven’t used social media in more than 12 years. I’m super adamant about blocking ads, blocking YouTube comments, Shorts, and suggested videos, and sanitizing YouTube titles and thumbnails. For things I must use, like LinkedIn1, I use browser extensions to block the news feed completely.
So I took it personally.
I wanted to see if I could extract the QR-code logic without all the extra bloat of the app.
So I started digging. I quickly found out that the code changes every 15 seconds. Screenshots are also blocked on that screen, consistent with Android’s FLAG_SECURE. I wondered if it was some kind of TOTP. Was the generation happening server-side?
I did the simplest thing: turned off Wi-Fi. The app immediately told me the codes would remain valid for N days without reconnecting2.
Okay, so it could generate them locally.
I used GLM 5.3 and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. In my sessions, GLM was burning something like 10–20 times as much in token cost without making that much progress. DeepSeek seemed to move much faster.
To be clear, I’m leaving out some details to keep the gym and myself anonymous. I don’t want to lose my gym subscription. I actually like that gym.
The app was written in Flutter, with most of the logic compiled into Dart native code. We used blutter to inspect that, jadx for the Android-side code, and Android’s SDK tools to inspect the package. Later, we used OpenSSL and WebCrypto to check the encryption, and zbar to decode the QR codes independently.
I was prompting DeepSeek here and there, mostly from intuition, because I’d never done this before. Sometimes it seemed to get lost in a direction where I felt the implementation must be simpler than that. Just telling it my guesses, or saying that I thought there must be a simpler way, helped steer it in the right direction.
We quickly understood that the QR code was a URL containing four things: an encoded account handle, an encrypted expiry timestamp, a random nonce, and a checksum.
The expiry was encrypted using AES-128-CTR. A separate secret was used to calculate the checksum. So we needed those two secrets for my account.
My first idea was to let DeepSeek drive an Android emulator, sign in, and extract the keys. But I quickly realized that my ten-year-old laptop, borrowed from a friend, wasn’t going to handle Android software emulation at any reasonable speed.
DeepSeek suggested a rooted phone. That’s when I remembered I had a functional rooted Android phone lying around.
I booted it, connected over wireless ADB, and let DeepSeek investigate. It turned out that the app logged the request and response payloads for the calls we cared about. The key material was sitting in a plain text log file on the phone.
Half of this project was ripgrep.
With the keys extracted, we built a simple SvelteKit web app to generate the QR codes.
There were a few wrong assumptions along the way. The expiry timestamp needed to be in milliseconds, not seconds. The encoding was base64url, not standard base64, and it kept the padding.
We also had an incorrect AES implementation that passed its own round-trip tests. It encrypted something, decrypted it, and got the original input back. But both directions shared the same mistakes, so that didn’t prove it was AES.
Comparing against WebCrypto exposed the discrepancy. OpenSSL and known test vectors confirmed it. The browser app uses WebCrypto.
We then checked against actual output from the original app. Given the same inputs, our implementation produced a byte-identical URL. We also decoded the QR image independently to check that it contained the right URL.
At that point, we had a working prototype. The web app could generate the codes locally from the extracted keys. This didn’t solve standalone login or remove the need to obtain fresh keys when they rotated, but it was enough to try it at the gym.
The next day, I headed there, very proudly showing my friend what I’d built, but still a bit uncertain whether it would work at the gate.
And voilà, it did!
Check-in and check-out.
No more being forced to get my attention hijacked by dark-patterned, manipulative social media just to enter an establishment to lift some metals.
Footnotes
- For the longest time, my LinkedIn bio was “I HATE LINKEDIN.” Someone told me LinkedIn combines the worst of the corporate world with the worst of social media, and I think that only half describes how bad it really is. But alas, I’m in the job market right now, and I need a LinkedIn profile for applications.↩
- I’m not revealing the exact number of days to help keep the app anonymous.↩

articles.title: My gym forced a social media down my throat. So I reverse-engineered its app
articles.body:
My gym forced a social media down my throat. I reverse-engineered its app.
I recently joined a new gym. It’s a pretty good gym, with nice equipment, nice management, nice branding.
And an app.
Now, it’s not some random shitty vibe-coded app. It’s actually pretty good as a product. It has pretty slick UI/UX and a well-thought-out, consistent design language. I found only one bug in it.
For me, though, the only use case is to show a QR code at the turnstile for checking in and out.
However, there is a problem. The home screen of the app is a social feed. Once you check out, it prompts you to post a story of your session. The home feed is full of people’s gym selfies. Every time I open the app, I’m forced to see something that essentially looks like Tinder.
Now, my friend thinks this is a genius business idea. According to her, people who work out really want to flaunt their bodies, but posting that on normal social media is frowned upon. So this gym company really found a good product-market fit.
I think she’s right.
However, I’m super aggressive about social media and feeds I don’t control. Any app that shows me a feed I can’t turn off, sort, or filter—I take that as psychological warfare against me.
I haven’t used social media in more than 12 years. I’m super adamant about blocking ads, blocking YouTube comments, Shorts, and suggested videos, and sanitizing YouTube titles and thumbnails. For things I must use, like LinkedIn1, I use browser extensions to block the news feed completely.
So I took it personally.
I wanted to see if I could extract the QR-code logic without all the extra bloat of the app.
So I started digging. I quickly found out that the code changes every 15 seconds. Screenshots are also blocked on that screen, consistent with Android’s FLAG_SECURE. I wondered if it was some kind of TOTP. Was the generation happening server-side?
I did the simplest thing: turned off Wi-Fi. The app immediately told me the codes would remain valid for N days without reconnecting2.
Okay, so it could generate them locally.
I used GLM 5.3 and DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. In my sessions, GLM was burning something like 10–20 times as much in token cost without making that much progress. DeepSeek seemed to move much faster.
To be clear, I’m leaving out some details to keep the gym and myself anonymous. I don’t want to lose my gym subscription. I actually like that gym.
The app was written in Flutter, with most of the logic compiled into Dart native code. We used blutter to inspect that, jadx for the Android-side code, and Android’s SDK tools to inspect the package. Later, we used OpenSSL and WebCrypto to check the encryption, and zbar to decode the QR codes independently.
I was prompting DeepSeek here and there, mostly from intuition, because I’d never done this before. Sometimes it seemed to get lost in a direction where I felt the implementation must be simpler than that. Just telling it my guesses, or saying that I thought there must be a simpler way, helped steer it in the right direction.
We quickly understood that the QR code was a URL containing four things: an encoded account handle, an encrypted expiry timestamp, a random nonce, and a checksum.
The expiry was encrypted using AES-128-CTR. A separate secret was used to calculate the checksum. So we needed those two secrets for my account.
My first idea was to let DeepSeek drive an Android emulator, sign in, and extract the keys. But I quickly realized that my ten-year-old laptop, borrowed from a friend, wasn’t going to handle Android software emulation at any reasonable speed.
DeepSeek suggested a rooted phone. That’s when I remembered I had a functional rooted Android phone lying around.
I booted it, connected over wireless ADB, and let DeepSeek investigate. It turned out that the app logged the request and response payloads for the calls we cared about. The key material was sitting in a plain text log file on the phone.
Half of this project was ripgrep.
With the keys extracted, we built a simple SvelteKit web app to generate the QR codes.
There were a few wrong assumptions along the way. The expiry timestamp needed to be in milliseconds, not seconds. The encoding was base64url, not standard base64, and it kept the padding.
We also had an incorrect AES implementation that passed its own round-trip tests. It encrypted something, decrypted it, and got the original input back. But both directions shared the same mistakes, so that didn’t prove it was AES.
Comparing against WebCrypto exposed the discrepancy. OpenSSL and known test vectors confirmed it. The browser app uses WebCrypto.
We then checked against actual output from the original app. Given the same inputs, our implementation produced a byte-identical URL. We also decoded the QR image independently to check that it contained the right URL.
At that point, we had a working prototype. The web app could generate the codes locally from the extracted keys. This didn’t solve standalone login or remove the need to obtain fresh keys when they rotated, but it was enough to try it at the gym.
The next day, I headed there, very proudly showing my friend what I’d built, but still a bit uncertain whether it would work at the gate.
And voilà, it did!
Check-in and check-out.
No more being forced to get my attention hijacked by dark-patterned, manipulative social media just to enter an establishment to lift some metals.
Footnotes
- For the longest time, my LinkedIn bio was “I HATE LINKEDIN.” Someone told me LinkedIn combines the worst of the corporate world with the worst of social media, and I think that only half describes how bad it really is. But alas, I’m in the job market right now, and I need a LinkedIn profile for applications.↩

articles.title: The Verge’s 2026 holiday gift guide
articles.body:
Gift-giving isn’t just about grabbing something solid under a determined spending limit. It’s an expression of love, a way to show someone how well you really know them. That doesn’t mean you have to do it all on your own, though. Sometimes you just need a push in the right direction to get things rolling.
The Verge’s 2026 holiday gift guide
Our latest holiday cheat sheet is jam-packed with our favorite tech, along with Play-Doh, vinyl, and plenty of analog picks.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
This year, we spent hours collecting our favorites to help you get ahead of your holiday shopping. This list has everything: minimalist smart rings, Play-Doh flowers, sleek beat machines — you name it. Whatever your needs, no matter how demanding the recipient, you’ll find something exceptional below for that special someone on your list.
Most of us have thousands of photos in the cloud, but if a photo never makes it into the real world, did it really happen? Existentialism aside, the Cricut StickerPix offers a new way to play with photos, providing you with everything you need to turn any picture into a pro-quality print or sticker.
AirPods 5
If you’re a fan of Apple’s open-ear standard AirPods, the AirPods 5 are the best model yet. The higher-end pair (there are two models) offers upgraded sound, better noise cancellation, and swipe-based volume controls, bringing some Pro-level features to the buds that started the wire-free revolution.
Busy Bar
It’s rare for a product to boast that it’s “hacker-friendly,” but the Busy Bar isn’t your average device. Equipped with a pixelated LED screen, fantastically fun buttons, and intriguing ways to play, Flipper’s open-source productivity tool breeds efficiency by, among other things, keeping coworkers from interrupting your flow with their weekend plans.
Espresso in the woods? Yes, please. The GR2’s magical mechanics make it possible, letting you turn 12 ounces of grounds into espresso without power. Its carrying case houses all the accessories needed to get that sweet shot of bean, making real coffee available virtually anywhere.
Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo
Digital photos changed everything, but there’s still something wonderful about the visceral touch and nostalgia of analog. Fujifilm’s Instax Mini Evo provides an intriguing hybrid that bridges these worlds, with a retro design, intuitive dials and controls, and the ability to filter like it’s 1989 (or 1889?).
TP-Link Roam 7 portable router
What if you could give the gift of stress-free Wi-Fi on the go? That’s the promise of TP-Link’s dual-band Roam 7, a portable Wi-Fi 7 router that simplifies connecting to public portals so travelers can connect everything to a single device and be done with it.
For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.
The company that brought gaming to the masses still defies the odds, thanks in large part to its creative roots. Those roots run deep, and journalist Keza MacDonald’s fascinating book traces them to their source, from a simple card game company to the minds behind the biggest hits of all time.
Akai MPC Sample
You can give the gift of creativity with this do-it-all digital music maker. Akai’s portable sampler, beat maker, and all-around sound machine blends tactile quick keys and pads with an onboard screen so musicians can build it all in a box and send the results to their DAW of choice.
For those who enjoy clever devices that just work, we give you Nimble’s “breakable” SharePower Portable Charger. The magnetically joined power bank quickly snaps into a pair of 20W batteries, letting two people charge their phones, or works as a single 10,000mAh unit for larger top-offs.
New Zealand artist Aldous Harding has another eccentric album on her hands with this year’s Train on the Island. The slow-burning LP is gorgeously recorded and delightfully weird, and it feels tailor-made for vinyl, making it an easy pick for Harding fans (or anyone who loves quirky indie jams).
For those in smaller dwellings, efficient living means maximizing space. That’s where combo appliances like Ninja’s newest microwave / air fryer combo come in. The handy countertop gadget lets you zap your food, then crisp it at the end so your pizza or French fries don’t turn into a soggy mess.
Perhaps no game in history is more anticipated than the latest entry in Rockstar’s sprawling, intricate, and absolutely bonkers open-world series. Grand Theft Auto VI is said to offer a more obsessively dense map, more realism in details like weather and passing time, and more realistic NPCs (non-player characters) than ever before. Here’s hoping those 13 years were worth the wait.
Open-style earbuds aren’t just for the sporty; they’re an entirely different way to listen that keeps you environmentally aware without the plugged-up feeling of traditional buds. The OpenFit Pro take a balanced approach, with seamless open-ear performance and even a touch of noise reduction to dampen the din on crowded commutes.
The old Ironman Timex was a staple for ’80s and ’90s kids, and while you can’t bring back those carefree days, remakes like the Retroware can bring back that carefree feeling. No smarts, no notifications, just a takes-a-licking Timex watch with tactile keys, 50 meters of water resistance, and totally tubular digital graphics.
Serious gamers need a serious controller, and few take gaming more seriously than 8BitDo’s Elite-style Xbox gamepad. From its drift-proof TMR joysticks and motion support to its customizable buttons and remappable bumpers, the Ultimate 3E is the gift for that lovable control freak in your life.
Play-Doh Blooms
There’s regular Play-Doh for kids, but did you know that Play-Doh makes kits for adults, too? We’re not scoffing. The new Blooms sets take on Lego’s floral bouquets with more realistic-looking flower arrangements, and they include a vase. They’re equal parts nostalgic kitsch and stylish decor.
For on-the-go content creators, it’s all about capturing the moment in the highest video quality possible. Insta360’s Luna Pro steadycam offers plenty of features to get the job done right, including 4K vertical video, swift file transfers, four hours of battery life, and a detachable touchscreen that conveniently doubles as a remote.
The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.
Most mobile controllers have a serious size limit. Not Razer’s Kishi V3 Pro XL, which lets you throw a big ol’ tablet between the handles for a major visual upgrade. It also has high-quality joysticks, great grips, and customizable keys for USB-C tablets, along with haptics for Android models.
KPop Demon Hunters (4K Blu-ray)
So what if you’ve heard “Golden” more times than you can count? Netflix’s massive animated hit is a lot easier to gift now that it’s officially available on 4K Blu-ray disc. The story about three pop stars who band together to save humanity from a demonic boy band is an instant classic, with fantastic music and striking animation.
If you’re contemplating a pricey pair of sleep buds for your loved one, we urge you to halt and consider a softer (and cheaper) alternative. Piercing pillows, designed with pockets for freshly pierced ears, also work great for regular earbuds. Blissbury’s comfy and adjustable Ear Pillow is our favorite. Problem — and sleep issues — solved.
The Concrete Edition of Keychron’s K2 HE is not your average mechanical board. Cased in actual concrete, it offers standard keycaps to match its industrial aesthetic, both Bluetooth and 2.4GHz connectivity, and several other advanced features. This includes the ability to adjust the actuation distance of the individual Hall effect switches (hence the “HE”).
We all do it: pay a ton for a monthly streaming service for just a few series. It’s better to own the real thing, and Hacks, a hilarious drama that follows a comedian (Jean Smart) and her young writer (Hannah Einbinder) in the tumultuous “biz,” is one of HBO’s best series in years.
Hoto’s soldering iron is super cool — and by that we mean hot, as it’s able to reach nearly 400 degrees Fahrenheit in about three seconds. The cordless, adjustable iron makes the perfect gift for your favorite DIYer, especially since it features customizable presets for virtually any job.
Knockaround Premiums sunglasses
For the person on your list whose hatred for smart glasses runs deep, Knockaround’s hip, tech-free sunglasses should hit the spot. They’re available in a variety of fun styles and offer lightweight frames and polarized lenses, with both UVA and UVB shielding for attractive eye protection.
The first 3D Zelda game has been remade for the modern era. And if you fear it will diverge too much from the Nintendo 64 original, fear not: This carefully crafted remake delivers updated graphics and improved controls alongside the same stellar adventure we remember.
Wuben G5 rechargeable flashlight
Everyone needs a good flashlight, and perhaps your recipient’s next one should ditch the replaceable batteries. Wuben’s rechargeable G5 has a pocketable, spy-tech-inspired design, USB-C charging, and adjustable brightness. More importantly, the 400-lumen light is super compact, making it easy to stow or clip onto your bag.
If you haven’t been bombarded by the Hulken yet, it’s a rolling tote that’s blown up online. Designed to hold everything from laundry to an impromptu picnic, the durable bag is beloved for its seemingly bottomless capacity and colorful style, making it a thoughtful gift for fashionable folks on the move.
Xteink X4 Pro e-reader
If a Kindle won’t quite fit into your favorite traveler’s tight pack job, consider the Xteink X4 Pro. The tiny e-reader is easy to pop into your bag or pocket thanks to its 4.3-inch display, and the latest model offers a backlit touchscreen for a more intuitive way to explore the literary world.
For the coffee or tea lover in your life who’s always headed to the microwave for a heat zap, Ember’s fancy-schmancy smart mug is a luxurious way to keep things toasty. With the ability to set the temperature on the mug or in the app, the Mug 3 makes it simple to keep liquids perfectly hot indefinitely.
Not all reusable water bottles are created equal. Give the gift of a narrow-mouthed bottle, like this 16-ounce Nalgene pick, which makes it easy to take measured sips on the go. Take this advice from someone (me) who bought the wide-mouthed version and regularly spills water all over themself.
If your giftee is into New York City memorabilia or wants a more unique way to light up a room, this cube-shaped lamp, designed around the old MTA entrance beacons, is sure to delight. Locals will recognize the vintage symbol, which still survives in the wild, and everyone will dig the old-school vibe.
Pokémon Pokopia
Pokopia brings Pokémon to life in a cozy worldbuilding game that borrows the best from predecessors like Minecraft and Animal Crossing. The twist? The slow-burning Switch 2 title eventually rolls into an expansive adventure that lets you customize as you go.
Petkit Fresh Element Solo Automatic Feeder
When it comes to keeping your pet happy and healthy while you’re away, the details matter. Petkit’s most basic auto feeder offers peace of mind with dual-power protection, meal monitoring via the Petkit app, and a generous 12-cup capacity that should keep an adult cat fed for up to 15 days.
Fairphone 6 Plus
Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.
In many ways, the Pebble Index 01 is the gadget of our times. The stripped-back smart ring has a microphone and, with a tap of a button, records and sends your thoughts to the Pebble app over Bluetooth. You can also use it to start a timer or even add a calendar event to your phone.
Cast iced tea glass
Sure. You could put iced tea in them, but no one’s stopping you from sipping pulpy OJ or rich chocolate milk from Kinto’s stylish glassware, which was crafted with an “uninterfering design” in mind. Needless to say, a full set makes a lovely addition to any minimalist’s ensemble.
The hippest thing in audio right now is… the hippest thing from a long time ago. Enter the modded iPod Classic from Player Mods, which refreshes Apple’s media player with some 21st-century upgrades. The 5th-gen model can be customized with several color options (including a transparent case) and up to 2TB of storage.
For those tired of experiencing Joy-Con drift with their Nintendo Switch (or stick drift on any controller), there’s the TT Pro. Loaded with the latest anti-drift tech for joysticks and customizable triggers that let picky gamers have it their way, GuliKit’s customizable wireless controllers work with PlayStation, Nintendo, PC, iOS, and Android devices.
Do you like… scary movies? That’s just one of many catchphrases that pair well with the Key Pocket, which can alter voices in real time. The tiny device sticks to the back of Apple or Android devices via magnets, granting you multiple effects for gaming, voice calls, or streaming.
OhSnap Grip Stand
Pricey yet endlessly useful, this is the kind of item you might not buy for yourself, which makes it a fantastic gift. Offering a brilliantly thin yet durable framework in a stand that also hangs, pops, and never needs to come off, it’s the ultimate phone accessory.
If someone on your list collects Game Boy, Game Boy Color, or Game Boy Advance cartridges, the GB Operator might be the perfect gift. The slick, transparent USB-C device makes it easy to play and manage classic titles on a macOS or Windows machine via emulation, with or without achievements.
Dock & Bay’s blankets are a great choice for almost everyone. They provide a soft space on which to relax or entertain, whether at the park or on your hardwood floors at home, and they’re incredibly easy to pack. Plus, they have a water-resistant bottom and come in an array of fun colors.
Sonos Beam Ultra
This radical upgrade of the middle child in Sonos’ soundbar lineup may be the best (little) soundbar you can buy. It delivers musical sound, surprisingly full and cinematic bass, and brain-tricking immersion thanks to drivers that now point every which way; it can also expand or connect with other Sonos speakers and stream almost anything.
The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.
Your favorite gamer needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.
Lego PlayStation
Few devices evoke more sheer nostalgic joy than Sony’s OG PlayStation console from ’94. If you know a gamer, Lego’s latest replica brings it all flooding back with several brick-ified details, including a pop-up hinge, a gamepad, and a number of hidden surprises waiting to be discovered.
Nothing can replace our furry friends, so for pets that tend to wander, only the best tracking tech will do. Enter the Fi Ultra, which uses Starlink technology via T-Mobile to track pets almost anywhere, even in cellular dead zones.
If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.
Gardyn Studio 2
If there’s someone on your list who loves plants but can’t seem to take care of them, the Gardyn Studio 2 can bring life to their living room. The smart hydroponic garden is easy to set up and features automated, AI-powered lighting, helping anyone maintain a green thumb.
Bissell ProHeat 2X Revolution Pet Pro carpet cleaner
You create a home for your pets; they create a mess for your home. It’s the circle of life (or carpet, anyway). Thankfully, Bissell’s pro-grade cleaner uses a concentrated stream of formula and 12 rows of rotating brushes to do the dirty work for you, keeping your carpets in good order.
Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.
Soundcore makes some of the best wireless earbuds you’ve never heard of — and the Liberty 5 Pro may be its best pair yet. The sleek buds deliver powerful noise-canceling, good sound, and surprisingly fabulous call quality for way less than Apple’s latest AirPods Pro.
Matic robot vacuum
It’s time for a smarter robovac. Thankfully, there’s the Matic, which looks less like the rambling discs that pervade the space and more like an actual robot that, well, vacuums. It doesn’t get under beds, but it also doesn’t get stuck under them, and it does a great job providing truly no-fuss cleaning thanks to its superb mapping.
OhSnap MCON controller
There’s no shortage of mobile gaming controllers, but few are as stealthy or as compact as the MCON. The sliding gamepad quickly attaches to any MagSafe- or Pixelsnap-ready phone, letting you game with a set of satisfying controls that feel more natural than most rivals.
Big Walk
It can be hard to keep in touch with friends, but Big Walk might be the game that gets the gang back together. The cooperative multiplayer title drops players into a wacky world as spherical humanoids who must solve puzzles by chatting and teaming up. You’ll want at least two copies, and sessions support up to 12 players.
The future is now, so of course we’ve got screens in sunglasses. The Viture Pro 2 are a slick pair of augmented-reality shades with speakers, micro-OLED screens, and a bonus feature: diopter-adjusting dials, which can sharpen the focus of whatever they’re mirroring from a phone or other device over a USB-C tether. Fancy!
BYOK
The BYOK (Bring Your Own Keyboard) is a distraction-free way for creatives to get their thoughts down without the allure of silly YouTube videos or notifications about their dog’s flea meds. No frills, just a low-resolution LCD screen that works with most keyboards and provides plenty of power for the long haul.
The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.
WiiM is a popular Sonos alternative, thanks in part to excellent software that works across its multiple streaming amplifiers and other products. The WiiM Sound is the brand’s sharpest smart speaker, with accessible controls, Alexa and Google smarts, and the ability to connect to other WiiM gear in surround sound or throughout your home.
When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like the pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.
Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.

articles.title: I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable this year — here’s how the iPhone Duo compares
articles.body:
When I first read Allison and Nilay’s Verge review of the iPhone Duo, I was immediately struck by one of their complaints: that the cover display is too small. That’s not how the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels, I thought. Had they got it wrong?
I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable this year — here’s how the iPhone Duo compares
Apple’s first foldable matches its Android rivals in a few key areas, but it falls short in others.
After a week and a half using the Duo, I know exactly what they mean — and it’s not the screen’s fault at all. Apps that feel comfortable on Samsung’s short foldable and the similarly sized Xiaomi 18 Fold are often cramped and compact on the Duo’s cover screen, robbed of screen space by a right-hand rail that most apps don’t make use of anyway.
That’s just one of the ways that Apple’s first foldable feels fundamentally different from the Android alternatives. I’ve reviewed almost every Android foldable that was released this year, from Samsung and Google to Honor and Oppo, and I’ve been surprised to realize that the Duo holds its own against them all on hardware, but is let down by iOS itself. For now at least, Android is slicker for folding phones — though I don’t know how long that will last.
Size, shape, and build quality
The iPhone Duo feels great. Mostly. Its curved frame and Ceramic Shield back have that ineffable Apple feeling, a sense of polish that helps justify the $2,000 price tag. The hinge in particular is satisfyingly smooth, closing and opening with a comforting magnetic click. Compared with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 or Xiaomi 18 Fold, the Duo just feels better.
But part of that is down to the Duo’s big drawback: its weight. At first it feels encouraging, the reassuring heft of all that glass and metal. Then I started using the phone, and I realized it’s just plain heavy. It weighs more than all of its rivals — even ones with larger screens — and any attempt to use the Duo one-handed makes that obvious quickly. It’s a little thicker than some other foldables, too, though in practice that bothers me far less.
The squat shape won’t be for everyone. The Duo is even shorter and wider than the Z Fold 8, though almost identical in dimensions to Xiaomi’s 18 Fold. I’m a fan of this design, which is both cute and comfortable when folded shut and gives you a natural choice of portrait or landscape orientations when open. The major downsides are that the short cover screen makes some apps awkward to use, and it’s wide when you need to stretch across to the other side — a problem worsened by some of Apple’s software choices. More on that later.
And while the Duo’s IP68 rating is an obvious advantage over much of the competition (only Google and Honor can match it), we’ve not seen many recent Android foldables struggle with hinge and display damage quite like the Duo. It’s still not clear how widespread Duo screen failures really are — they don’t seem to be as ubiquitous as Samsung’s first-generation failures back in 2019 — but non-impact damage like this is almost unheard of in modern Android foldables. It’s a reminder that the Duo is still a first-gen product while some Android rivals are into their eighth iteration.
The crease and screen
The screen is the Duo’s smartest hardware trick, and easily my favorite thing about the phone compared with other foldable phones. No rival offers anything like the “nano-texture” (read: matte) finish on the inner screen, which is easy on the eyes in more ways than one.
Crucially, it also helps mask the phone’s crease, which isn’t quite invisible but is well-hidden. The Duo’s crease is somewhere in the middle of the Android pack: subtler than Google’s and Honor’s, more obvious than Samsung’s. Oppo’s near-invisible crease remains the best, but not by much. The Duo’s matte screen means it’s harder than most to see (though visible from an angle), but it’s still easy enough to feel, and a couple of friends have immediately remarked on it when trying the phone. Still, I don’t want to over-egg it: The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is probably the only one out of this year’s foldables with a crease I’d say is a problem. The Duo’s crease is easy to ignore.
I’d actually say the Duo’s under-display camera is more of an annoyance. It’s not only inside an extra-pixelated circle of screen, but that’s the only patch without the matte coating, which makes it a little more distracting. I can mostly tune it out, but not entirely. I’d probably prefer a regular selfie camera tucked right into the corner, as on the Xiaomi 18 Fold and a few others, but I suspect opinions will differ here.
Finally, the Duo benefits from stylus support, letting you use a USB-C Apple Pencil on the central screen. This isn’t unique — Samsung used to offer the same, and both of Honor’s and Oppo’s latest foldables work with their styli — but plenty of the current Android crop don’t offer the option. I don’t have an Apple Pencil, so I haven’t been able to test it myself, but my colleague Allison is clearly a fan.
Cameras and battery life
The iPhone Duo’s cameras, like those on most foldables, are fairly basic, with a pair of 48-megapixel rear lenses, one main and one ultrawide. It’s a setup comparable to the Z Fold 8, and both phones’ cameras are good, but not great. Most other Android foldables (including Samsung’s Z Fold 8 Ultra) instead offer triple rear cameras, netting you a big boost in photographic flexibility. They often use larger sensors than either Apple or Samsung, so their main cameras are better, too. Still, Vivo is the only manufacturer getting close to slab flagship quality in its foldable cameras, and its hardware lags behind in a few other respects that would prevent it from being my foldable recommendation overall.
As for selfies, the front-screen camera is pretty basic, but you can take better shots using the rear cameras by opening the phone up and flipping it round. That under-display camera is worse than a regular selfie camera, but good enough so long as you only use it for video calls.
As for battery, Nilay and Allison had different experiences in our Duo review. I’ve mostly found the battery long-lasting, easily running a full day of mixed use. It’s got a higher capacity than either of Samsung’s foldables, so that’s no real surprise. It still pales in comparison to the two-day battery of Honor’s Magic V6, but once you’re past lasting a day, I think you get diminishing returns anyway.
Software support and multitasking
So far, the Duo looks like a competitive foldable, albeit a little middle-of-the-pack. It beats its rivals in some hardware areas, falls behind in others, and has one truly unique selling point in the matte foldable display.
Unusually for Apple, the software is what lets it down.
The biggest problem isn’t Apple’s own software, but everyone else’s: Most apps still aren’t optimized for the Duo. In the best case, that means apps that don’t make full use of the Duo’s new right-hand rail, showing an empty black bar instead of app controls. Worse are the ones that don’t even scale to the larger screen — apps like Bluesky or Duolingo can use the whole display on other foldables, but appear in thin strips with huge black bars on the Duo.
This will improve with time. I’ve seen Google Maps, Google Translate, and Instagram update in the last few days alone, and no doubt more will follow. Some are already better on the Duo: Slack uses a helpful desktop-style two-column layout, while on Android foldables you just get the mobile UI but bigger. But for now at least, most apps run better on my Android foldables than on my Duo.
OS-level improvements are harder to predict. At first I loved the idea of Apple moving key controls to the right-hand edge, but it takes up so much space that it leaves the Duo’s cover screen feeling smaller than it needs to: You get all the awkward stretching of a wide phone without the expansive screen space. Samsung and Xiaomi’s wide foldables may be about the same size, but in use they feel much bigger. I wonder how many software developers will follow Google’s lead in app optimization — it essentially ignored the right rail entirely while updating Google Maps, instead just spreading the map to the edge of the screen. It feels bigger and better than most other Duo apps as a result.
And this is partly the Android user in me, but the lack of a persistent back-swipe gesture seems to grate more on the Duo than on other iPhones. Sometimes, moving backward in an app requires a button in the right rail, sometimes one in the top-left corner, sometimes a swipe from the left-hand edge of the screen. It’s annoyingly inconsistent, and more often than not requires stretching across the phone’s width, whether it’s open or closed. Being able to swipe back from either side of the screen gives Android foldables a huge advantage in one-handed use.
As for multitasking, the Duo is well behind the competition. You can run two apps at once in split-screen, but only in landscape mode, and each must take up exactly half the display. Compare this to Oppo, which allows you to fluidly move between multiple split-screen apps and floating windows; or Xiaomi, which allows up to six apps to run side by side in split-screen, and Apple’s implementation feels downright basic. These are the extreme end of Android, and probably overkill for most (they certainly are for me), but I’d take them over Apple’s half-hearted multitasking any day.
The bottom line
Apple hasn’t waded into the foldable market and fixed all its flaws. If anything, “crackgate” is proof that it’s still playing catch-up with the Android alternatives, which have a few years of fine-tuning behind them. Many are still lighter, and thinner, and have subtler creases than the Duo, or bigger batteries and better cameras. In broad strokes, though, this hardware is up to scratch — and, crucially, on par with its most direct worldwide rival, the Galaxy Z Fold 8.
For now, though, Android has the software edge. Google has worked hard to make its OS adaptable to various screen sizes so most apps take full advantage of the bigger inner screen while individual OEMs have designed ambitious multitasking tools. That isn’t yet true for iOS, and some of Apple’s own software tweaks in the OS make things more awkward still. It’s those that I’m worried about long term. The best thing about foldables is their flexibility — something Apple itself often lacks. If the Duo is going to catch up to Android, Apple might have to adapt.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
articles.body:
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
Here’s an overview of what’s new:
Fast and cost-effective at scale
Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
Longer clips up to 15 seconds
You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
Better reference adherence
You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.
Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.
More consistent results
You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.
Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.
Easier editing in conversation
You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.
Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.
More natural speech
You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow, creating video explainers in Gemini for business, or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids.
Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.
More controllable, cinematic look
You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.
Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.
Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.
Real-world results, from creatives to global brands
Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.
Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:
- For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio, explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing.
- For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console, and build enterprise solutions with the API.
- For everyone using Google apps: Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in Flow, generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the Gemini app (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in Google Ads.

articles.title: Blender's UI and Runtime: Much Faster Than GPUI
articles.body:
Blender's user interface, as a library you can use from Python, Rust, JavaScript (React, Svelte), C, C++ and Dear ImGui. People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat! Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in docs/ or on the website when there's more to say. BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU. At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it. What BUI is not: - Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it. - Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network. - Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui. Blender's interface is famous for how it feels. You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands. That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency. - You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged. - You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect. - You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser. - You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag. - You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words. You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they all get the same widgets and interactions: Not sure which to pick? If you already have code, use the row that matches it. If you're starting fresh in Python, the Blender components are the friendliest. - Number fields you drag with a hidden, continuous cursor: Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap. - Math in number fields, with Blender's own expression evaluator: 2*pi, min(4, 3), round(1.7), x if c else y. - Ctrl+Wheel steps values, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy values, Backspace resets. - Drag across checkboxes to set them all. - Press-drag-release menus, pie menus, and Blender's fuzzy menu search: "ad cu" finds "Add Cube", typos are forgiven, recent picks rank first. - Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type; Tab between fields. - Blender's float display precision, multi-field vertical drags, and panels that collapse with Blender's animation. - The HSV color wheel, color ramps, curves, trees, lists, text areas, canvases, a node editor and Blender's File Browser. - Blender's Dark and Light themes, switchable at run time. - tkinter: all 7,846 public names of tkinter and ttk. Nine real programs behave identically on the standard library and on BUI. - Qt syntax: widgets, layouts, signals, QPainter, menus and timers. - Components: 45 Blender widgets, editors and templates. - Dear ImGui: from blenderui import imgui, pyimgui-style. - One pip install, no Qt or Tk widgets drawing anything. - All 113 HTML elements, drawn like a browser draws them; styled gives any subtree Blender's look, and Blender components (, {/* a Blender component */} ) } render(, { title: "Counter", width: 360, height: 200, gpu: true })bun app.jsx # run it (Bun reads JSX directly) npx bui build app.jsx # or ship it: app.exe, one 7 MB file Without React, @blender-ui/native gives you a DOM-like API: const { App, signal } = require("@blender-ui/native") const app = new App({ gpu: true }) const win = app.window({ title: "Hello", width: 360, height: 200 }) win.body.className = "m-0 p-6 flex flex-col gap-3 bg-[#2b2b2b] text-[#e6e6e6]" const clicks = signal(0) const label = win.createElement("span") label.textContent = clicks // follows the signal const button = win.createElement("button") button.textContent = "Add one" button.addEventListener("click", () => clicks.value++) win.body.appendChild(label) win.body.appendChild(button) A task list in React (examples/site/js/todo_react.js); the DOM-like version draws the same Node.js 18+ or Bun. Prebuilt for Windows x64; on Linux, build the addon from source (npm run build in bindings/node) and windows are native. Guide: docs/javascript.md. The real Dear ImGui 1.93 runs on BUI: BUI's windows, input, CPU/GPU renderer, Blender's theme and the Inter font. Existing ImGui code compiles unchanged. C++: #include "imgui.h" #include "imgui_impl_bui.h" // see examples/imgui_demo.cpp static void frame(void*) { ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); ImGui::Begin("Hello"); static float v = 0.5f; ImGui::SliderFloat("Value", &v, 0.0f, 1.0f); ImGui::End(); } int main() { ImGui::CreateContext(); ImGui_ImplBUI_App* app = ImGui_ImplBUI_CreateApp("Demo", 1280, 800, frame, nullptr); ImGui_ImplBUI_RunApp(app); ImGui_ImplBUI_DestroyApp(app); ImGui::DestroyContext(); } Python: import blenderui.imgui as imgui # C: cimgui.h · Rust: the blenderui-imgui crate state = {"value": 0.5} def frame(): imgui.show_demo_window() imgui.begin("Hello") _, state["value"] = imgui.slider_float("Value", state["value"], 0.0, 1.0) imgui.end() imgui.run(frame, title="Hello", size=(1280, 800)) C (cimgui.h, cimgui conventions: ImGui_Button, ImGui_ButtonEx, and the backend in cimgui_impl_bui.h) and Rust (blenderui-imgui) work the same way: use blenderui_imgui as imgui; fn main() { let mut value = 0.5f32; imgui::run("Hello", [1280, 800], move || { imgui::show_demo_window(); imgui::begin("Hello"); imgui::slider_float("Value", &mut value, 0.0, 1.0); imgui::end(); }); } Build with -DBUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON (or the Rust feature blender-widgets) and ImGui's widgets become Blender's own: DragFloat is Blender's drag-to-scrub number field (Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap), SliderFloat Blender's number slider, checkboxes drag-toggle, menus and combos get Blender's menus. The rest of the ImGui API is unchanged. (The PyPI wheel is built without it, so from Python you get ImGui's own widgets in Blender's theme unless you build from source.) Dear ImGui's own demo with BUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON: number fields, sliders, color rows and panel headers are Blender's The same ImGui code: ImGui's widgets (left) and the Blender-widgets build (right) (examples/site/imgui_inspector.cpp) Guide, coverage and the stock look: docs/imgui.md. The kit's API is one header, kit/include/BUI_kit.h, and it doubles as the reference: every function has a one-line comment. This is a shortened examples/kit_hello.c: a slider and a button in a native window. #include #include "BUI_kit.h" static void on_event(void *data, BKNode *node, int kind, void *ref, double a, double b) { if (kind == BK_EV_CLICK) printf("clicked %s\n", BK_get_str(node, "text")); else if (kind == BK_EV_CHANGE) printf("%s = %g\n", BK_get_str(node, "label"), BK_get_num(node, "value")); } int main(void) { BKNode *root = BK_node_new("frame"); /* everything is a node */ BK_set_num(root, "padding", 8); /* configured by property name */ BKNode *size = BK_node_new("slider"); BK_set_str(size, "label", "Size"); BK_set_num(size, "max", 10); BK_set_num(size, "value", 2.5); BK_node_add(root, size, -1); BK_geom_set_manager(size, BK_GEOM_PACK); /* Tk's packer, in C */ BK_geom_set(size, "fill", 1); BKNode *apply = BK_node_new("button"); BK_set_str(apply, "text", "Apply"); BK_node_add(root, apply, -1); BK_geom_set_manager(apply, BK_GEOM_PACK); BKContext *ctx = BK_context_new(root); /* input, focus, popups, undo */ BKHost host = {0}; host.emit = on_event; /* the window fills in the rest */ BK_context_set_host(ctx, &host); if (BK_window_supported()) { /* Win32, X11 or Cocoa */ BKWindow *win = BK_window_new(ctx, "BUI from C", 320, 120); BK_window_show(win); BK_window_run(); BK_window_free(win); } BK_context_free(ctx); BK_node_free(root); return 0; }cmake -S . -B build -DBUI_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON cmake --build build --target bui_kit_hello A bigger C program: a modifier stack (examples/site/kit_modifiers.c) Without a window system, render into a raster instead (BK_render(ctx, raster, w, h, full)), which is also how tests and screenshots work. Guide: docs/c-api.md. your code: tkinter Qt components Dear ImGui (C++/C/Python/Rust) Rust: rsx! / HTML / CSS / Tailwind / hooks JS / React │ │ │ │ │ │ └──── Python: options, signals │ ImGui core + BUI backend └── style cascade + taffy layout ◄────┘ │ │ │ C kit (kit/): node tree · geometry · input & interaction · Blender widget drawing · undo · animation · themes · Blender search/expr │ renderer: damage-driven software raster (parallel) or GPU (Direct3D 11 / OpenGL 3.3, instanced, opt-in) │ window: native Win32 / X11 / Cocoa window · stdlib Tk window · headless (tests, screenshots) - Your code, in any language above, creates widgets and says what happens when they change. - The kit keeps them in one tree, lays them out and handles input, following Blender's rules. - The renderer draws them, on the CPU by default or on the GPU if you ask. - Damage rendering keeps it cheap: a change redraws only the rectangle it touched, and an idle window uses no CPU at all. What's under the hood: - Blender's real UI code. Widget drawing is a C port of Blender's interface_widgets.cc (round_box_edges, widgetbase_draw, the shape tables), and interaction follows interface_handlers.cc. Color math, rects, text cursors, string search and expression evaluation are Blender's blenlib, copied in. A few interface files (string search, text-edit undo, float precision) are copied into kit/intern/blender/ and edited for the kit. The X11 and Cocoa hosts follow Blender's GHOST; the Win32 host is BUI's own. - One node tree. Every widget is one kit node. The C kit owns layout, hit testing, hover, focus, drags, menus, tooltips, undo and animation. - Damage rendering. A change marks only its widget's rectangle, and only changed tiles reach the screen. - Thin bindings. Python, Rust and JavaScript keep only what their syntax layer needs. More: ARCHITECTURE.md and How it works. These rules live in the C kit, so they work the same everywhere Blender widgets are drawn: the Python components, tkinter and Qt syntax, the Rust and JavaScript Blender components and form controls inside styled, ImGui's Blender-widgets build, and every C kit widget. - Drag to scrub. Press a number field and drag sideways. The cursor hides and wraps, so you never hit the screen edge, and comes back where the drag started. A float moves one click step per pixel; Shift moves at a tenth of the speed; Esc cancels and restores the value. - Ctrl snaps with Blender's rules: unbounded floats to whole units, angles to 10°, sliders to 0.1, 1 or 10 depending on their range, integers to multiples of 10. - Click to type, and type math: Blender's expression evaluator (expr_pylike_eval.cc) turns 2*pi, 90/4, min(4, 3) or x if c else y into numbers. This works in Blender number fields and sliders; plain text fields keep what you type as text. - Shortcuts on any value: Backspace resets to the default, - negates, Ctrl+Wheel steps, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy and paste, right-click opens Copy, Paste and Reset. - Several fields at once. Drag down over a column of number fields to collect them, then sideways to change them together. Drag across checkboxes (or panel headers) to set them all in one stroke. - Panels collapse with Blender's animation; Ctrl+click opens one and closes the others; drag the grip to reorder. - Menus work press-drag-release or click; hover switches menu-bar menus; pie menus open around the pointer. - Menu search is Blender's string search: start typing in any open menu. It matches word initials ("ad cu" finds "Add Cube"), forgives typos, and ranks your recent picks first. - Undo everywhere. Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z work on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type. A burst of typing or a multi-field drag is one step. - Float precision follows Blender: small values show the decimals they need. - Tooltips appear after Blender's half-second delay. Coming soon: typing values with units ("2 m"), Blender's search-as-you-type popups, and widget drag and drop. More: Blender's widgets. articles.title: Blender's UI and Runtime: Much Faster Than GPUI
articles.body:
Blender's user interface, as a library you can use from Python, Rust, JavaScript (React, Svelte), C, C++ and Dear ImGui. People spent decades building and optimizing Blender's GUI. It's battery and memory efficient, and super duper fast. We decoupled it, to give everyone a chance to build their own products with it. It supports multiple languages and frameworks, so you won't miss a beat! Website and full documentation: bui.preetham.top · Chat: Discord This README is a small book. Read it front to back for the whole story, or jump to the chapter you need. Every chapter links to a longer guide in docs/ or on the website when there's more to say. BUI takes the user interface of Blender (its widget drawing, its interaction rules and its look) and turns it into a standalone UI library with a small C core. Your code builds the widget tree and handles callbacks. Layout, input, drawing and presenting all happen in fast native code, on the CPU or the GPU. At the heart of BUI is the kit: a small runtime written in C. The kit holds every widget in one tree, lays them out, handles the mouse and keyboard, and draws them the way Blender does. The drawing code is a C port of Blender's own widget code, and the interaction follows Blender's rules. On top of the kit sit bindings: thin layers that let Python, Rust, JavaScript, C++ and Dear ImGui talk to it. What BUI is not: - Not Blender. It contains the parts of Blender's UI code it needs and builds on its own. You don't need Blender installed, and you don't need to know Blender to use it. - Not a browser. The Rust and JavaScript sides use HTML and CSS as a UI language, but there's no browser engine, no webview and no network. - Not a re-imagining. The widget drawing is ported from Blender's interface_widgets.cc, and the Dear ImGui support runs the real Dear ImGui. Blender's interface is famous for how it feels. You press a number field and drag: the cursor vanishes, the value glides under your hand, and you never hit the edge of the screen. You type 2*pi into a field and it just works. You type "ad cu" into a menu and it finds "Add Cube". Millions of artists have these habits in their hands. That interface is also fast and frugal. It redraws only what changed, sleeps when nothing does, and starts in milliseconds. BUI exists so that any app, in any language, can have both: Blender's feel, and Blender's efficiency. - You have a tkinter app and wish it looked less like 1998. Run it on BUI, unchanged. - You're building a tool for artists who already know Blender. Give them the panels, sliders and shortcuts their hands expect. - You write Rust or React and want a native desktop UI without shipping a browser. - You use Dear ImGui and want it to look and feel like Blender, with one build flag. - You're curious how a UI toolkit works. The source is readable, and the concepts are explained in plain words. You can drive BUI many ways, and all of them share the same C runtime, so they all get the same widgets and interactions: Not sure which to pick? If you already have code, use the row that matches it. If you're starting fresh in Python, the Blender components are the friendliest. - Number fields you drag with a hidden, continuous cursor: Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap. - Math in number fields, with Blender's own expression evaluator: 2*pi, min(4, 3), round(1.7), x if c else y. - Ctrl+Wheel steps values, Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V copy values, Backspace resets. - Drag across checkboxes to set them all. - Press-drag-release menus, pie menus, and Blender's fuzzy menu search: "ad cu" finds "Add Cube", typos are forgiven, recent picks rank first. - Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z on every UI edit, and inside a text field while you type; Tab between fields. - Blender's float display precision, multi-field vertical drags, and panels that collapse with Blender's animation. - The HSV color wheel, color ramps, curves, trees, lists, text areas, canvases, a node editor and Blender's File Browser. - Blender's Dark and Light themes, switchable at run time. - tkinter: all 7,846 public names of tkinter and ttk. Nine real programs behave identically on the standard library and on BUI. - Qt syntax: widgets, layouts, signals, QPainter, menus and timers. - Components: 45 Blender widgets, editors and templates. - Dear ImGui: from blenderui import imgui, pyimgui-style. - One pip install, no Qt or Tk widgets drawing anything. - All 113 HTML elements, drawn like a browser draws them; styled gives any subtree Blender's look, and Blender components (, {/* a Blender component */} ) } render(, { title: "Counter", width: 360, height: 200, gpu: true })bun app.jsx # run it (Bun reads JSX directly) npx bui build app.jsx # or ship it: app.exe, one 7 MB file Without React, @blender-ui/native gives you a DOM-like API: const { App, signal } = require("@blender-ui/native") const app = new App({ gpu: true }) const win = app.window({ title: "Hello", width: 360, height: 200 }) win.body.className = "m-0 p-6 flex flex-col gap-3 bg-[#2b2b2b] text-[#e6e6e6]" const clicks = signal(0) const label = win.createElement("span") label.textContent = clicks // follows the signal const button = win.createElement("button") button.textContent = "Add one" button.addEventListener("click", () => clicks.value++) win.body.appendChild(label) win.body.appendChild(button) A task list in React (examples/site/js/todo_react.js); the DOM-like version draws the same Node.js 18+ or Bun. Prebuilt for Windows x64; on Linux, build the addon from source (npm run build in bindings/node) and windows are native. Guide: docs/javascript.md. The real Dear ImGui 1.93 runs on BUI: BUI's windows, input, CPU/GPU renderer, Blender's theme and the Inter font. Existing ImGui code compiles unchanged. C++: #include "imgui.h" #include "imgui_impl_bui.h" // see examples/imgui_demo.cpp static void frame(void*) { ImGui::ShowDemoWindow(); ImGui::Begin("Hello"); static float v = 0.5f; ImGui::SliderFloat("Value", &v, 0.0f, 1.0f); ImGui::End(); } int main() { ImGui::CreateContext(); ImGui_ImplBUI_App* app = ImGui_ImplBUI_CreateApp("Demo", 1280, 800, frame, nullptr); ImGui_ImplBUI_RunApp(app); ImGui_ImplBUI_DestroyApp(app); ImGui::DestroyContext(); } Python: import blenderui.imgui as imgui # C: cimgui.h · Rust: the blenderui-imgui crate state = {"value": 0.5} def frame(): imgui.show_demo_window() imgui.begin("Hello") _, state["value"] = imgui.slider_float("Value", state["value"], 0.0, 1.0) imgui.end() imgui.run(frame, title="Hello", size=(1280, 800)) C (cimgui.h, cimgui conventions: ImGui_Button, ImGui_ButtonEx, and the backend in cimgui_impl_bui.h) and Rust (blenderui-imgui) work the same way: use blenderui_imgui as imgui; fn main() { let mut value = 0.5f32; imgui::run("Hello", [1280, 800], move || { imgui::show_demo_window(); imgui::begin("Hello"); imgui::slider_float("Value", &mut value, 0.0, 1.0); imgui::end(); }); } Build with -DBUI_IMGUI_BLENDER_WIDGETS=ON (or the Rust feature blender-widgets) and ImGui's widgets become Blender's own: DragFloat is Blender's drag-to-scrub number field (Shift for precision, Ctrl to snap), SliderFloat Blender's number slider, checkboxes drag-toggle, menus and combos get Blender's menus. articles.title: Cuban: Facebook knowingly runs AI deepfake scam ads; docs say $16B fraud revenue
articles.body:
Mark Cuban keeps getting emails about a $294 diabetes cure he has never sold.
"Every single week I get emails from little old men and ladies saying, 'Will my cure for diabetes work?' or 'I just ordered your cure for diabetes for $294,'" the 68-year-old billionaire investor said on an August episode of Pivot, the podcast hosted by Kara Swisher and Scott Galloway.
Must Read
- Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one
- Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP
- A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change
Those ads are deepfakes built with an AI copy of his face and voice, Cuban said, and Meta (NASDAQ:META) runs them anyway. "Facebook knows the little old ladies are getting ripped off," he said. He called the platform "the worst of the worst."
The ads Cuban says Meta waves through
Cuban said some of the ads even include a disclaimer admitting the person on screen is AI-generated and the clip is meant as entertainment. By the time anyone gets to it, he argued, the pitch has already worked. "And to Facebook, that's good enough," he said.
"The point is, that defines the culture of the organization," Cuban said. A company that lets scammers go after people's grandparents, he argued, has shown what it will tolerate at every level.
Cuban does run a drug company — he co-founded Cost Plus Drugs, an online pharmacy that sells low-cost generic medications.
What Meta's documents showed
On Nov. 6, 2025, Reuters reported on internal Meta documents showing the company expected roughly $16 billion, or about 10% of its 2024 revenue, to flow in from ads pushing scams and prohibited products. By Meta's own internal count, users across its apps were seeing some 15 billion "higher risk" ads a day — the ones with obvious markers of fraud. One late 2024 document put that category's value at about $7 billion a year.
In a May 2025 presentation, Meta's own safety staff estimated the company's platforms play a part in a third of the scams that succeed in the U.S. Before Meta bans an advertiser, its automated systems must peg the account as at least 95% likely to be running a scam, the documents say. Below that threshold, the suspected scammer simply pays more per ad and stays live.
Meta spokesman Andy Stone told Reuters the documents "present a selective view that distorts Meta's approach to fraud and scams," and called the company's 10% estimate "rough and overly-inclusive." Complaints from users about scam ads had fallen 58% over the prior 18 months, he said at the time, and the company pulled down more than 134 million scam ads in 2025. The same documents note the Securities and Exchange Commission is looking into Meta over advertising tied to financial fraud.

articles.title: California Gov Newsom commutes death sentences for all 548 people on death row
articles.body:
California governor commutes sentences for state's 548 death row inmates
California Governor Gavin Newsom has commuted the death sentences of all 548 people on death row in the state, changing them instead to life in prison.
"We can now let these offenders die in obscurity while we forever remember and honour the victims," he said in a letter.
The decision to spare death row inmates is largely symbolic in a state that has not executed an inmate since 2006, though experts say it could save millions of dollars in court costs each year. Only 13 inmates have been executed since voters reinstated the death penalty in 1978.
The decision comes as Newsom, the Democratic leader of the most populous US state, has been discussed as a possible 2028 contender for president.
Newsom, who is term limited, is winding down his final months in office. Fellow Democrat Xavier Becerra is projected to take over after the midterm elections on Tuesday.
Newsom explained in his letter that he is exercising his constitutional clemency authority to commute the sentences to life without the possibility of parole.
"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom said. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system and diminishes each of us".
California has historically had the largest population of death row inmates. Newsom had previously ordered a halt to the death penalty in the state in 2019.
Describing his decision as a difficult but "righteous action", Newsom said that although many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die, he has concluded that "the state cannot morally kill them".
He said that by every measure, California's system for administering the death penalty "is a failure", and that it has not and cannot be fairly applied, resulting in the conviction of innocent people.
Life without the possibility of parole is the most severe punishment he can lawfully impose and that the state can ethically enforce, he said.
He acknowledged that his clemency action will anger and hurt some Californians and said that it will "always weigh heavily on me".
"As governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," he wrote.
"For this reason, I am compelled to follow my conscience and, as authorised by our Constitution, take this action for the welfare of the State of California."
Because individual states have the power to prosecute crimes and order executions, much of the power lies with state governors.
Bernard E Harcourt, a law and civil liberties professor at Columbia University, told the BBC that it is not unprecedented for a potential presidential candidate to come out as an abolitionist in the run up to elections - despite the overall popularity of the death penalty in the US.
He noted that François Mitterrand did precisely that in his presidential campaign in France in 1981, taking "the higher ethical ground and was rewarded by the public for that".
"I detect a very similar ethical positioning in Governor Newsom's statements about the commutations. And here too, it may well be something that the voters respect," he said.
Newsom's decision comes after the high-profile botched execution of a woman in Tennessee in late September and while executions have been on the rise in the US. There are three executions scheduled for Thursday in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.
At least four of seven judges on the California Supreme Court will have to sign off on the commutations, CalMatters reported.
It is unclear how Newsom's decision will affect condemned inmates like Keith Doolin, 53, who was sentenced to death in 1996 for murdering two sex workers, Inez Espinoza and Peggy Tucker, and shooting four others. He maintains his innocence.
Doolin lived on death row at San Quentin for decades, until he was moved to another prison in 2025 when the governor announced the state would reform the prison for all but those on death row.
Doolin's mother, Donna Larsen, told the BBC that the news of Newsom's commutations - which includes Doolin - brought mixed emotions.
"At least the execution chamber will not be reconstructed, and no more killing by the people of the state of California," she said.
Anthony D Romero, the executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, applauded Newsom's action.
"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," Romero said.
"By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialised injustice head-on."
Nathan Hochman, the top prosecutor in Los Angeles County, said that while Newsom has the power to commute sentences, only state legislature or voters can eliminate the death penalty.
"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," Hochman said in a statement.
On the federal level, President Donald Trump, a long-time supporter of the death penalty, has described capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".
In 2020, during his first term, he ended a nearly two-decade moratorium on the federal death penalty, by ordering 13 executions over a six-month period.
While the moratorium returned under President Biden, on the first day of Trump's second term in 2025, he signed an executive order that re-instated the death penalty.
No federal executions have been carried out since he signed it, however. In the US, both the federal government and local states authorities can order executions.
The death penalty is legal in 27 states, but has been abolished in 23 states and Washington DC, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a national non-profit.
California, which primarily uses lethal injection for executions, used to house male death row prisoners in San Quentin State Prison north of San Francisco, and female inmates in the Central California Women's Facility in the Central Valley.
But a 2016 ballot measure allowed for their transfer to other facilities that provide a necessary level of security, according to the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.
