A few years passed by, and we saw Apple release the first ARM-based Mac in 2021, the M1 MacBook Air. The timing was impeccable, Intel was unable to create competitive processors (due to being stuck on the 14nm node), and Apple had powerful and efficient ARM chips already being shipped in their iPhones. The long battery life, the fanless design, the instant wake, what's not to like? The benefits of switching to ARM were clear, however to most, this was thought to be the final chapter in the hackintosh community. x86 versions of macOS would soon be discontinued, and the hackintosh community would slowly fade away. The latest version of macOS 27 (Golden Gate) was released this year, and is no longer compatible with x86...
Just a few days ago, I decided to create an iOS app for the first time. It required XCode 26 for development, so I used my spare ThinkPad T490 as my development machine and installed macOS 26 using a posted guide. The installation was smooth and painless. XCode 26 has integrations with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, and this was my first foray into AI-assisted coding. After some initial tinkering with x86 workarounds, I was pleased that I had a functional iOS app within a day, without touching a single line of code!
So how does this all tie in? Well, this is exactly what the Hackintosh community could hardly envision five years ago: the rise of AI. Waiting patiently and gently until now, the hackintosh and the hackios community has seen an absolute explosion in development, activity, and success in the past few weeks! As one person aptly wrote, this is the power of Claude Code with Ghidra on steroids. To list a few recent developments, we have:
macOS 27 running on the Snapdragon Laptop:
macOS 27.2 Beta on an ARM SBC RK3588 with Mali drivers:
iOS 17 running on the Nintendo Switch OLED:
Support for 50-series Nvidia GPUs with nullmoth:
I'm barely scratching the surface, with further developments in AirDrop, accelerated video decode, and even running translated macOS 27 on x86. As much as we lament the cost of AI, there are some glimmers of hope: you just might be able to have your hardware and own it too.
Join the discussion on Hacker News: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50383057

articles.title: The New York Times is in talks to buy Letterboxd for around $330 million
articles.body:
The New York Times Company is in talks”exclusive negotations” to acquire Letterboxd, the social network for film lovers, for around $330 million, The New York Times reports. The Times Company, Sony Pictures Entertainment, and A24 were all recently rumored to be among those interested in buying Letterboxd.
The New York Times is in talks to buy Letterboxd for around $330 million
Rumors have been swirling about the film lover’s social network for a while, but the NYT reports it’s the buyer.
The negotiations with the Times Company have included the potential for Letterboxd’s co-founders to stay in charge but report to a Times Company executive. Letterboxd would likely remain standalone for the “foreseeable future,” according to the NYT. The company would also integrate the Times Company’s ad tech.
NYT spokesperson Charlie Stadtlander declined to comment. Letterboxd and current parent company Tiny Ltd. didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment from The Verge.
If the NYT does acquire Letterboxd, it would follow other major purchases like Wordle (in a deal in “the low seven figures”), Wirecutter (“slightly more than $30 million”), and The Athletic ($550 million).

articles.title: TikTok launched a dedicated TikTok Shop app
articles.body:
TikTok has released a standalone app for TikTok Shop in a few countries, as spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra. According to its App Store listing, the TikTok Shop app offers:
TikTok launched a dedicated TikTok Shop app
The new TikTok Shop app is now available in a few countries, but not the US.
- Personalized picks inspired by your interests
- LIVE streams & short videos to see products in action
- App-only deals, free shipping offers & exclusive first-order benefits that make every order feel worth it
- Secure payments for safe checkout
- Easy order tracking & 24/7 support from purchase to delivery
But it appears the app, which is also available on Android, hasn’t launched widely yet. Navarra says it’s currently listed in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines, and not in the UK or US App Store. (I’m personally not seeing it on the US App Store on my iPhone.) Still, the fact that the dedicated app exists at all could signal that TikTok is planning to make an even bigger push into online shopping.
TikTok didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

articles.title: Brazilian Credit Guarantor Fund Data Breach Affecting PII and Payout Data
articles.body:
Comunicado importante
Atualização em 05/11/2026.
O FGC informa sobre um incidente de segurança envolvendo dados pessoais tratados pela entidade e esclarece o que foi identificado, as providências adotadas e os cuidados que recomendamos.
Identificamos acesso não autorizado a informações pessoais em ambientes relacionados aos processos internos do fluxo de pagamento de garantia do FGC. Até o momento, não foi identificada nenhuma evidência de que os dados tenham sido divulgados ou utilizados de forma indevida. Também não foi identificada nenhuma perda financeira decorrente do evento. A investigação prossegue, com apoio de empresas especializadas, para esclarecer a extensão do acesso e verificar se houve cópia, divulgação ou utilização indevida das informações.
A suspeita de incidente foi identificada em 26 de outubro de 2026. Desde então, foram adotadas restrições de acesso aos ambientes envolvidos, bloqueio de contas indevidas, preservação de evidências e revisão das permissões e dos controles de segurança.
A Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) foi devidamente comunicada, em conformidade com a legislação vigente. A apuração continua, com apoio de especialistas, e as informações complementares pertinentes serão encaminhadas à Agência conforme o avanço das investigações. Os titulares afetados também foram comunicados.
Reunimos aqui as informações disponíveis e confirmadas nesta etapa. Caso a apuração identifique novos elementos relevantes relacionados a dados pessoais ou as medidas de proteção, atualizaremos as orientações pelos canais oficiais.
Quais dados foram afetados:
- Dados pessoais: nome, CPF, e-mail e data de nascimento;
- Dados relacionados ao pagamento da garantia: informações sobre os tributos retidos no pagamento e sobre o canal de distribuição pelo qual o investimento garantido foi realizado na instituição liquidada.
Principais cuidados e como se proteger
As informações envolvidas podem ser utilizadas para tornar contatos fraudulentos mais convincentes, inclusive em tentativas de uso indevido de identidade ou de obtenção de pagamentos e outras informações pessoais.
Por essa razão, enviamos comunicação aos titulares afetados e recomendamos atenção redobrada a mensagens, ligações e e-mails que mencionem informações pessoais ou relacionadas ao pagamento da garantia, especialmente quando realizadas por pessoas que se apresentem como representantes do FGC ou de outras instituições. Qualquer pessoa, ao receber algum contato suspeito, pode entrar em contato com o FGC.
Destacamos alguns cuidados importantes para a segurança de todos:
- Desconfie de contatos que solicitem pagamentos, senhas, códigos de autenticação ou instalação de aplicativos, mesmo quando mencionarem informações corretas sobre você;
- Não clique em links em mensagens suspeitas. Para acessar informações do processo de pagamento, use diretamente o aplicativo do FGC;
- Confirme informações relacionadas ao processo de pagamento de garantia pelos canais oficiais do FGC;
- Preserve as mensagens suspeitas e registre ocorrência perante as autoridades competentes se identificar tentativa de fraude. Neste caso, avise imediatamente o FGC.
Como os dados são protegidos e o que estamos fazendo
A segurança da informação é prioridade para o FGC que possui arquitetura robusta de proteção, além de equipes especializadas que atuam no monitoramento, na detecção e resposta a ameaças. Os ambientes utilizavam mecanismos de autenticação e controle de acesso. Após a identificação do incidente, restringimos os acessos aos ambientes envolvidos, desabilitamos contas indevidas, reforçamos o monitoramento e preservamos evidências para a investigação. A revisão de permissões e a validação dos controles de segurança permanecem em andamento.
O tema está sendo tratado com a máxima prioridade, tendo como principal preocupação o apoio aos titulares de dados afetados e a revisão contínua dos mecanismos de proteção de dados e de segurança da informação.
Atualizações e orientações sobre o incidente serão disponibilizadas nesta página: fgc.org.br/comunicado.
Para obter mais detalhes sobre dados pessoais ou esclarecer dúvidas específicas, entre em contato com nossa central de atendimento pelo e-mail: atendimento.credores@fgc.org.br.
 
Seguimos à disposição para prestar esclarecimentos e apoiar você nas medidas de prevenção.
Atenciosamente,
Fundo Garantidor de Créditos - FGC
Encarregado de dados – DPO
privacidade@fgc.org.br

articles.title: App Store 2026 in numbers: AI, pricing, abandoned apps
articles.body:
Research · Data as of November 6, 2026
App Store 2026 in numbers
We looked at 178,637 apps that appeared in the App Store top charts of 173 countries and regions since October 9, 2026. Here are the answers to five questions.
Key findings
- About 1 in 10 apps in the charts mention AI in their store listing (9.8%); in Graphics & Design it is 43%.
- Apps that sell in-app purchases or subscriptions are 3 times as likely to mention AI as plain free apps (19.9% vs 6.6%).
- 26.7% of free-to-download apps sell in-app purchases or subscriptions; most in Graphics & Design (60.2%), fewest in Shopping (11.5%).
- 20.3% of apps in the charts have not been updated for a year or more; 9.8% for over three years.
- In 1-2 star reviews the most common complaint is subscription & price (12.7%), ahead of bugs & broken features (10.9%) and login & account (10%).
1. How many apps talk about AI
17,456 apps (9.8%) mention AI, GPT, machine learning, generative or chatbot in their name or the start of their description. They cluster in Graphics & Design, Photo & Video and Developer Tools. Ratings barely differ: among apps with at least 50 ratings, those mentioning AI average 4.49 stars and the rest 4.4.
Show the numbers
2. How free apps make money
Of 164,056 free-to-download apps, 26.7% say in their description that they offer in-app purchases, a subscription, a trial or a Pro unlock. Graphics & Design and Photo & Video lead; Shopping and News come last; many of those are apps of businesses that most likely earn their money outside the app.
Show the numbers
3. How much of the charts independent developers hold
By our definition (see the notes below), 67.3% of apps in the charts come from independent developers. Their ratings match the larger publishers': 4.41 against 4.41 stars for apps with at least 50 ratings. The share is highest in Developer Tools, Sports and Navigation and lowest in Games.
Show the numbers
4. How many apps are no longer maintained
70.9% of apps in the charts were updated in the last six months, yet 20.3% have gone a year or more without an update and 9.8% more than three years. Books, Reference and News have the most apps left alone; Finance the fewest (10.9%).
Show the numbers
5. What bad reviews complain about
We read 165,735 US App Store reviews of 3,912 apps. Among 1-2 star reviews, 12.7% complain about subscription & price, 10.9% about bugs & broken features and 10% about login & account. One review can fall under several themes.
Next edition
We will refresh this report every quarter. From the next edition it will show change over time: which apps moved to subscriptions, how fast the AI share grows, and whether abandoned apps come back.
How to read these numbers
- Scope: 178,637 iPhone, iPad and Mac apps that appeared in an App Store top chart since October 9, 2026. In 12 large markets that means the overall and category charts for free, paid and top grossing apps; elsewhere the overall free chart. Apps never seen in a chart are left out.
- Categories: the app's primary App Store category, with names in other languages merged. Categories with fewer than 1,500 apps have no row of their own.
- Mentions AI: the name or the first 1,500 characters of the description contain AI, GPT, artificial intelligence, machine learning, generative, LLM or chatbot. It shows the app markets itself with AI, not that its features depend on it.
- Sells in-app purchases or subscriptions: free to download, and the description mentions a subscription, in-app purchase, premium, trial, unlock, Pro or a monthly or yearly price. Apps that say nothing may still sell something, so this share is on the low side.
- Independent developer: at most 5 of the developer's apps seen in the charts, no app with 30,000 ratings or more, and a seller name that does not read as a company (Inc, Corp, GmbH and the like). We only see apps that charted, so this share may run high.
- Last update: the release date of the current version on the US App Store.
- Reviews: recent public reviews on the US App Store. Themes come from keywords (for example subscription, ads, crash); shares are of 1-2 star reviews, except feature requests, which are of all reviews. Recent reviews lean negative, so we do not publish the overall share of bad reviews.
- Ratings: only apps with at least 50 ratings count.
Cite and download
The charts and data are free to use, commercial use included (CC BY 4.0). Please credit “Obelisk Club” and link to this page.
Suggested citation
Obelisk Club, “App Store 2026 in numbers”, November 6, 2026, https://obelisk.club/research/app-store-2026

articles.title: Chip stocks get slaughtered as Wall Street in worst post-midterm day since 1896
articles.body:
Wall Street's midterm celebration lasted one day. Chip stocks got taken to the woodshed Thursday, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) fell 3.4%, its worst second session after a midterm election in data going back to its start in 1896.
It took the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) six minutes to erase its entire post-election rally. Then the selling got worse.
The tech-heavy index closed down 5.5%, and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) lost 4.4%. It was the worst day for both since the April 2025 tariff crash.
Investors bought stocks Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, helped by falling oil prices and lower Treasury yields. Thursday, the focus shifted to what a Democratic Congress could mean for the AI build-out, and in particular for the data centers driving it.
It was also the S&P 500's worst second day after a midterm in data going back nearly a century. The previous low came in 2002, when the index fell about 2.3%.
This week has an echo from 1896. The day after William McKinley won the White House that November, the Dow jumped about 4.5%, then gave back about 2% the next session. On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 3%, its best day after a midterm since 1982.
The Nasdaq-100 (^NDX), in correction territory since Monday, fell 6.4% for its worst day since March 2020. The broader Nasdaq Composite joined it, closing nearly 12% below its Oct. 6 record. Both indexes also closed below their 200-day moving averages for the first time since April. Many traders treat that line as the boundary between an uptrend and a downtrend.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) sank 12%, its worst day since March 2020, leaving it about 38% below its June record.
The S&P 500 shed about $3 trillion in market value. Nvidia (NVDA) alone lost about $450 billion, and chipmakers as a group gave up more than $1.5 trillion.
Memory and storage stocks took the worst of it, with SanDisk (SNDK), Western Digital (WDC), Seagate (STX), and Micron (MU) all suffering steep double-digit losses. AMD (AMD), Marvell (MRVL), Arm (ARM), and Lam Research (LRCX) fell sharply too. Even the biggest names, Nvidia, Broadcom (AVGO), and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM), fell 9% or more.
The damage spread across the AI supply chain. Cloud provider Nebius (NBIS) fell double digits and CoreWeave (CRWV) nearly 10%, along with networking and optical names Astera Labs (ALAB), Lumentum (LITE), Coherent (COHR), Dell (DELL), Corning (GLW), and Quanta Services (PWR).
Speculative favorites went down with them. Tesla (TSLA), SpaceX (SPCX), Robinhood (HOOD), Coinbase (COIN), and Strategy (MSTR) each fell 9% or more. (Disclosure: Yahoo Finance has a partnership with Coinbase.)

articles.title: Ember’s smallest self-heating mug is on sale for just $33
articles.body:
We’ve been fans of Ember’s temperature-controlled mugs for years, though given the price tag, we admit that they’re somewhat of a luxury purchase. Thankfully, if you’ve been looking for a more affordable option, Woot is selling the Ember Cup in black for $32.99 ($67 off) with a 90-day warranty through November 7th. You can potentially save even more as part of Woot’s larger Home and Kitchen Sale, which lets you save an additional $20 off orders of $100 or more when you use code COOK at checkout.
Ember’s smallest self-heating mug is on sale for just $33
It may only hold six ounces, but it offers the same customizable temperature settings as Ember’s pricier drinkware.
Granted, six ounces isn’t much, but the smaller, handle-free cup is well-suited for cappuccinos, cortados, flat whites, and other espresso-based drinks. It’s also a perfectly fine option if you don’t mind refilling your cup of coffee, cocoa, or tea throughout the day. I’m actually tempted to pick one up myself at this price, especially since I’ve been trying (with varying degrees of success) to cut back on coffee.
Like Ember’s larger mugs, the smart cup lets you choose and set your drinking temperature between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit using a companion app, then remembers your setting for future drinks. It can then maintain that temperature for up to 95 minutes on a charge, up to four hours with a lid, or even all day if you leave it on the included charging dock. The cup also automatically enters sleep mode after two hours of inactivity to conserve power. Just keep in mind that, despite its IPX7 water-resistance rating, the cup is hand-wash only.

articles.title: How to Get Signed & Personalized Books From Me For the Holidays, 2026 Edition
articles.body:
How to Get Signed & Personalized Books From Me For the Holidays, 2026 Edition
Posted on November 6, 2026 Posted by John Scalzi 1 Comment
We’ve come to that time of the year again, where folks begin to think about their holiday gift giving, and at least some of you think about books as the perfect gift. Well, they are! But would make them even more perfect is getting those books signed and personalized. Every year I join forces with Jay and Mary’s Book Center in Troy, Ohio, to sign and personalize books so that you’ll have them available to give to the people you love, including yourself.
From today (Nov. 6) through Friday, December 4, you can order books I have written from Jay and Mary’s and I will come in and sign them for you, and then the bookstore will ship them to you (US only). I strongly encourage you to get your orders in early, so there are no delays in shipping the books to you this holiday season.
Here’s how to do it!
1. Call Jay & Mary’s at their number (937 335 1167) and let them know that you’d like to order signed copies of my books. Please call rather than send e-mail; they find it easier to keep track of things that way.
2. Tell them which books you would like (For example, Monsters of Ohio ), and what, if any, names you would like the book signed to. If there’s something specific you’d like written in the books let them know, but for their sake and mine, please keep it short. Also, if you’re ordering the book as a gift, make sure you’re clear about whose name the book is being signed to. If this is unclear, I will avoid using a specific name.
3. Order any other books you might think you’d like, written by other people, because hey, you’ve already called a bookstore for books, and helping local independent bookstores is a good thing. I won’t sign these, unless for some perverse reason you want me to, in which case, sure, why not.
4. Give them your mailing address and billing information, etc.
5. And that’s it! Shortly thereafter I will go to the store and sign your books for you.
Again, the deadline for signed/personalized books for 2026 is December 4. After December 4 all Scalzi stock will still be signed and available, but I will likely not be able to personalize.
Also, this is open to US addresses only. Sorry, rest of the world. It’s a cost of shipping thing.
What books are available?
CURRENT HARDCOVER: The current hardcover is Monsters of Ohio. There might be hardcovers of When the Moon Hits Your Eye and The Shattering Peace, both of which came out last year, but you should inquire because stock on those would be limited.
CURRENT TRADE PAPERBACK: As of now, all seven books the Hugo-winning Old Man’s War series (Old Man’s War, The Ghost Bridages, The Last Colony, Zoe’s Tale, The Human Division, The End of All Things, The Shattering Piece) are available in trade paperback with matching cover treatments, so if you wanted to give those seven books as a gift, they are all now a matching set. Other books in trade paperback: When the Moon Hits Your Eye, Starter Villain, The Kaiju Preservation Society, The Android’s Dream, Agent to the Stars and Fuzzy Nation, Redshirts (the 2013 Hugo Award winner), Twenty-First Century Science Fiction (which features a story of mine), Metatropolis (which I edited and contribute a novella to) are all also available in trade paperback format. Also available: Robots Vs. Fairies, the anthology that features the story of mine that was adapted for the “Three Robots” episode of the Netflix animated series Love, Death and Robots.
CURRENT MASS MARKET PAPERBACK: The Mass Market Paperback format is being phased out and stocks of it will become increasingly scarce over time (and the series I have in the format will migrate to trade paperback format eventually). That said, at the moment both my Interdependency series (The Collapsing Empire, The Consuming Fire, The Last Emperox) and my Lock In series (Lock In, Head On, companion novella Unlocked) are still available for purchase.
CURRENT NON-FICTION: Your Hate Mail Will Be Graded (essay collection, Hugo winner).
AUDIOBOOKS: The Kaiju Preservation Society, The Last Emperox, The Consuming Fire, The Collapsing Empire, The Dispatcher, The End of All Things, Lock In, Head On, The Human Division, Redshirts, Fuzzy Nation, The God Engines, Metatropolis and Agent to the Stars are all available on CD and/or MP3 CD, and Jay & Mary’s should be able to special order them for you. Check with them about other titles, which may or may not be currently available on CD.
Two things regarding audiobooks: First, if you want these, you should probably call to order these as soon as possible. Second, and this is important, because the audiobooks come shrinkwrapped, I will have to remove the shrinkwrap in order to sign the cover. You ordering a signed audiobook means you’re okay with me doing that and with Jay & Mary’s shipping it to you out of its shrinkwrap.
If you have any other questions, drop them in the comment thread and I’ll try to answer them!

articles.title: OpenAI Responds to US Midterm Elections With New Commitment to Communities
articles.body:
OpenAI Responds to US Midterm Elections With New Commitment to Communities 71
			
		 	
				"OpenAI has published a new National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint, apparently in response to the Blue Wave Midterm Elections," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. "Instead of moving into communities like a juggernaut, they say they will be dangling friendly carrots going forward." Here's an excerpt from OpenAI's article:  Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We'll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we're doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:
- Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We'll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we'll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.
- Protect local resources and report on our impact. We'll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We'll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.
- Create opportunities for local workers and businesses. We'll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We'll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.
[...] The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That's what we're committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

articles.title: Major Digital Bank In Paraguay Collapses With Half of Population's Savings
articles.body:
Major Digital Bank In Paraguay Collapses With Half of Population's Savings (apnews.com) 81
			
		 	
				Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned Thursday amid mass protests and impeachment threats following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital lender with close ties to his administration and more than 60% of the country's adults as customers. Regulators seized the bank after uncovering risky insider lending and accounting irregularities that left its capital below legal requirements, locking millions of customers out of their savings. The Associated Press reports:  Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium. Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Pena. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender. As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies. Pena repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets. Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left. Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.  Officials say they had begun repaying depositors and opening accounts at other banks for the roughly 280,000 customers who had banked exclusively with Ueno.
"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Pena's request.
Meanwhile, eight senior Ueno executives have been detained, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. "Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud," reports the AP.

articles.title: Microsoft's Imagine Cup 'Evolves' From Student Competition To AI Startup Contest
articles.body:
Microsoft's Imagine Cup 'Evolves' From Student Competition To AI Startup Contest (geekwire.com) 11
			
		 	
				theodp writes:  That Was Then: The Imagine Cup competition, Microsoft explained in a 2003 press release, "seeks to provide students [aged 16-and-up] around the world with resources to use technology and Web services to solve everyday problems [...] Imagine Cup is about empowering students to apply their creativity and knowledge toward making the world a more-connected place."
This Is Now: "Building is Hard. Selling is Harder." begins the "Why Imagine Cup?" promo video for the 2027 Imagine Cup competition, which is pivoting to an AI startup-first focus in recognition that "A new era for founders is here." "Since 2003, Imagine Cup has empowered emerging innovators to turn ambitious ideas into real-world solutions with Microsoft technology," Microsoft writes of the Imagine Cup Evolution. "Now part of Microsoft for Startups, Imagine Cup enters its next chapter in 2027, opening the competition to eligible early-stage startups and founders everywhere."
An Eligibility FAQ drives home the point that Imagine Cup is no longer a student-only competition: "Imagine Cup 2027 welcomes eligible early-stage startups across seven categories; founders do not need to be students." And if you think making high school students compete against seasoned full-time employees of startup companies seems a tad unfair, Microsoft advises: "Eligible student-led startups are encouraged to enter the Student Startup category but may choose an industry category instead." The #1 overall startup will win a $250,000 cash award and $1,000,000 in startup credits. However, Student Startup category entrants are ineligible for the open category prizes (where the 2nd-place winner gets $50,000 cash and $350,000 in credits, while 3rd place is good for $25,000 and $350,000 in credits); they will instead compete for a single prize of $25,000 cash and $250,000 in credits. The Official Rules (PDF) note that all startups must have a valid Azure Subscription ID and a Microsoft for Startups account.

articles.title: The Enough Phone is made by and for people fed up with big screens
articles.body:
It’s a bad time and maybe also a great time to make a new smartphone.
The Enough Phone is made by and for people fed up with big screens
It’s a little phone with a big challenge ahead of it.
Brennan Jordan and Austin Boer are two-thirds of the trio behind the Enough Phone, a small phone that will run your choice of stock Android or the minimalist OdysseyOS. They’re currently seeking funding on Kickstarter, and just a day after launching, the project is over halfway to its $250,000 goal.
The Enough Phone’s target specifications include a 5.3-inch display, 3,500mAh user-replaceable battery, MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chipset, a 50-megapixel Sony sensor in the rear camera, and 8GB of RAM. The dimensions listed on the Kickstarter page suggest an iPhone Mini-ish size; Jordan and Boer also happen to be former iPhone Mini users themselves.
The two of them cofounded a software startup called Sleke, which sells refurbished phones loaded with OdysseyOS, their minimalist, low-distraction version of Android. Putting the software on existing phones is a win for sustainability, but it also helps them get their software to market faster, Boer tells me. The pair offers small batches of Pixel 8 and 9 phones right now through the Sleke website, but the large devices didn’t feel quite right to some customers.
“One of the biggest things that we get is, ‘I don’t want this large of a phone for a minimal operating system,’” says Boer. They’d wanted to make a small phone, and the opportunity arrived when Will Stults approached them about creating one. Stults operates an online store for non-smartphones called Dumbwireless. He also brings familiarity with the smartphone manufacturing process to the mix thanks to some previous work with a “big” phone brand.
But hardware is hard in the best of times, and 2026 has proven extremely challenging for phone companies big and small. The chip shortage has driven prices up and made RAM scarce. Jordan and Boer are feeling the pressures, particularly around pricing. The Kickstarter campaign offers some discounts for early backers, but after that the Enough Phone will sell for $599. “We don’t want to be charging as much as we are,” says Boer, “but as a startup you can only do so much.” They’re a self-funded operation and want to keep it that way, he says, so they can choose their own priorities. Outside funding would change the dynamic and might put pressure on them to shorten their promised five years of software support or cut other costs.
As it stands, the project is on schedule. According to the Kickstarter page, it’s in the production tooling phase, with plans to ship phones to customers in May 2027 — though a footnote says that the RAM shortage’s “ripple effects across the entire electronics manufacturing industry” could still throw a wrench in the works.
Prospects for small phone fans (disclosure: I am one) were bleak even before the chip crisis. Apple’s last Mini was released five years ago, and there’s no indication of another one in sight. Asus’ Zenfone used to be a nice, small-ish Android option before the company made it bigger and quit selling it in the US. Pebble founder Eric Migicovsky made a lot of noise about launching a small phone, but has since shifted priorities. And there’s Unihertz’s Jelly Max — certainly small, but its specs lag behind a modern midrange phone.
Boer sees this gap as an opportunity, even in the midst of a global RAM crisis. “Nobody was doing it, and we’re kind of seeing why — because it’s not the ideal time to start. But that also kind of makes it the ideal time to start, because no one else is doing it,” he says. “Let’s just do it ourselves.” Enough is enough. At least that’s what they’re hoping.

articles.title: OpenAI Finds 948 Local Privilege Escalation Bugs in the Linux Kernel
articles.body:
OpenAI Finds 948 Local Privilege Escalation Bugs In The Linux Kernel
OpenAI published a blog post outlining their work on autonomous vulnerability discovery. To showcase their AI potential, they found 948 valid local privilege escalation vulnerabilities within the Linux kernel.
OpenAI's prototype found 2,308 candidate vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and ultimately found 948 local privilege escalation exploits for allowing unprivileged local users to gain root access. They also generated candidate patches for maintainer review.
Discovering nearly one thousand local privilege escalation vulnerabilities consumed $1.2 million USD in API credits.
OpenAI researchers noted in their blog post:
"Within the next few years, we believe that if there are vulnerabilities in a given software project, frontier models will likely be able to discover them and even less capable models may be able to develop exploits once disclosed. In a world of no unknown vulnerabilities, it will be critical to build and maintain high assurance software, especially core software such as operating systems, browsers, image parsing libraries, the TCP/IP stack, and more. Investing in training models to write secure code by default, minimizing attack surface by removing unnecessary features, and formal verification are promising areas of future research to effectively scale software security, in addition to finding and fixing existing vulnerabilities."
Another interesting takeaway is that their GPT-5.5 Cyber model is finding more than 5x more novel LPEs than their GPT-5.6 Sol model despite three months of hardening/patches in the Linux kernel between scans.
Those wanting to go through this OpenAI showcase in more detail can do so via their blog post.

articles.title: We've built an open-source feature flag server for 11 years
articles.body:
Unleash is a powerful open-source solution for feature management. It streamlines your development workflow, accelerates software delivery, and empowers teams to control how and when they roll out new features to end users. With Unleash, you can deploy code to production in smaller, more manageable releases at your own pace.
Feature flags in Unleash let you test your code with real production data, reducing the risk of negatively impacting your users' experience. It also enables your team to work on multiple features simultaneously without the need for separate feature branches.
Unleash is the most popular open-source solution for feature flagging on GitHub. It supports 15 official client and server SDKs and over 15 community SDKs. You can even create your own SDK if you wish. Unleash is compatible with any language and framework.
To get started with Unleash, you can either explore Unleash Enterprise with a free trial or get started locally with our open-source solution.
To start with Unleash Enterprise, request a free trial. This gives you access to a hosted instance with unlimited projects and environments and features such as role-based access control, change requests, single sign-on, and SCIM for automatic user provisioning.
To set up Unleash locally, you'll need git and docker installed on your machine.
Execute the following commands:
git clone git@github.com:Unleash/unleash.git
cd unleash
docker compose up -d
Then point your browser to localhost:4242 and log in using:
- username: admin
- password: unleash4all
If you'd rather run the source code in this repo directly via Node.js, see the step-by-step instructions to get up and running in the contributing guide.
Find your preferred SDK in our list of official SDKs and import it into your project. Follow the setup guides for your specific SDK.
If you use the docker compose file from the previous step, here's the configuration details you'll need to get going:
- For frontend SDKs, use:
  - URL: http://localhost:4242/api/frontend/
  - clientKey: default:development.unleash-insecure-frontend-api-token
- For backend SDKs, use:
  - Unleash API URL: http://localhost:4242/api/
  - API token: default:development.unleash-insecure-api-token
If you use a different setup, your configuration details will most likely also be different.
Checking the state of a feature flag in your code is easy! The syntax will vary depending on your language, but all you need is a simple function call to check whether a flag is available. Here's how it might look in Java:
if (unleash.isEnabled("AwesomeFeature")) {
  // do new, flashy thing
} else {
  // do old, boring stuff
}
Want to explore Unleash without setting it up locally? Here are two easy ways to see it in action.
Open a running Unleash environment in your browser with no signup or setup required. This shared demo instance includes the core functionality so you can quickly get a feel for how Unleash works.
Get your own dedicated instance with a free 14-day cloud trial. This includes the full Unleash Enterprise feature set; ideal when evaluating Unleash for production use.
To self-host Unleash in a production environment, you need to deploy it to a persistent server.

For more advanced configurations options, check out our documentation on:

💻 Create a GitHub issue if you have found a bug or have ideas on how to improve Unleash.
📚 Visit the documentation for more in-depth descriptions, how-to guides, and more.
📖 Learn more about the principles of building and scaling feature flag solutions.
Unleash is the largest open-source feature flag solution on GitHub. Building Unleash is a collaborative effort, and we owe a lot of gratitude to many smart and talented individuals. Building it together with the community ensures that we build a product that solves real problems for real people. We'd love to have your help too: Please feel free to open issues or provide pull requests.
Check out the CONTRIBUTING.md file for contribution guidelines and the Unleash developer guide for tips on environment setup, running the tests, and running Unleash from source. Before a pull request can be merged, contributors must read and agree to the Unleash Contributor License Agreement.
You can visit the Unleash documentation at https://docs.getunleash.io. As of 2 February 2026, the Unleash documentation source code lives in its own repository: Unleash/unleash-documentation.

- Targeted releases using activation strategies to enable and disable features for certain users or segments without having to redeploy your application.
- Canary releases / gradual rollouts
- Kill switches
- A/B testing
- 2 environments
- Organize feature flags using tags
- Out-of-the-box integrations with popular tools (Slack, Microsoft Teams, Datadog) + integrate with anything with webhooks

- Privacy by design (GDPR and Schrems II). End-user data never leaves your application.

- Flexible hosting options: host it on premise or in the cloud (any cloud)
- Scale with Unleash Edge independently of the Unleash server to support any number of frontend clients without overloading your Unleash instance

- tighter security

articles.title: Hardcoded credentials and other issues in Tata Motors App
articles.body:
Original Issue Date:November 04, 2026 Severity Rating: HIGH
Systems Affected
Overview
Multiple vulnerabilities have been reported in Tata Motors iRA and iRA.ev applications, which could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive credentials or access to vehicle related information and services.
Target Audience: Users of the affected iRA 2.0 and iRA.ev mobile applications.
Risk Assessment: Risk of unauthorized access to sensitive information, user impersonation and unauthorized modification of application data.
Impact Assessment: Potential for unauthorized access and modification of data with the privileges of the impersonated user.
Description
Solution
Upgrade to latest versions:

articles.title: Claude was faster and cheaper. We took the scenic route anyway
articles.body:
Verify, Then Vote
We gave five small local models the same questions and checked their sources before picking an answer. Our first paper reports what got better, a safety test that failed and how we can rerun decisions without asking the models again.
When five models disagree
We wanted to see how far a few small models could get running on one machine. We gave five of them the same question, let them look things up and compared their answers. They often disagreed. The obvious fix is a vote, but models can share the same mistake and a vote can’t catch that.
So we tried something else: check the sources each model cited, then use a fixed rule to pick the answer. We called the paper Verify, Then Vote. We kept answering, checking and choosing as separate steps and saved the results of each, so we could go back and reuse them.
Five local models and one checker
We used Llama 3.2 3B, Mistral 7B, Gemma 2 2B, Phi-3 mini and Qwen 2.5 3B, running through Ollama on an Apple M3 Pro with 36 GB of RAM. We left it running overnight and it finished in about eight hours.
Each model wrote a search query and got back five passages: Wikipedia for general questions, research abstracts for science claims. It then gave an answer, said how confident it was and cited up to three passages. We saved everything before any answer was picked.
To check sources, we used Claude Sonnet 5.5 as a separate hosted model. It saw only one sentence stating the answer and one cited passage and said whether the passage supported the answer, contradicted it or didn’t say enough. It never saw the correct answer.
A supported answer can still be wrong
If a passage says Sydney is the capital of Australia, it supports the answer “Sydney,” even though the capital is Canberra. Our check asks whether the passage backs up the answer. It doesn’t ask whether the passage is true.
Our rule starts with the answer that got the most votes and breaks ties the same way every time. It only switches to a different answer if the checker says a cited passage supports it. Every switch keeps a record of the passage and the check behind it, so we can see why it happened.
We also proved one thing about the rule using Lean 4, software that checks mathematical proofs: if the rule ever swaps a correct answer for a wrong one, a source check must have backed the wrong answer. That tells us where to look when something goes wrong. It doesn’t prove the source was true or that the checker read it correctly.
91 fixes, 12 new mistakes and a failed test
We tuned the settings on a separate practice set, then ran the rule on 1,000 main questions. Accuracy went from 77.1% with a simple majority vote to 85.0% with our rule.
On 526 of those questions, the models gave a mix of right and wrong answers. There, the rule fixed 91 answers the vote got wrong and broke 12 the vote got right, raising accuracy from 71.5% to 86.5%. One caveat: the vote broke ties at random, while our rule always broke them the same way, so part of the gain came from how ties were handled.
Before we started, we set a limit on how many right answers the rule could break. Of 376 answers the vote got right, the rule made 12 wrong (3.2%). Allowing for chance, the true rate could be as high as 5.5%, above our 5% limit. So the original rule failed our test. We had written down the plan and analysis before collecting data, though we didn’t file them in a public registry.
We also wanted to know whether the checker was really reading the passages. So we ran it again with the cited text removed or swapped for unrelated text. Either way, 76 of the 91 fixes disappeared. The passages mattered, though Sonnet may still lean on what it already knows when the right text is in front of it.
Keep the answer if it’s already backed up
That result suggested a more careful rule: if the starting answer already has a source backing it, keep it. We wrote down that change before collecting answers from five different models on the same questions and reused existing checks wherever the answer and passage were the same.
With the new models, 547 questions had a mix of right and wrong answers. The revised rule fixed 73 and broke three, raising accuracy from 73.1% to 85.9%. Of 400 answers the vote got right, three became wrong (0.75%) and the worst-case rate was 2.2%, well under our 5% limit.
So the revised rule passed with a new set of models. Because the questions were the same and we designed the change after seeing the first results, this shows the rule carries over to other models, not that it works on new questions.
Why not just let Sonnet choose?
We tried that too. Given the same answers and passages, Sonnet picked the right one 93.9% of the time on the first group’s 526 mixed questions, compared with 86.5% for our rule. It was also cheaper: about $0.014 per question, versus $0.021 for checking sources. Neither number includes the cost of the models writing their answers.
So Sonnet is better at making the first call. Our approach helps afterward. Because every check is saved, we can see exactly why an answer was picked and try a different rule without paying for new checks. You can log a judge’s choice too, but asking it to choose again means another call.
Rerun decisions without another model call
Across all 1,100 questions, including a separate set of 100 from TruthfulQA, the models disagreed on 702. To see how much each model mattered, a Python script dropped one model at a time and handed the remaining saved answers to our Rust program to choose again. Five reruns per question came to 3,510 in total.
All of them took 23 seconds with no new model calls. The chosen answer changed 9.4% of the time, which shows how much the outcome depends on which models take part. Rerunning all 1,100 original decisions gave exactly the same output.
This works because answering, checking and choosing are kept separate. We can change how answers are chosen while the saved answers and checks stay the same. New answers or sources would need new checks.
What we want to try next
Next we need new questions, not just new rules. Because we keep every run, we can dig into a decision, change the rule and measure the effect before paying to collect more answers.
The paper, code, proofs and saved runs are on GitHub, with scripts to reproduce our results and try your own rules on the same data.
The record
Sources & methods
These links point to the paper, code and saved experiment records on GitHub.

articles.title: MoofTCP – A modern replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs
articles.body:
A modern, memory-lean replacement for MacTCP on 68k Macs running System 6.
MoofTCP is a drop-in replacement for Apple's MacTCP. Programs written for MacTCP run on it unchanged, but underneath it is a fresh TCP/IP stack written from scratch in portable C, with its own control panel, installer and DHCP client. It was built for a Mac Classic with 4 MB of RAM, so every byte counts.
MacTCP is wonderful, but it is old, and on a 4 MB Mac Classic with a SCSI Wi-Fi/Ethernet adapter like BlueSCSI it can be slow to answer, hungry for memory, and awkward to set up. MoofTCP aims, in this order, for:
- Reliability. No hangs, no leaks, no surprises when apps quit.
- Low latency for interactive use, like typing in a telnet session.
- Throughput, for handling quasi-modern use cases.
...all while using no more resident memory than MacTCP does.
- Drop-in compatible. Implements the MacTCP .IPP driver interface (TCP, UDP, ICMP echo) and the dnrp name resolver. Your existing MacTCP programs just work.
- DHCP or a fixed address. Pick either in the control panel. Don't need to manage static IP anymore.
- MoofTCP Lite. A build without DHCP that saves about 5 KB of system memory, for tight machines. One installer holds both; a checkbox picks which one.
- A friendly installer. It moves MacTCP's files aside, installs MoofTCP, and its Remove button puts everything back exactly as it was. An interrupted install repairs itself.
- MultiFinder-aware. Quitting an app that had connections open cleans up after it.
- Built-in diagnostics. An optional in-memory log and a small MoofDiag tool for bug reports.
- A portable core. The TCP/IP stack in core/ has no malloc and no global state, and is tested on the
desktop with sanitizers and fuzzers.
- Download MoofTCP-1.0.dsk, MoofTCP-1.0.hqx or MoofTCP-1.0.sit from the
Releases page and get it onto your Mac (a BlueSCSI shared folder works well).
- Open MoofTCP Installer, leave Lite version (no DHCP) unticked, and click Install.
- Restart the Mac.
- Open Control Panels, MoofTCP, enter your IP address, mask, router and DNS server (or tick Get the address by DHCP), and save.
- Restart again. You're online.
To go back to MacTCP, run the installer and click Remove. The Read Me file in the release has the
details, including how to switch between MoofTCP and MoofTCP Lite.
StuffIt Lite 3.6 is tested as working for expanding the .hqx packages.
- A 68k Mac with System 6.0.8 (the version it was tested on). Please report back if it works on other versions!
- An Ethernet adapter that provides the .ENET0 driver, such as a BlueSCSI v2 WiFi with DaynaPORT. MoofTCP
does not include an Ethernet driver.
Tested on a real Mac Classic (System 6.0.8, 4 MB, BlueSCSI v2 WiFi with DaynaPORT) and in the Snow emulator.
Have a program that doesn't work? Please open an issue (see below).
MultiFinder grows the system heap on demand, so free memory varies more there.
MoofTCP keeps a small diagnostic log in memory. If a program misbehaves but the Mac keeps running, run
MoofDiag right away (it is in the release's diagnostic tools download), and open an issue with the
MoofDiag.out file it writes next to itself, plus a note about what you were doing. Feel free to ask your LLM
to analyze the codebase and the diagnostic output as well and to submit fix PRs.
- No IPv6.
- Tested only with the DaynaPORT Ethernet driver on System 6.0.8.
- DHCP is basic: no lease RELEASE, no INIT-REBOOT and no address-conflict probe. While it runs, programs cannot use UDP port 68. With no DHCP server, the first open waits about 10 seconds and then fails.
You only need Docker. The pinned Retro68 cross-compiler image is pulled automatically.
scripts/build-mac.sh MoofTCP              # the MoofTCP file -> build-mac/moof/
MT_LITE=1 scripts/build-mac.sh MoofTCP    # MoofTCP Lite -> build-mac-lite/
scripts/release.sh --force 1.0            # one installer with both -> dist/MoofTCP-1.0.{dsk,hqx,sit}
release.sh also needs hfsutils, macutils, unar, gcc and Python 3.
The portable core and the glue logic are tested on your desktop with gcc and CMake (AddressSanitizer and UBSan are on by default):
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
cmake -S . -B build-lite -DMT_NO_DHCP=ON   # the Lite configuration
The emulator tests (Snow) need Apple system software and the BlueSCSI DaynaPORT image. Those are not in this
repository and you must supply them yourself; the scripts in scripts/ (setup-home.sh, golden-stage.sh) show
what is expected.
core/      portable TCP/IP stack (no malloc, no globals), host-tested
mac/       Mac glue: .IPP driver, INIT, resolver, control panel, installer, diagnostic apps
tests/     host tests (ctest), including fuzzers
scripts/   build, release, emulator and hardware-session scripts
tools/     pinned tool versions; tools/sit is a small StuffIt-format writer
Bug reports, compatibility reports ("program X does/doesn't work") and pull requests are welcome. For code
changes, please read CONTRIBUTING.md and run the host tests first (see above). CLAUDE.md is a
detailed map of the code and its rules. Security problems: see SECURITY.md.
- Retro68 for the 68k cross-compiler.
- Snow for the Mac emulator the tests run in.
- BlueSCSI and DaynaPORT for the network hardware this was built around.
- Claude Code was used to develop this project, with human planning and testing.
- More comprehensive bake-in testing on real hardware as we use it
- Remake Daynaport similarly (stay tuned for MoofPort)
- Review the BlueSCSI codebase for opportunities to integrate more tightly for better performance
- There is potential for further algorithm optimization for added performance on smaller or older systems.
MIT. "MacTCP" and "StuffIt" are trademarks of their owners and are used here only to describe compatibility. MoofTCP contains no Apple or third-party code; building it uses Apple's interfaces as shipped in the Retro68 toolchain.

articles.title: Meta’s warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
articles.body:
Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has “not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments.”
Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people’s feelings about AI technology overall.
“The visible sort of manifestation of AI is a data center, and it’s something that people can say, ‘I don’t want this in my community,’” she explained. “I think there’s an underlying bigger issue, which is how people feel about AI in general.”
Meta believes it could turn around the negative consumer sentiment around AI if it’s able to demonstrate the value, not only of the data centers coming to local communities, but also in the technology itself.
“The stakes of who builds the technology that cures cancer, that gives access to education, that is also a very fundamental difference … Mark [Zuckerberg, Meta CEO] is very ‘long human,’ and he’s betting on humans more than machines,” Powell McCormick explained. “And that’s what we mean when we say the future is for everyone. That people should not be left behind. But the way to ensure that is that this technology is democratized, that people have access to it in a very fair and transparent way,” she said.
The exec also touted Meta’s experience in building data centers, saying that the company has been doing so for 20 years, as it takes a lot of compute power to offer the products it does in the social networking space. Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.
But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.
“I think it’s going to be harder,” Powell McCormick said, describing what the future of building data centers looks like. “It has been hard, I should say, but I also think that it’s becoming clear what models work, and the states want those models that work.”
Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today uses to close its data center deals in local communities.
Successful projects see Meta paying for its own electricity, directing any tax surpluses as a result of the data centers toward teachers and first responders, keeping the labor force local, and getting bipartisan support for the project, among other things.
Going forward, she expects data center projects to come under more review and be weighed against whether the constituents actually want them.
Meta has pinned its hopes on its AI investments, particularly its consumer AI agent Muse scaling far beyond the 10 million users it has today, to become a business that one day serves billions. But even if that’s not the case, it believes that its investments in data centers will not be for nothing, as the compute itself will be valuable.
“We’re getting calls every day to lease that compute [we’ve built], and so one way or another, we’re seeing a path to monetization,” Powell McCormick said.

articles.title: NTS: Authenticated Time at Meta
articles.body:
- Meta’s public time service now speaks NTS (Network Time Security, RFC 8915) at nts.meta.com. Packets are authenticated, so a device can verify the time came from us and was not modified on the way.
- Our NTS servers hold no per-client state. Cookie keys are derived, not stored and not replicated.
- We’ve open sourced everything, including the protocol, server, client through Meta’s Time library on GitHub.
- We’re also encouraging everyone, particularly those who maintain an NTP client on Android or iOS, to join us in enabling NTS support.
We’ve previously written about building a more accurate time service at Meta scale – migrating from ntpd to chrony, going from 10 milliseconds to 100 microseconds, and opening time.meta.com to everyone.
That work made time precise. This work makes it verifiable.
Why NTS?
NTP has been unauthenticated since 1985, like a lot of the internet’s foundational protocols. But it is also the one every certificate, token, and signature is checked against. The client sends 48 bytes, something sends 48 bytes back, and the client believes it. There is no signature and no identity.
It is not alone in that. Plenty of the internet’s foundational protocols were designed for a network where nobody was assumed to be hostile, and the industry has been retrofitting them ever since. What makes time different is that it is not just another protocol to secure. It is the input every other security decision is measured against.
For most of NTP’s life that did not matter much, because a clock being a few seconds off was an operational annoyance. Today it is load-bearing:
- Certificate validation: notBefore and notAfter are compared against the local clock. Wrong clock, wrong answer.
- Token and credential expiry: “Valid for 15 minutes” is a claim about a clock.
- Replay windows: Rejecting a request older than N seconds requires knowing what time it is.
- Log correlation and ordering: Two hosts that disagree produce a timeline that never happened.
And the check itself is circular. You can’t do X.509 notBefore/notAfter validation without knowing the current time. Effectively you’d have to disable cert time validation, or implement one of the suggested work-arounds.
There are two common workarounds. Both are bad. You can skip validation until the clock is set, which leaves a device unprotected exactly when it is most exposed. Or you can build in-slack: A certificate issued at 12:00:00 is rejected by a client whose clock reads 11:59:30, so issuers backdate notBefore by a few minutes and validators quietly widen the window at their end. Both sides are guessing at how wrong the other one is.
That was survivable when a certificate lasted 398 days. CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3 changed that. The cap on newly issued publicly trusted TLS certificates dropped to 200 days in March 2026, falls to 100 days in March 2027, and reaches 47 days in March 2029 — with domain validation reuse dropping to 10 days at the same point.
At 47 days, manual certificate management stops being viable at any scale. Renewal moves to roughly monthly, and it happens unattended — usually over ACME. An automated renewal loop on a host with a skewed clock does not raise a ticket. It reissues, or it fails, on a schedule nobody is watching.
How NTS Works
NTS works in phases, and separating them is what makes it deployable.
Phase 1 – Key Establishment (NTS-KE): TLS 1.3 over TCP/4460, negotiated with ALPN ntske/1. The client and server agree on an AEAD algorithm, then derive two directional session keys (C2S and S2C) straight from the TLS session using the RFC 5705 exporter. The server issues eight cookies, tells the client which NTP server to actually use via a server negotiation record, and closes the connection. This happens once, not per packet.
We negotiate three AEADs: AES-SIV-CMAC-256 (ID 15), which RFC 8915 makes mandatory to implement and is what an unknown client is most likely to ask for; AES-SIV-CMAC-512 (17); and AES-128-GCM-SIV (30). Client preference wins.
Phase 2 – Authenticated NTP: Standard NTPv4 over UDP/123 to the advertised server, with NTS extension fields. A request carries a unique identifier, a cookie, and an authenticator; the authenticator covers everything before it, but encrypts nothing. The server opens the cookie to recover the session keys, verifies that authenticator, and replies with the unique identifier echoed back plus an authenticator of its own – and that one does carry a payload: the fresh cookies, encrypted inside it.
A forged packet fails verification and is dropped. We do not send an NTS NAK, so a failure is indistinguishable from packet loss and cannot be used to push a client into a fresh key exchange. A replayed response carries the wrong unique identifier and matches no outstanding request. Because the replacement cookies ride inside the response authenticator rather than in the clear, an observer sees a different opaque blob every exchange and cannot follow a client between networks. Spending each cookie once is the client’s side of that bargain – the server is stateless and does not track them.
Cookies Without State
A cookie is a server state handed to the client for safekeeping. It holds the session keys, sealed with AES-SIV so only the server can open it. The obvious implementation is a key ring replicated to every server, which turns time service into a distributed state problem.
We do not replicate keys. Each server derives the sealing key from a shared master secret and the current day:
Since the Unix epoch, day is measured as whole 24-hour periods,  not a calendar day. So there is no timezone and no DST, and every host computes the same integer for the same instant. That integer is the cookie’s key ID and travels in the clear. A server that has been handed a cookie it has never seen or sealed by a host it has never talked to, re-derives the key and opens it. We accept two days back and one forward to cover skew around a rotation boundary.
The result is no key ring, no replication, no session table, no shared state to fall out of sync, and nothing for an attacker to exhaust. It is also what makes the split above work – the KE server and the NTP servers it hands you off to are different machines in different places, and they never exchange anything. Adding a server is adding a server.
The plain NTP path is untouched. The responder parses extension fields only when they are present, so unauthenticated clients hit the same code as before at the same cost.
Using NTS
One line of chrony config:
nts.meta.com terminates key exchange only. During the handshake it advertises an NTP responder in a server negotiation record, so the client is steered to time.meta.com and sends its authenticated NTP there. The host you configure is not the host you end up talking to.
That indirection is why we use pool rather than server. A single server line gives you one association and one responder, which is a single point of failure – and NTP is a protocol that wants several sources so it can outvote a bad one. pool asks for maxsources independent associations. Each runs its own key exchange over its own TLS session, so each ends up with a distinct pair of session keys:
Five rows, five independent authenticated sources, from one line of config and one KE endpoint.
Reading across: Type 30 is the negotiated AEAD, AES-128-GCM-SIV, with KLen 128 bits of session key — chrony lists it first and client preference wins. CLen 68 is the cookie: 36 bytes of envelope around the two 16-byte keys inside. Cook 8 is cookies in hand and NAK 0 means none has been rejected.
The more interesting half is not in the table. Each row’s session keys came out of its own TLS handshake and work only for that association. The key that seals them into a cookie is the shared one – the epoch day number from the derivation above, identical on every responder we run, stamped inside each cookie and never visible to the client. That split is what lets a single key exchange hand a client five different responders that have never spoken to each other.
When a pool member completes key exchange and moves to its negotiated responder, the freed KE address is handed to the next unresolved member, repeating until maxsources responders have answered. Five sources come up in about 20 minutes as each member completes its own key exchange in turn.
NTS Protects Against Attacks
Unlike NTP, NTS stops a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack from forging the answer. A classic MITM attack doesn’t need to break any cryptography, it just has to answer a client before a real server does. If an attacker rolls the clock backward they can make expired certificates validate again or revoked tokens work again. Any control that relies on something having expired is reset. If they roll the clock forward everything expires at once. This is the more difficult direction to address because beyond a certain point the failure stops being recoverable.
Let’s look at an example of what happens to a device that gets convinced it is the year 2037. NTP counts seconds in a 32-bit field that wraps in February 2036, and a client stranded on the far side of that boundary computes its correction into the wrong era – so the mechanism that exists to fix a wrong clock now moves it further away. Meanwhile every certificate the device holds is long expired, so TLS fails, therefore it cannot reach anything that might help, including its own update service. The patch that would fix it cannot be delivered, because delivering it needs the clock that is broken.
The device is not damaged. Every component works exactly as designed. It is simply holding a number that puts it outside the reach of the network. And no amount of waiting or rebooting fixes it. Recovery means a factory reset, or a trip to a service center. Multiply that by a fleet and the cost of a wrong integer becomes a logistics problem.
Now, consider a clock forward attack on a host that issues credentials. Short-lived credentials are considered safe because they expire quickly, which means short lifetime is doing the job revocation would otherwise do. That property is entirely a function of the issuing host’s clock. An issuer convinced it is next year signs credentials that outlive the window you designed for.
What NTS Does Not Fix
Delay attacks. RFC 8915 is explicit. An attacker who holds your packets shifts your clock by up to half the delay introduced, and no cryptography in the protocol detects it, because every byte is genuine. Authentication tells you who wrote a packet, not how long it spent in flight. Mitigations are the usual ones – multiple independent sources, sanity limits, bounded steps.
So the claim is narrow: An on-path attacker can still delay your packets and can still drop them. What they can no longer do is lie about the contents.
Bootstrapping. NTS-KE runs over TLS and TLS wants a working clock, which is the same circular problem as above. A device with a dead RTC still has to get roughly correct before its first handshake.
Wrong servers. NTS authenticates the path, not the answer. A server that is correctly configured, correctly authenticated, and simply wrong will hand you the wrong time with a perfect signature on it. Quorum, sanity checks, and monitoring are still required.
Monotonicity. Authenticated time is still wall-clock time, and wall clocks move backward — at a leap second, or whenever a correction lands. Cloudflare’s authoritative DNS hit this at the end of 2016: a resolver round-trip measured across the leap second came out negative, propagated into upstream selection, and panicked Go’s rand.Int63n(). Nothing was forged and nothing was misdelivered. If your code measures elapsed time, use a monotonic clock.
Adoption
RFC 8915, Network Time Security for the Network Time Protocol, was published on the IETF Standards Track as a Proposed Standard in September 2020. Cloudflare had launched time.cloudflare.com with NTS 15 months earlier, in June 2019, against the then-current draft, and showed it works at scale.
Server-side, the public NTS list today runs to a few dozen entries, mostly national metrology institutes and internet infrastructure operators such as PTB, Netnod, and time.nl. We are adding one more.
The bigger gap is on the client. NTS support exists where you would expect it in the server world – chrony and ntpsec implement it. It is absent entirely from the stock time client on the platforms that account for most of the endpoints on the internet.
Android’s platform time sync is plain SNTP over UDP/123 – a fixed 48-byte packet with no extension-field handling, alongside NITZ and GNSS – so there is no NTS path in it. Apple devices sync through timed against time.apple.com, where we are not aware of any NTS support either.
Those two stacks set the clock on billions of phones, watches and headsets, and every one of them is trusting an unauthenticated UDP packet. A device vendor can ship a separate NTS-capable client today — chrony runs perfectly well on Android – but that is a workaround for something the platform should do itself.
The protocol is finished, the servers are appearing, the client implementations exist.
What is missing is mobile.
Join Us in Enabling NTS
nts.meta.com is live and free. The code is in github.com/facebook/time.
If you run a public time service, turn NTS on. If you maintain an NTP client, implement RFC 8915. If you own the time stack in a mobile OS, this is the gap – Android and iOS are where most of the world’s clocks get set, and both of them are still doing it over an unauthenticated packet.
We have spent years making time more precise. Precision without authenticity only gets you a very accurate number from an unknown source. Now it can be both.
Acknowledgements
We’d like to thank Sofia Scalzo, Pablo Mazzini, Vadim Fedorenko, Patrick Cullen, and Yixin Wei for their support on this project.

articles.title: Vibe Coding Keypad
articles.body:
Kick-start your next idea
Open a new chat with one press. Explore a different approach or start the next task in its own conversation.
Shipping will start within 2 working days.
Keychron F4 HE 8K Vibe Coding Keypad - White is backordered and will ship as soon as it is back in stock.
Keychron F4 HE 8K Vibe Coding Keypad is a compact four-key keypad featuring Ultra-fast Lime magnetic switches and an 8K polling rate. Customize each key for macros, keyboard inputs, gaming controls, or shortcuts through Keychron Launcher for faster, more efficient control.
Color: White
The Keychron F4 HE 8K is a four-key controller for working with AI. Send the prompt. Dictate the next one. Accept the change. Reject the bad idea. Each action is one press, so you stay in the review-and-refine loop instead of hunting for shortcuts across a full keyboard.
COMING SOON
Keychron T1 HE
Wireless Trackball Mouse
Be first in line for the launch update
Meet the First Trackball Mouse with 3-Axis Adjustment.
Be first in line for the launch updates
Working with an AI assistant collapses into a few moves you repeat all day: send a prompt, speak the next one, approve what came back, or throw it out and go again. The F4 gives each move its own key with an icon cap to match, so the loop runs through your fingers, not through menus.
Off the clock, the same four keys handle whatever you repeat most: copy/paste, meeting mute, window snapping, or a macro chain.
Start voice input with a tap. Talk through a feature idea or describe what went wrong while it’s still fresh in your mind.
Turn the prompts you use most into one-press shortcuts. Ask AI to review a code change for bugs without typing out the same request again.
Thanks to Dynamic Keystrokes (DKS), you can now assign up to 4 distinct actions per key based on press depth. A light press moves your character, a deeper press makes them run, and releasing the key enables additional commands. This layered control lets you execute multiple moves with ease.
Plug in, open launcher in your browser, and the F4 is ready to configure. Choose a ready-made preset for Codex or Claude and go, or remap the keys, record macros, adjust the actuation point. Prefer to just say it? The built-in AI assistant sets keys up from a plain-language request. 
The Codex and Claude presets each include a key for voice input. Follow the Start guide to set it up.
*The F4 does not have a built-in microphone. For voice input, use your computer's built-in microphone or an external one.
* Please use the latest version of Chrome / Opera / Edge browser to open the Launcher and connect it to your device via USB-C cable. The version of Keychron Launcher shown here is in beta. The official release is scheduled for November 9, 2026.
1.  Plug in via USB-C.
2. Open launcher.keychron.com. 
3. Pick a preset or ask the AI assistant.
Every key you program gets a cap to match. Pick from 15 icon legends in Cherry-profile dye-sub PBT. Set up a loadout for the way you work.
*The image shows suggested keycap combinations. Remap the keys in Keychron Launcher to assign the corresponding actions.
Your layout saves to the F4 itself. Plug into a different computer and your four actions are already there. No account, no sync, no setup twice.
With per-key RGB, give each key a color that matches its job, such as green to accept, red to reject, or choose from 22 backlight effects to make your setup your own.
Map the keys to your in-game moves, such as weapon swaps, abilities, push-to-talk, and tune how deep each press registers. Magnetic switches and wired 8,000 Hz polling keep every action responsive.
Comes with Keychron Ultra-Fast Lime Magnetic Switches, it delivers smooth, stable keystrokes with adjustable actuation point from 0.20 to 3.30 mm with 0.1 mm sensitivity. Choose a shallower setting to register a press sooner or a deeper setting for more deliberate input.
*8,000 Hz polling requires a USB-C cable that supports an 8K polling rate.
With a wired polling rate of 8,000 Hz, the F4 HE 8K can report key inputs to your computer up to 8,000 times per second, delivering responsive input. Pair it with an 8K-rated cable like the Keychron Coiled Aviator Cable 8K since standard USB-C cables cap the polling rate.
Need a break? The F4 taps like a fidget piece — smooth keystrokes, soft sound. And at 44.94 mm square with a lanyard, it leaves the desk as easily as it lives on it: clip it to your bag and take your shortcuts along.

October 2026
