articles.title: Building a Multi-Agent System from Scratch: Architecture Patterns
articles.body:
Building a Multi-Agent System from Scratch: Architecture Patterns
Orchestrator-worker, blackboard, and pipeline patterns for coordinating multiple AI agents — with the failure modes that only show up once you go past a single-agent demo.
A single well-tuned agent is easy to demo. Give it a clear goal, a handful of tools, and a generous system prompt, and it'll look impressive in a five-minute walkthrough. I wrote about exactly that kind of agent in an earlier post — a single agent that turned natural-language restaurant queries into structured search filters. It worked well because the problem had one shape: understand the query, call some tools, format the answer.
Multi-agent systems are a different animal. The moment you have more than one agent, you've introduced a coordination problem on top of the reasoning problem, and coordination is where almost all of the real engineering effort goes. Nobody warns you about this in the demos, because demos are built to succeed once, not to run in production for six months against inputs nobody anticipated.
This post is about the three architecture patterns I keep coming back to when splitting work across multiple agents, and — more importantly — the failure modes that only show up once you're past a single-agent demo and into something that has to run unattended.
Why split into multiple agents at all?
Mostly for the same reason you split code into functions: a single agent juggling retrieval, domain reasoning, validation, and formatting in one prompt tends to do all four things a little worse than four agents each doing one thing well. Narrower responsibility means a shorter, more focused system prompt, which means more predictable behavior and easier evaluation.
Pattern 1: Orchestrator-Worker
This is the pattern most people reach for first, and for good reason — it maps cleanly onto how a human manager delegates work. One orchestrator agent receives the task, breaks it into subtasks, dispatches each subtask to a specialized worker agent, and aggregates the results into a final answer. Workers don't talk to each other; they only talk to the orchestrator.
Task → Orchestrator
              ├─→ Worker A (research)
              ├─→ Worker B (code generation)
              └─→ Worker C (validation)
                     ↓
             Orchestrator aggregates → Final answer
This pattern fits when the task decomposition is clear upfront — you know in advance that answering the question requires "look something up," "generate something," and "check it," even if you don't know the specifics until runtime. The orchestrator's only job is planning and aggregation, which keeps its prompt small and its behavior predictable. The tradeoff is that the orchestrator becomes a bottleneck: every piece of context has to flow through it, and if it misjudges the decomposition, every worker downstream inherits that mistake.
Pattern 2: Blackboard
The blackboard pattern drops the strict hierarchy. Instead of a central orchestrator directing traffic, agents read from and write to a shared state store — the "blackboard" — and each agent decides for itself when it has something useful to contribute. There's usually a lightweight scheduler that decides which agent gets to act next based on what's currently on the blackboard, but there's no single agent that owns the plan.
         ┌────────────────────────┐
         │   Shared Blackboard    │
         │  (partial state,      │
         │   hypotheses, facts)  │
         └───────────┬────────────┘
        read/write    │    read/write
     ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
     ↓                 ↓                 ↓
 Agent A           Agent B           Agent C
(hypothesis)      (evidence)        (critique)
I reach for this pattern when the solution path genuinely isn't known ahead of time — debugging a subtle production issue, for instance, where one agent proposes a hypothesis, another gathers evidence for or against it, and a third critiques the reasoning. Nobody could have written that as a fixed sequence of steps beforehand, because the next useful action depends entirely on what's already been discovered.
The cost of that flexibility is that blackboard systems are much harder to reason about and to test. There is no single place where "the plan" lives, so debugging a bad outcome means reconstructing the entire sequence of reads and writes after the fact — closer to debugging a race condition than debugging a function call stack.
Pattern 3: Pipeline
The pipeline pattern is the simplest of the three, and it's the one I default to whenever the workflow is well-understood and repeatable. A fixed sequence of specialized agents, each handing its output to the next: retrieve, extract, validate, format. No delegation logic, no shared scratch space — just a chain.
Input → Retrieve Agent → Extract Agent → Validate Agent → Format Agent → Output
Pipelines are the easiest of the three patterns to evaluate, because each stage has a well-defined input and output contract, which means you can test and version each agent independently. The obvious limitation is rigidity: if a task doesn't decompose into a fixed sequence — if step three sometimes needs to loop back and redo step one — a pipeline will either fail outright or you'll end up bolting ad hoc branching logic onto it until it quietly turns into an orchestrator with extra steps.
Picking a pattern
If you can write the decomposition down as a checklist before you start, use a pipeline. If the decomposition is knowable but the specifics depend on the input, use orchestrator-worker. If you can't know the solution path until agents start finding things out, use a blackboard — and budget more time for evaluation.
Failure Modes You Won't See in a Demo
Every one of these showed up for me only after moving past a controlled demo into something running against real, messy inputs.
Infinite delegation loops
Two agents that can each decide "this isn't my job, pass it back" will occasionally pass a task back and forth indefinitely. An orchestrator delegates to a worker; the worker decides it needs clarification and delegates back to the orchestrator; the orchestrator, seeing an unclear request, delegates it right back out. Neither agent is wrong in isolation — the loop only exists at the system level, which is exactly why it's invisible when you're testing agents individually.
Runaway cost from re-invocation
Every agent-to-agent call is a model call, and model calls cost money and time. A blackboard system with three agents each re-checking the board after every write can spiral into dozens of model calls for a task that a human would resolve in three steps. This is easy to miss in development, where you're running one task at a time and eyeballing the transcript. It's very much not easy to miss on the invoice.
Conflicting concurrent writes
When two agents can act on shared state at the same time — two workers both trying to update the same record, two blackboard agents both trying to "resolve" the same open question — you get the same class of bug as an unguarded race condition in concurrent code, except the two writers are language models instead of threads, which makes it much harder to reproduce reliably.
Error propagation between agents
The most insidious one. If Agent A hallucinates a fact and passes its output to Agent B, Agent B has no way to distinguish that hallucination from a verified fact — it just sees text in its context window and reasons from it as if it were true. In a single-agent system, a hallucination is a wrong answer. In a multi-agent system, a hallucination is an input that gets compounded by every downstream agent that trusts it.
Guardrails That Actually Work
None of the failure modes above are solved by "better prompting." They're solved by hard limits enforced in code, outside the agents' control.
Hard caps on delegation depth
Track how many times a task has been re-delegated and refuse further delegation past a fixed limit — typically 3 to 5 hops in my experience. When the cap is hit, escalate rather than loop.
A token or cost budget per task
Set a hard ceiling on total tokens or dollars spent per task, tracked centrally, not per agent. When a task hits the ceiling, it stops — it does not get "one more try."
A defined human-escalation path
When confidence is low or a cap is hit, the system needs a real exit that isn't "let the agents keep trying" — surface the partial state to a human, don't let the system quietly retry into a low-quality answer it presents as confident.
The Honest Summary
Multi-agent architecture buys you task decomposition — the ability to break a large, fuzzy problem into smaller, more tractable pieces that are each easier to prompt, test, and reason about. It does not, on its own, buy you correctness. A system of five agents that each hallucinate 5% of the time doesn't average out to more reliable behavior; it compounds. The pattern you choose determines how the work is split. The evaluation harness and the guardrails you build around it determine whether the system is safe to actually put in front of users. Spend your engineering time accordingly.
Continue Reading
Explore more articles on software engineering and technology
Combo Maker: Building a Budget-Aware Meal Recommender
Give it a budget and a diet preference, and Combo Maker assembles the best meal combo it can afford from a sample menu — a live demo, how the allocator works, and an honest look at what a real AI-backed version would need.
Building Agentic Workflows for Restaurant Discovery
Learn how to create intelligent AI agents that help users discover nearby restaurants based on specific queries like lunch buffets, continental breakfast, and more using modern AI frameworks.
Model Context Protocol (MCP): How to Plug AI Agents into Your Product
What MCP is in plain terms, how hosts, clients and servers talk, how to design tools AI agents use well, and the security rules that matter, with an interactive walkthrough of real MCP messages and a hidden prompt-injection attack.

A blackboard system with three agents each re-checking the board after every write can spiral into dozens of model calls for a task that a human would resolve in three steps. This is easy to miss in development, where you're running one task at a time and eyeballing the transcript. It's very much not easy to miss on the invoice.
Conflicting concurrent writes
When two agents can act on shared state at the same time — two workers both trying to update the same record, two blackboard agents both trying to "resolve" the same open question — you get the same class of bug as an unguarded race condition in concurrent code, except the two writers are language models instead of threads, which makes it much harder to reproduce reliably.
Error propagation between agents
The most insidious one. If Agent A hallucinates a fact and passes its output to Agent B, Agent B has no way to distinguish that hallucination from a verified fact — it just sees text in its context window and reasons from it as if it were true. In a single-agent system, a hallucination is a wrong answer. In a multi-agent system, a hallucination is an input that gets compounded by every downstream agent that trusts it.
Guardrails That Actually Work
None of the failure modes above are solved by "better prompting." They're solved by hard limits enforced in code, outside the agents' control.
Hard caps on delegation depth
Track how many times a task has been re-delegated and refuse further delegation past a fixed limit — typically 3 to 5 hops in my experience. When the cap is hit, escalate rather than loop.
A token or cost budget per task
Set a hard ceiling on total tokens or dollars spent per task, tracked centrally, not per agent. When a task hits the ceiling, it stops — it does not get "one more try."
A defined human-escalation path
When confidence is low or a cap is hit, the system needs a real exit that isn't "let the agents keep trying" — surface the partial state to a human, don't let the system quietly retry into a low-quality answer it presents as confident.
The Honest Summary
Multi-agent architecture buys you task decomposition — the ability to break a large, fuzzy problem into smaller, more tractable pieces that are each easier to prompt, test, and reason about. It does not, on its own, buy you correctness. A system of five agents that each hallucinate 5% of the time doesn't average out to more reliable behavior; it compounds. The pattern you choose determines how the work is split. The evaluation harness and the guardrails you build around it determine whether the system is safe to actually put in front of users. Spend your engineering time accordingly.

Give it a budget and a diet preference, and Combo Maker assembles the best meal combo it can afford from a sample menu — a live demo, how the allocator works, and an honest look at what a real AI-backed version would need.
Building Agentic Workflows for Restaurant Discovery
Learn how to create intelligent AI agents that help users discover nearby restaurants based on specific queries like lunch buffets, continental breakfast, and more using modern AI frameworks.

articles.title: FAA Begins Retiring Decades Old Floppy Disks from Air Traffic Control
articles.body:
Trump’s Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy Begins Retiring Decades Old Floppy Disks from Air Traffic Control as Part of Ongoing Modernization Effort Deployment of Brand New Air Traffic Control Continues at Record Pace
WASHINGTON, D.C. - U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy today announced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is continuing its historic modernization of America’s air traffic control system by replacing outdated floppy disks that contain vital weather and other critical information with a streamlined, 21st-century system.
The Enterprise – Information Display System (E-IDS) replaces four systems dating back to the 1980s that are in more than 400 FAA facilities. E-IDS provides a single, secure system that gives air traffic controllers faster access to information they need. It also will reduce costly repairs and workarounds while enhancing safety for the American flying public.
The first five facilities to receive these upgrades include:
- Atlantic City International Airport
- Nashville International Airport
- Greater Rochester International Airport
- Data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City
The FAA plans to install E-IDS in 435 sites by the end of 2028.
“Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” said U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy. “The greatest nation in the world deserves a state-of-the-art air traffic control system, and under President Trump, we’re delivering just that. The installation of E-IDS is just the latest signal that America’s brand new air traffic control system is coming at lightning speed.”
Click HERE or above to watch a video on the new technology.
“E-IDS gives air traffic controllers the information they need to make timely decisions and keep the flying public safe,” said FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford. “We’re moving away from outdated, manual processes and replacing technology that once relied on floppy disks with a modern system that allows controllers to instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports across the National Airspace System.”
You can track the progress of the Brand New Air Traffic Control System (BNATCS) by state and airport on our Modern Skies website.
Additional information:
E-IDS is a digital display board that puts important operational information in one place so controllers can quickly see updates, status information, and alerts they need to keep air traffic moving safely and efficiently. This information includes notices about equipment issues and disruptions, air traffic conditions, weather impacts, and important advisories.
E-IDS will also improve how Pilot Reports (PIREPS) and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) are collected and distributed. PIREPs are first-hand reports on weather conditions from pilots to air traffic controllers. Both provide vital information on real-time pilot conditions and improve situational awareness for controllers.
Reminder:
Under Secretary Duffy’s leadership, the FAA is rapidly moving to make upgrades to our air traffic control system nationwide. We have already:
- Replaced 69% of copper wires
- Installed Surface Awareness Initiative (SAI) systems at 143 towers
- Transitioned 26 towers to electronic flight strips
- Installed 226 IP Voice Switches

articles.title: OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
articles.body:
Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion, OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials.
OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
The ChatGPT maker won’t use NDAs with public officials as part of its new data center community commitments.
Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects.
OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

articles.title: The Big Idea: Daryl Gregory
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Daryl Gregory
Posted on November 5, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 4 Comments
Being the middle child isn’t easy, but the bonds you form with your siblings can be some of the closest and most impactful relationships in your life. Author Daryl Gregory shares memories of his sisters from his childhood, and talks about how their bond played a roll in creating his newest novel, The Porcelain Sisters.
DARYL GREGORY:
Is there something wrong with me that I find two sisters fighting with each other to be hugely entertaining? I was the middle child, the boy sandwiched between two girls—one who was seven years older than me, and the other sixteen months younger. We grew up in a small ranch house in the suburbs of Chicago, and we fought what I assumed was a normal amount.
Ninety percent of the time, it was me versus one of them. With my older sister, this was often when she ordered me to do something, and my go-to response was to slam a door and shout, “You’re not the boss of me!” (She was absolutely the boss of me.)
My younger sister and I were closer in age and so spent more time together, which meant more opportunities to torture each other. I liked to hide in her room and jump-scare her. She’s the finest screamer in the family, and terrifying her is extremely satisfying. She knew how to hit back, though. One time she kidnapped my prized possession, a G.I. Joe with lifelike hair and Kung Fu grip, and he reappeared days later with a bald spot, as if his forced marriage to Barbie had driven him into middle age. I still have him—and the damage is outrageous.
So it was a delight—a delight, I tell you—when my sisters fought with each other, and I got sit on the sidelines munching my proverbial popcorn.
But here’s the thing I found amazing—their fights were so short. They’d pivot from shouting at each other to calmly hanging out in their shared bedroom. They didn’t hold grudges. (I, however, was a champion pouter.) Even now, if they have an argument, they repair the damage quickly. I love my sisters, and they’ve assured me that they love me back, but they have a bond with each other that I find mysterious and enviable.
So perhaps it’s not a surprise that sisters turn up a lot in my books. Ruth and Isabel, the two main characters in my new novella, The Porcelain Sisters, are not exactly like my siblings—for one thing, neither of mine is a haunted doll—but let’s just say there are… similarities.
Ruth (the flesh-and-blood sister) and Isabel (the porcelain one) first appeared as teenagers in my YA Lovecraftian horror novel, Harrison Squared. They were my favorite characters to write dialog for, because they operated almost like a vaudeville ventriloquist act—Ruth was shy and soft-spoken, while Isabel spoke the truth and cut everyone down to size.
But in that book I never explained why Isabel could talk, or how they were sisters, or where Isabel came from. That was for a good reason: I didn’t know. I wrote this book to find out—and to get the chance to hang out with them some more.
Ruth, now in her twenties, is trying to make rent while taking college classes, but feeling adrift. She seems to have some latent magical ability, but doesn’t know what her purpose in life is beyond taking care of her sister. She’s never even had a long-term romantic relationship because Isabel deliberately freaks out anybody she brings home.
Isabel’s anger issues stem, of course, from being trapped in a porcelain body. She can’t grow up and may never live on her own. When her body’s accidentally damaged during a fight with Ruth—a seaside cliff is involved—a mundane toy repair shop won’t cut it. They have to go on the road to find the Dollmaker, the French witch who made her.
As I wrote that last sentence I realized the sisters are literally repairing each other. I wish I’d thought of that in time to put it on the back cover copy.
The girls head to Marseille, where they face off with an unkillable assassin with the resilience of a ragdoll, a pair of demons (one a chain-smoking crow, the other a black cat) and their human familiars, as well as a small army of haunted dolls. Oh, and the Dollmaker turns out to be the head of Le Clan des Sorciéres, a kind of witch mafia. I know, it’s a lot.
At the root of the mystery is why their mother, an enforcer for Le Clan called Godless Annie, abandoned them. What the sisters discover about themselves suggests there may be a way for them to live apart—but do they want to?
Another thing occurred to me as I’m typing this: is that ending about my current relationship with my sisters? Since our mom passed we don’t see each other like we used to. We live on opposite sides of the country, and our lives are busy. Did I write this book because I miss them?
I suppose I could talk to a therapist about this. Or write another book about sisters. Or—and hear me out—I could go on the road with the Gregory girls, solving mysteries and fighting the occasional demon.
The Porcelain Sisters: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Powell’s

articles.title: KPop Demon Hunters on 4K Blu-ray costs less than a month of Netflix Premium
articles.body:
Buying the 4K Blu-ray disc version of KPop Demon Hunters was already going to be a wise idea for some people, especially those who primarily keep their $26.99 Netflix Premium subscription just to watch the hit animated flick in 4K. But at just $24.99 from Barnes and Noble instead of its original $49.95 price, it’s easier than ever to recommend.
KPop Demon Hunters on 4K Blu-ray costs less than a month of Netflix Premium
The 4K Criterion Collection set is available to pick up at Barnes and Noble for $25.
One important thing to note: it’s unavailable to ship from Barnes and Noble, but you can find a discounted copy at most retail stores, and the site makes it easy to reserve a copy online to pick up later. Amazon was matching the price earlier today, but is currently offering a slightly less tempting deal.
The Criterion Collection version of the film recently launched, and comes with a bunch of extras in a gorgeous set. In addition to the 4K digital master, complete with Dolby Vision HDR and Dolby Atmos sound, you also get two standard 1080p Blu-rays, one containing the film, and the other packed with special features (a full feature-length animatic, a making-of documentary, lyric videos, and more). It includes physical goodies, too, like collectible postcards, as well as an essay by Polygon alum Karen Han.
Kpop Demon Hunters was on my list of physical movies to buy, and this deal just turned it into a must-buy ahead of the holiday season.

articles.title: Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
articles.body:
Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot “where did my money go this month,” for example, and it’ll create an overview with a breakdown of spending by category, including rent and utilities, shopping, and food. Claude can also answer broader questions around what bills are left before your next payday, if you can afford big purchases like holiday trips, and how much money you could be saving each month.
Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
With access to your bank account via Plaid, Anthropic’s chatbot will try to explain where your money is going and what you can afford.
Its access is read-only, and with Plaid facilitating the connection, Claude doesn’t see your banking passwords and your bank doesn’t have to deal with unvetted AI bots crawling around your accounts.
Claude can’t move, manage, or invest your money, according to Anthropic, and it “isn’t designed to give investment advice.”, but it can see the bank’s name, account names, account type, the last four digits of the number associated with it, your balances and credit limits, and up to two years’ worth of your transaction history.
If you choose to give it access to all that, Claude can explain financial terms you don’t understand and answer questions about your balances and transactions.
Personal Finance in Claude is rolling out in beta this week to Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plan subscribers in the US. Anthropic’s announcement follows OpenAI introducing a similar feature for ChatGPT in May, which also plugs into your bank accounts through Plaid. Allowing AI to have oversight into your finances might ring some alarm bells, but according to the sign-off in Anthropic’s press release, it’s just the beginning:
“Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.”

articles.title: Fox bought Roku
articles.body:
Fox has officially closed its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, the companies announced on Friday. With Roku under its umbrella, Fox now controls a major streaming platform that reaches more than 100 million households in the US.
Fox bought Roku
Fox now has control of Roku’s streaming platform, which reaches more than 100 million US households.
First announced in June, the deal will allow Fox to bring Fox Sports, news content, and local stations to Roku. “I would expect that we can grow our viewership in the US with a combination of Roku technology, Roku’s platform, the tremendous content that’s on The Roku Channel, and the content that Fox brings to it as well,” Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch said at the time. Along with Roku, Fox also operates its own Fox One streaming service and the free streamer Tubi.
Though the deal might change what Roku showcases on its platform, it doesn’t look like it will affect the open nature of its streaming ecosystem. “We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources,” Roku founder Anthony Wood said. “Fox has a deep respect for Roku’s culture and wholly shares our commitment to staying open to every content partner.” Wood now serves on Fox’s board of directors.

articles.title: Stranger Things is getting a live-action spinoff called Other Worlds
articles.body:
Netflix isn’t done with Hawkins, Indiana just yet. The streamer just announced a live-action spinoff of Stranger Things which is expected to debut in 2028. It’s called Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure.
Stranger Things is getting a live-action spinoff called Other Worlds
The prequel series is set in the 1950s, and is expected to start streaming in 2028.
There aren’t a lot of details, but the show will be going back in time quite a bit. According to Netflix, Other Worlds is “a prequel set in the 1950s, before Stranger Things and before the stage play Stranger Things: The First Shadow.“ Franchise creators the Duffer brothers are back on board, and Stranger Things veteran Kate Trefry will serve as showrunner. British director Joe Wright is set to helm the first three episodes.
In a statement, the Duffers described the series as “Stranger Things, but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new… actually, we’re not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting.“
It’s been clear that Netflix has been looking for ways to keep its most impactful series alive ever since Stranger Things wrapped up with its final season last year. So far that has included the animated spinoff Tales From ‘85, but a live-action series appears to show a much bigger effort behind expanding the franchise.

articles.title: Tesla is ‘winding down’ production of the Cybertruck next year
articles.body:
Tesla is getting the Cybertruck ready for retirement in an effort to ramp up its robotaxi output. In an X post on Friday, Tesla CEO Elon Musk said that the company will be “winding down” Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory sometime around the middle of next year, “to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
Tesla is ‘winding down’ production of the Cybertruck next year
Cybertruck production at the Texas Gigafactory is being axed to make way for more Cybercabs.
The production plant in Austin, Texas, is the only Tesla facility that’s known to assemble the Cybertruck, and that’s equipped to make the specialized components required to build the vehicles. Musk hasn’t mentioned if Cybertruck production will be moved elsewhere, but doing so would be arduous, especially for a car that’s never sold well. While Tesla doesn’t break out individual Cybertruck sales figures, even the highest analyst estimates place the total number of deliveries at roughly 70,000 since its launch in 2023 — significantly below the 250,000 that Musk once predicted would be sold annually.
The Cybertruck has also been mired in controversy since it was introduced, from its divisive design (that isn’t road legal in many parts of the world), the numerous recalls for faulty or outright dangerous components, and the fatal accidents it’s been involved in. It’s an unusually long and complicated history for a vehicle that’s only been on the road for three years. If the Cybertruck does meet its demise in 2027, Tesla still has another ridiculous vehicle on the horizon to serve as its spiritual successor.

articles.title: OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts
articles.body:
OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts (bleepingcomputer.com) 45
			
		 	
				A newly disclosed OpenSSH flaw dubbed "*sshole" can allow attackers to log in to password-disabled accounts on certain musl-based Linux systems simply by submitting a password longer than 256 bytes. "Apparently certain varieties of musl Linux (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, etc.) have had this OpenSSH vulnerability for about a decade," writes longtime Slashdot reader AlteredEgg. "Upgrade now!" BleepingComputer reports:  Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes.
To prevent attackers from identifying valid usernames through different response times, OpenSSH was modified to perform password hashing even when an account had no usable password hash, including accounts configured with * to block password logins. The problem is that the musl C library's crypt() function also returns * when password hashing fails, including when a submitted password exceeds its 256-byte limit. This means an attacker can submit an oversized password and cause OpenSSH to compare the returned * against the account's stored *, resulting in a successful login.
To be clear, the flaw does not allow attackers to bypass passwords on accounts with valid password hashes. [...] Admins who can't immediately install the update can mitigate the issue by turning off SSH password authentication with PasswordAuthentication no in their SSH server configuration and restarting SSH. Kultekin says admins can also check for signs of exploitation by examining SSH authentication logs for password-based logins for accounts that should not allow them.

articles.title: Salon.com shutters suddenly after 31 years
articles.body:
Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.
When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.
Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.
The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.
We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.
The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.
Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.
Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.
Salon

articles.title: Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
articles.body:
Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space.
Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
Blue Origin had been aiming for a launch at the end of this year after a launchpad explosion in May, but now it’s reportedly targeting January.
In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process.
“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

articles.title: RIP Cybertruck. You Were Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd
articles.body:
Elon Musk, in a post on X, has officially called time on the Cybertruck, stating that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”
Produced for less than four years, the polarizing pickup is seemingly dying as it lived, with the news being greeted in a flurry of replies in praise of the EV as well as deriding it. James Star, claiming to be a Tesla employee, posted that it was “the saddest news! Cybertruck (was) the best car Tesla sold,” right next to a user called Captain Ford who simply replied to Musk with “Fuck that shitbox.”
Tesla has not responded to WIRED’s request for comment and clarification that the Cybertruck will no longer be made at all. The Cybertruck is exclusively made at Gigafactory Texas, as this is apparently the only Tesla facility equipped with the machinery required to manufacture the truck’s unique stainless steel body, which supposedly started to rust in some cases.
Despite whipping up a fevered number of reservations—allegedly more than a million according to Musk, who at the end of 2023 crowed that demand was “off the charts!”—the truck failed to sell, shifting less than 50,000 units in total by March last year.
EVWire cites Kelley Blue Book data suggesting that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first three quarters of this year in the US, down 28 percent year-over-year, adding that Musk’s announcement post came about 80 minutes after Tesla raised US Cybertruck prices and paused new orders for the entry-level Dual-Motor AWD version.
The Cybertruck proved not only to be wildly unpopular, it was also beset by troubles before it even reached customers. In 2023, WIRED covered a leaked Tesla report dated January 25, 2022, that showed the Cybertruck had basic design flaws, and that the preproduction “alpha” version was struggling with problems with its suspension, body sealing, noise levels, handling, and braking.
In November 2019, when Musk stepped onto a stage in California to launch his new cyberpunk-styled electric pickup, he decided to demonstrate the strength of the “unbreakable” glass windows by hurling a steel ball at them. In what has now entered into public relations folklore, the demo truck’s windows smashed not once, but twice. Musk swore, then joked: “There’s room for improvement.”
There most certainly was. In April 2024, a recall was issued for the Cybertruck because its accelerator pedal pad could come loose and get trapped by interior trim, which had the frightening potential of pushing the car to full speed.
In March last year, Tesla had to recall nearly all the Cybertrucks it had then produced because a stainless steel trim panel could become detached from the vehicle while driving, blaming the problem on the wrong type of glue, a new adhesive “not prone to environmental embrittlement.”
Back in May this year, Cybertrucks were struck down by the wrong type of grease, which meant that their wheels could potentially fall off. In what was then the EV’s 11th recall, it was declared that the Rear Wheel Drive (RWD) Cybertruck Long Range model might have faulty brake rotors. In a notice posted by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla stated that “brake rotor stud holes may crack and allow the stud to separate from the wheel hub.” Such a situation might have seen some RWD Cybertruck owners merrily driving along only to then be disconcertingly overtaken by their own wheels.
Musk even tried to get President Donald Trump to buy one of his Cybertrucks, creating an impromptu Tesla showroom on the White House South Lawn, no less. But, sadly, even President Trump must have smelt something was off about the truck as instead he shunned the pickup and opted for a 200-mph Model S Plaid in ultra red, clearly impressed with the interior, remarking that “Everything’s computer!”
At the end of 2024, Karl Brauer, executive analyst at car ranking service iSeeCars, told WIRED that he’d calculated that the Cybertruck’s six recalls to date at the time made the EV “worse than 91 percent” of all other 2024 vehicles.
Yet, despite supposedly being so unreliable, the Cybertruck did find a small but loyal audience. WIRED profiled a number of owners last year, all fervently in love with their vehicles, but who were periodically forced to endure insults and taunts that they were Nazis, perhaps referring to an on-stage gesture Musk made at the start of 2025.
However, despite evidence seemingly to the contrary, Musk claims he is killing the Cybertruck, not because of its unreliability and staggering unpopularity, but because he wishes to focus instead on Cybercab, an autonomous EV that is central to Tesla’s robotaxi ambitions but itself has had a rocky start.
Currently operating in Austin only, with a fleet supposedly numbered only in the hundreds, Musk apparently wants to ramp up production dramatically since he confirmed on an earnings call the first cab came off the line in February.
Musk sees Cybercab as very much the vision of Tesla’s future. The CEO has even said that Tesla should no longer be regarded as an automaker but as a robotics and autonomous vehicle company. “Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab,” Cybertruck lead engineer Wes Morrill said on X.

articles.title: Goodbye from Salon
articles.body:
Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.
When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.
Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.
The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.
We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.
The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.
Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.
Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.
Salon
